Hypercontractivity and entropy decay for infinite-dimensional quantum Gibbs samplers
Simon Becker
Address: Bocconi University, Milan, Italy
Email address: simon.becker@unibocconi.it
,
Cambyse Rouzé
Address: Inria, Télécom Paris–LTCI, Institut Polytechnique de Paris, 91120 Palaiseau, France
Email address: cambyse.rouze@inria.fr
and
Robert Salzmann
Address: Department of Physics, RWTH Aachen, Otto-Blumenthal-Strasse 20, 52074 Aachen, Germany
Email address: robert.salzmann@rwth-aachen.de
Abstract.
We derive rates of exponential relative-entropy decay for a broad class of infinite-dimensional quantum Gibbs samplers. A key technical ingredient is a perturbative stability theory for hypercontractive estimates and logarithmic Sobolev inequalities. For suitably chosen dissipative couplings, we obtain exponential entropy decay for full multimode Bose–Hubbard samplers with arbitrary hopping and repulsive density interactions. For harmonically confined quantum Coulomb gases and molecular systems, we prove exponential entropy decay for every fixed finite-rank low-energy truncation of the interaction. Finally, we exhibit a periodic charging model with a positive spectral gap but no finite-time  $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{p}$  bound for any  $p>2$ .
Key words and phrases: Quantum Markov semigroup, hypercontractivity, modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality, relative entropy, Gibbs sampler
1. Introduction and main results
Thermal-state preparation is a basic task in quantum statistical mechanics
and quantum computation. A Gibbs sampler drives an initial state towards thermal equilibrium
through a dissipative evolution. A spectral gap gives exponential decay of
deviations from equilibrium in a weighted  $L^{2}$  norm. In infinite
dimension, this estimate requires initial data in the weighted  $L^{2}$
space. Relative entropy measures distinguishability from equilibrium
and, for a Gibbs state, equals the excess free energy divided by the
temperature whenever these quantities are finite. Exponential
relative-entropy estimates can also apply to initial states outside the
weighted  $L^{2}$  space and control convergence in trace distance.
Boundedness of the semigroup from  $L^{2}$  to  $L^{p}$ ,  $p>2$ , connects  $L^{2}$  relaxation with relative-entropy decay. A finite  $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{p}$  bound is referred to as hyperboundedness, while a bound with operator norm at most one is the contractive form of hypercontractivity.
Both express an improvement in integrability after a finite time.
This smoothing property is not implied by a spectral gap alone. In classical probability, the
connection between hypercontractivity, logarithmic Sobolev inequalities,
and convergence to equilibrium has been studied extensively since
Gross’s foundational work; see [1].
These inequalities give estimates for diffusion and Markov-chain mixing.
For reversible quantum dynamics, we show that one bounded
$L^{2}$ -to- $L^{q}$  map gives an explicit exponential
relative-entropy bound. In the atomic setting considered here, this
endpoint already implies compact resolvent and, under primitivity, a
positive spectral gap. Its value enters the rate when the endpoint norm
exceeds one.
Efficient finite-dimensional quantum Gibbs samplers satisfying exact KMS detailed balance were developed in [2, 3], and the infinite-dimensional construction of [4] extends this framework to systems governed by unbounded Hamiltonians and jump operators.
We study when these samplers improve integrability and how this
gives entropy decay. We prove sufficient conditions and examples of
failure, showing what must be added to a spectral-gap estimate. The behavior depends on the choice of jumps, even when the
Hamiltonian is fixed.
1.1. Main results
We first state two criteria that turn a bounded  $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{q}$  map
into exponential relative-entropy decay. A state is a positive trace-class operator of trace
one; it is faithful if its kernel is zero. Let  $\Phi_{t}$ ,  $t\geq 0$ , be a
strongly continuous semigroup of completely positive, trace-preserving
linear maps on trace-class operators, and let  $\sigma$  be a faithful
invariant state. Write  $T_{t}$  for the dual evolution of observables.
For  $1\leq p<\infty$ , the equilibrium-weighted space  $L^{p}(\sigma)$  is
the completion of bounded observables in the norm
$\|X\|_{p,\sigma}=\|\sigma^{1/(2p)}X\sigma^{1/(2p)}\|_{p},$
where  $\|\cdot\|_{p}$  is the Schatten  $p$ -norm.
The space  $L^{\infty}(\sigma)$  consists of bounded observables with the
operator norm. We assume that  $T_{t}$  extends consistently to positive
contractions on these spaces, is self-adjoint on  $L^{2}(\sigma)$ , and
has only scalar observables in its  $L^{2}$  fixed space. These are the
reversibility and primitivity assumptions used below; reversibility
is in the Kubo–Martin–Schwinger (KMS) sense.
With  $\operatorname{Tr}$  denoting the operator trace, the spectral gap  $\lambda$  is
the optimal exponential contraction rate on observables
$X\in L^{2}(\sigma)$  of equilibrium mean zero:
$\|T_{t}X\|_{2,\sigma}\leq e^{-\lambda t}\|X\|_{2,\sigma},\qquad\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma X)=0.$
For  $X\in L^{2}(\sigma)$ , the mean  $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma X)$  denotes its
continuous extension from bounded observables.
The gap may vanish in infinite dimension. For a state  $\rho$ , its
relative entropy is
$D(\rho\|\sigma)=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(\rho(\log\rho-\log\sigma)\bigr)\in[0,\infty],$
interpreted in the extended sense when the separate traces are not
finite. The spaces and operator domains are specified in Section 2.
Theorem 1.1 uses the Stroock–Varopoulos comparison: entropy
production is at least four times the Dirichlet energy of the square
root of the state. The domain requirement is included in
(2.6) below.
Theorem 1.1.
In the reversible setting above, assume the Stroock–Varopoulos
comparison (2.6). Suppose that, for some  $s>0$
and  $C\geq 1$ ,
(1.1)
$\|T_{s}:L^{2}(\sigma)\to L^{4}(\sigma)\|\leq C.$
If  $C>1$ , let  $\lambda>0$  denote the spectral gap, which is
positive by the endpoint bound and primitivity. Then every state  $\rho$
satisfies, for  $t\geq 0$ ,
$D(\Phi_{t}(\rho)\|\sigma)\leq e^{-\alpha_{\rm HC}t}D(\rho\|\sigma),\qquad\alpha_{\rm HC}=\left(s+\frac{\log C+\frac{1}{2}}{\lambda}\right)^{-1}.$
If  $C=1$ , the same conclusion holds with  $\alpha_{\rm HC}=s^{-1}$
without a gap assumption.
The comparison can fail for the samplers considered here. The following
result extends the finite-dimensional endpoint criterion of
[5, Theorem 3.3] to the present setting, with the
same entropy-decay rate after normalization.
Theorem 1.2.
In the same reversible setting, let  $q_{0}>2$  and suppose that, for some
$s>0$  and  $C\geq 1$ ,
$\|T_{s}:L^{2}(\sigma)\to L^{q_{0}}(\sigma)\|\leq C.$
If  $C>1$ , let  $\lambda>0$  denote the spectral gap, which is
positive by the endpoint bound and primitivity. Then every state  $\rho$
satisfies, for  $t\geq 0$ ,
(1.2)
$D(\Phi_{t}(\rho)\|\sigma)\leq e^{-\alpha_{\rm KMS}t}D(\rho\|\sigma),\qquad\alpha_{\rm KMS}=\frac{1-2/q_{0}}{s+\lambda^{-1}(\log C+1-2/q_{0})}.$
If  $C=1$ , one may take  $\alpha_{\rm KMS}=(1-2/q_{0})/s$  without a gap.
In Section 3, we prove two stability results.
First, adding a bounded operator to the generator preserves the
$L^{p}$  bounds along a hypercontractive curve, provided its norm is
uniformly bounded on those spaces. We give the resulting norm estimate.
Second, a change of the Gibbs weight on a finite-dimensional energy
subspace, apart from normalization, preserves a tight  $2$ -logarithmic
Sobolev inequality when the Dirichlet forms are comparable and the new
generator has a positive gap.
The main applications are Bose–Hubbard and trapped Coulomb samplers.
In both cases we prove the smoothing estimate and the positive gap
needed by Theorem 1.2.
Bose–Hubbard models.
On a fixed lattice of  $k$  modes, Theorem 4.3 treats
$H=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\left[\frac{U_{j}}{2}N_{j}(N_{j}-I)-\mu_{j}N_{j}\right]+\sum_{i<j}V_{ij}N_{i}N_{j}-\sum_{i<j}\left(J_{ij}a_{i}^{\dagger}a_{j}+\overline{J_{ij}}a_{j}^{\dagger}a_{i}\right),$
where  $a_{j},a_{j}^{\dagger}$  are the mode operators,
$N_{j}=a_{j}^{\dagger}a_{j}$ ,  $U_{j}>0$ ,  $V_{ij}\geq 0$ ,
$\mu_{j}\in\mathbb{R}$ , and  $J_{ij}\in\mathbb{C}$ .
With the bare jumps  $a_{j},a_{j}^{\dagger},a_{j}^{3},(a_{j}^{\dagger})^{3}$  in
each mode and the filter (2.3), the sampler has a unique
invariant Gibbs state, a positive spectral gap, and a bounded map
$L^{2}(\sigma_{\beta})\to L^{p}(\sigma_{\beta})$  for every  $t>0$  and
finite  $p>2$ . It therefore satisfies
$D(\Phi_{t}(\rho)\|\sigma_{\beta})\leq e^{-\alpha t}D(\rho\|\sigma_{\beta}),\qquad\alpha>0.$
The theorem allows arbitrary hopping amplitudes and uses the full
bosonic space, without an occupation cutoff. The cubic jumps provide
losses of order  $n^{3}$  on the sector with  $n$  particles; these dominate
the quadratic energy and the errors caused by hopping. The same theorem gives a bounded endpoint after a positive waiting
time with the smaller jump family  $a_{j},a_{j}^{\dagger},a_{j}^{2},(a_{j}^{\dagger})^{2}$ .
The rate may depend on the lattice size and all model parameters.
Trapped Coulomb systems.
For  $n$  particles in  $d=2$  or  $3$  dimensions, Corollary 4.5
considers the Hamiltonian
$H_{n,M}=-\Delta+|x|^{2}+\Pi_{M}\left(\sum_{i<j}\alpha_{n,i,j}w_{d}(x_{i}-x_{j})\right)\Pi_{M},\qquad w_{2}(y)=-\log|y|,\quad w_{3}(y)=|y|^{-1},$
where  $\Pi_{M}=P_{M}^{\otimes n}$  and  $P_{M}$  projects onto the first  $M$
one-particle Hermite functions, and the couplings  $\alpha_{n,i,j}$
are real. Only the interaction is truncated;
the Hamiltonian acts on  $L^{2}((\mathbb{R}^{d})^{n})$ . With coordinate creation
and annihilation jumps and the Gaussian filter
$\widehat{f}_{\eta}(\nu)=e^{-\eta\nu^{2}-\beta\nu/4}$ ,  $\eta>0$ , the sampler
has a unique invariant Gibbs state and a positive gap. For each fixed
$n,M$ , we prove a contractive  $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{4}$  bound after a finite
time and exponential relative-entropy decay. The proof controls the
terms containing one ladder operator and one finite-energy coefficient
by a weighted oscillator estimate. The constants can depend on  $n$
and  $M$ .
The other examples explain when such smoothing estimates can fail.
For one-mode polynomial number Hamiltonians,
Theorem 4.2 compares the degree of the Hamiltonian
with the largest jump order. Bounded  $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{p}$  maps then occur
at every positive time, after a positive waiting time, or never;
the stated classification excludes the boundary time in the critical
case. A periodic charging model has a positive gap but no such bound
at any finite time.
1.2. Relation to earlier work
Our results build on finite-dimensional entropy criteria and on the
infinite-dimensional Gibbs samplers constructed in earlier work.
The finite-dimensional version of Theorem 1.2
is due to Gao and Wang
[5, Theorem 3.3]. Their entropy-decay rate agrees
with ours after converting their normalization
$D(\Phi_{t}(\rho)\|\sigma)\leq e^{-2\alpha_{1}t}D(\rho\|\sigma)$ .
They combine weighted interpolation, contraction of centred
observables, and a norm-to-entropy estimate. We extend their criterion to infinite dimension. We approximate
arbitrary states while preserving the limit of the relative entropy,
and prove the required  $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{q}$  bounds for our unbounded models.
Related finite-dimensional results for primitive KMS-symmetric
semigroups appear in [6, 7].
Noncommutative hypercontractivity and its connection with logarithmic
Sobolev inequalities go back to the weighted  $L^{p}$  theory of
[8]; see also
[9, 10]. Complete modified
logarithmic Sobolev inequalities and their tensor-stable
finite-dimensional forms were developed in [11],
while perturbative change-of-measure principles appear in
[12]. The equivalence between modified
logarithmic Sobolev inequalities and exponential relative-entropy
decay in the von Neumann algebra setting is treated in
[13]. Here one  $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{q}$  bound in infinite dimension gives an
explicit entropy-decay rate, involving the automatically positive
spectral gap when the bound has norm greater than one. One argument uses the
Stroock–Varopoulos comparison; the other uses only the KMS
reversibility assumptions above. The counterexample in
Proposition 2.10 shows why the KMS argument is needed for general cross-frequency generators.
Our earlier work [4] provides the
infinite-dimensional Gibbs-sampler construction used here. In [14], we established
spectral-gap results for mean-field and full multimode
Bose–Hubbard samplers and used them to obtain thermal-state
preparation guarantees. Here we prove the additional smoothing estimates needed for
exponential decay from every initial state of finite relative entropy. This requires control of the jump operators
as well as the Hamiltonian. For example, for  $H=N^{2}$  and the filter
used in Section 4.1, Theorem 4.2
shows that linear jumps alone have no bounded  $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{4}$
endpoint, whereas adding cubic jumps gives such a bound at every
positive time and yields the entropy estimate in
Theorem 4.3. Quadratic jumps already give an endpoint
after a positive waiting time, including with hopping; cubic jumps
give the every-positive-time conclusion.
The theorem does not give the same entropy estimate for the
linear-jump samplers of [14].
The Coulomb result complements the fixed-cutoff spectral-gap
analysis of [15]. We prove a weighted
oscillator estimate for the perturbed semigroup, controlling the mixed
terms that contain one unbounded ladder operator. This gives an  $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{4}$  bound directly. The form comparison
in Section 3 also preserves a tight  $2$ -logarithmic Sobolev inequality,
but obtaining hypercontractivity from that inequality would require
an additional regularity assumption.
Section 2 sets up the spaces and proves the entropy-decay criteria. Section 3 proves the stability results, and Section 4 treats the bosonic examples
and obstructions.
1.3. AI statement
We used OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra to help identify assumptions under which generators associated with bosonic Hamiltonians, particularly the Bose–Hubbard Hamiltonian, are hypercontractive. We also used these tools to assist with manuscript preparation. We reviewed and verified the AI-assisted material and take full responsibility for the content of this work.
2. Framework and entropy decay
We define the weighted spaces and prove the two entropy-decay
criteria from the introduction. The first proof uses a logarithmic Sobolev
inequality and the Stroock–Varopoulos comparison; the second obtains
entropy contraction directly from KMS symmetry and hypercontractivity.
We then show why the comparison can fail when different frequencies are
coupled, and give approximation conditions that extend it to infinite-dimensional
Davies generators.
2.1. Spaces and Gibbs samplers
We define the operator spaces, Gibbs samplers, and reversibility
assumptions used throughout the paper.
We use  $\mathbb{N}=\{1,2,\ldots\}$  and  $\mathbb{N}_{0}=\{0,1,\ldots\}$ .
For a separable Hilbert space  $\mathcal{H}$ , let  $B(\mathcal{H})$  be the algebra of
bounded operators and let  $I$  be its identity. The adjoint of an operator
$X$  is written  $X^{\dagger}$ .
For  $1\leq p<\infty$ , the Schatten class and its norm are
$\mathscr{T}_{p}(\mathcal{H})=\{X\text{ compact}:\operatorname{Tr}|X|^{p}<\infty\},\qquad|X|=(X^{\dagger}X)^{1/2},\qquad\|X\|_{p}=(\operatorname{Tr}|X|^{p})^{1/p}.$
Thus  $\mathscr{T}_{1}$  and  $\mathscr{T}_{2}$  are the trace-class and
Hilbert–Schmidt spaces, respectively;  $\|X\|_{\infty}$  is the operator
norm on  $B(\mathcal{H})$ ; see [16] for trace ideals
and their norm inequalities.
For operators  $X,Y$ , we write  $[X,Y]=XY-YX$  and
$\{X,Y\}=XY+YX$  whenever these products are defined.
Let  $H$  be a self-adjoint Hamiltonian bounded from below, let  $\beta>0$
be the inverse temperature, and assume that the partition function
$Z_{\beta}(H)=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H})$  is finite. The Gibbs state is
$\sigma_{\beta}(H)=Z_{\beta}(H)^{-1}e^{-\beta H}$ .
We omit the Hamiltonian argument when it is fixed.
For the sampler construction, assume in addition that
$\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-bH})<\infty$  for every  $b>0$ , as in
[4, Section 2], and let  $\{A^{\alpha}\}_{\alpha\in\mathcal{A}}$  be a
finite adjoint-closed family of bare jump operators: the index set has
an involution  $\alpha\mapsto\bar{\alpha}$  with
$A^{\bar{\alpha}}=(A^{\alpha})^{\dagger}$ . These operators specify the allowed
transitions. The jumps are closed on their respective domains and
contain a common spectral core. We impose the energy-bound and filter
hypotheses of [4, Condition A]; they
are verified for the applications in Section 4.
For a filter  $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}$ , our Fourier convention is
$\widehat{f}(\nu)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{it\nu}f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t,\qquad\nu\in\mathbb{R},$
with a distributional interpretation when the integral is not absolutely
convergent. The filtered jump operators  $L^{\alpha}$  are given formally by
(2.1)
$L^{\alpha}=\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{itH}A^{\alpha}e^{-itH}f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t,\qquad\overline{\widehat{f}(\nu)}=e^{-\beta\nu/2}\widehat{f}(-\nu).$
Let  $B=B^{\dagger}$  be the detailed-balance correction Hamiltonian
chosen in the infinite-dimensional construction of
[4].
The associated Gorini–Kossakowski–Lindblad–Sudarshan (GKLS)
generator is
(2.2)
$\mathcal{L}(\rho)=-i[B,\rho]+\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal{A}}\left(L^{\alpha}\rho(L^{\alpha})^{\dagger}-\frac{1}{2}\{(L^{\alpha})^{\dagger}L^{\alpha},\rho\}\right),$
Under the stated hypotheses, this choice of  $B$  makes
$\sigma_{\beta}$  stationary.
The examples below use the multiplier  $\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}$ , where
$\mathscr{M}$  labels the following filter:
(2.3)
$\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(\nu)=\exp\left[-\frac{\sqrt{1+(\beta\nu)^{2}}+\beta\nu}{4}\right]$
For  $k\in\mathbb{N}$  bosonic modes, we work in the occupation basis
$\{|n\rangle:n=(n_{1},\ldots,n_{k})\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{k}\}$  of
$\ell^{2}(\mathbb{N}_{0}^{k})$ . With  $e_{i}$  the  $i$ th coordinate vector,
the annihilation, creation, and number operators are
$a_{i}|n\rangle=\sqrt{n_{i}}\,|n-e_{i}\rangle,\qquad a_{i}^{\dagger}|n\rangle=\sqrt{n_{i}+1}\,|n+e_{i}\rangle,\qquad N_{i}=a_{i}^{\dagger}a_{i},$
where the first expression is zero when  $n_{i}=0$ .
The bare jumps in our examples are these operators or their higher
powers. For unbounded jumps or a nonintegrable filter,
(2.1)–(2.2) are formal expressions on the
common core specified by the construction. The sampler is the conservative quantum Markov semigroup obtained from
the closed Dirichlet form in [4]; its
$L^{2}$  realization is a self-adjoint operator. We compute unbounded products on the common core specified in that
construction and then take closures.
For the general quantum Markov semigroup (QMS) of
Section 1.1, let  $\mathcal{L}$  be its generator. Then
$\Phi_{t}=e^{t\mathcal{L}}\quad\text{on }\mathscr{T}_{1}(\mathcal{H}),\qquad T_{t}=\Phi_{t}^{*}\quad\text{on }B(\mathcal{H}),$
For  $t\geq 0$ , the duality between the Schrödinger and Heisenberg
pictures is  $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi_{t}(\rho)X)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho T_{t}(X))$ .
Assume that  $\sigma$  is a faithful invariant state. We use
primitive to mean that the fixed observables are exactly
$\mathbb{C}I$ ; in this setting  $\sigma$  is the unique invariant state.
For  $1\leq p<\infty$ , the map
$\iota_{p,\sigma}(X)=\sigma^{1/(2p)}X\sigma^{1/(2p)}$  on  $B(\mathcal{H})$
extends to an isometry from the weighted space  $L^{p}(\sigma)$  of
Section 1.1 onto  $\mathscr{T}_{p}(\mathcal{H})$ .
We call this the symmetric Schatten realization and put
$\iota_{\infty,\sigma}=\mathrm{id}$ .
For the weighted interpolation construction, see
[17, 8].
The  $\sigma$ -weighted mean is
$\langle X\rangle_{\sigma}=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma X)$ , extended continuously to
these spaces;  $X$  is  $\sigma$ -centred if this mean is zero.
We also write  $T_{t}$  for its consistent extensions to
$L^{p}(\sigma)$ , writing  $T_{t}^{(p)}$  when the exponent must be specified.
An operator norm  $\|T:L^{p}(\sigma)\to L^{q}(\sigma)\|$  is the supremum
of  $\|TX\|_{q,\sigma}/\|X\|_{p,\sigma}$  over nonzero  $X$ .
The KMS symmetry assumed in Section 1.1
[18] is self-adjointness of  $T_{t}$  for the inner product
$\langle X,Y\rangle_{2,\sigma}=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma^{1/2}X^{\dagger}\sigma^{1/2}Y).$
Transporting the  $L^{2}$  semigroup to Hilbert–Schmidt space through
$\iota_{2,\sigma}$  gives its standard form:
(2.4)
$\iota_{2,\sigma}T_{t}^{(2)}\iota_{2,\sigma}^{-1}=e^{-tL}\quad\text{on }\mathscr{T}_{2}(\mathcal{H}).$
Here  $L$  is a nonnegative self-adjoint operator on  $\mathscr{T}_{2}(\mathcal{H})$ .
It acts on Hilbert–Schmidt operators, whereas the jump operators
$L^{\alpha}$  in (2.1) act on  $\mathcal{H}$ .
For any operator  $A$ ,  $D(A)$  denotes its operator domain.
The closed quadratic form of  $L$ , its form domain, and its
complex-time semigroup are
$D(\mathcal{E})=D(L^{1/2}),\qquad\mathcal{E}(Y)=\|L^{1/2}Y\|_{2}^{2},\qquad e^{-zL}\quad(\operatorname{Re}z>0).$
A form core is a subspace dense in  $D(\mathcal{E})$
for the norm  $\bigl(\|Y\|_{2}^{2}+\mathcal{E}(Y)\bigr)^{1/2}$ .
For closed forms and form cores, see [19, Sections 10.1–10.2];
the correspondence with Markov semigroups in standard form is treated
in [20].
When  $\ker L=\mathbb{C}\sqrt{\sigma}$ , the spectral gap from
Section 1.1 has the variational expression
$\operatorname{gap}(L)=\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}Y\in D(\mathcal{E}),\ \|Y\|_{2}=1\\
\operatorname{Tr}(\sqrt{\sigma}\,Y)=0\end{subarray}}\mathcal{E}(Y).$
Compactness from one endpoint.
For  $2<q<\infty$ , the inclusion  $L^{q}(\sigma)\hookrightarrow L^{2}(\sigma)$
is compact. In symmetric Schatten coordinates it is
$J_{q}(Y)=\sigma^{a}Y\sigma^{a}$ , where  $a=1/4-1/(2q)>0$ .
For finite-rank spectral projections  $P_{n}\uparrow I$  of  $\sigma$ ,
Schatten Hölder with  $r=1/a$  and  $2/r+1/q=1/2$  gives
$\|J_{q}-P_{n}J_{q}(\,\cdot\,)P_{n}\|_{\mathscr{T}_{q}\to\mathscr{T}_{2}}\leq 2\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}((I-P_{n})\sigma)\bigr)^{a}\longrightarrow 0.$
The approximating maps have finite rank. Thus a bounded
$T_{s}:L^{2}(\sigma)\to L^{q}(\sigma)$  makes  $e^{-sL}$  compact.
The spectral theorem then gives compact resolvent for  $L$ ; if
$\ker L=\mathbb{C}\sqrt{\sigma}$ , zero is simple and isolated, so
$\operatorname{gap}(L)>0$ . This argument uses the atomic algebra
$B(\mathcal{H})$  and trace-class  $\sigma$ ; it does not assert compactness
for diffuse algebras or a uniform numerical lower bound on the gap.
Let  $\mathscr{L}^{(p)}$  denote the
generator of  $T_{t}^{(p)}$  on  $L^{p}(\sigma)$ . The minus sign in
(2.4) gives
$L=-\iota_{2,\sigma}\mathscr{L}^{(2)}\iota_{2,\sigma}^{-1}.$
The Bohr frequencies are the energy differences in
$\Omega(H)=\{E^{\prime}-E:E,E^{\prime}\in\operatorname{Sp}(H)\}$ .
Let  $\sigma_{E}\in(0,\infty]$  be an energy-resolution width:
the sampler couples energy differences  $\nu$  and  $\mu$  with
Gaussian factor  $\exp[-(\nu-\mu)^{2}/(8\sigma_{E}^{2})]$ , interpreted as
one when  $\sigma_{E}=\infty$ . With the filter  $\widehat{f}$  and
Hamiltonian  $H$  fixed, write
$\mathcal{L}_{\sigma_{E}}$  for the state-side generator and
$L_{\sigma_{E}}\geq 0$  for its standard-form operator.
The explicit finite-dimensional formula
is (2.20). At the Davies endpoint
$\sigma_{E}=0$ , only equal frequencies remain; its form is denoted by
$\mathcal{E}_{0}$  and is generated by  $L_{0}$ .
We call the family hyperbounded if for every  $1<p<q<\infty$  there
are  $\tau_{p,q}\geq 0$  and  $C_{p,q}\geq 1$  such that
(2.5)
$\|T_{t}^{(p)}:L^{p}(\sigma)\to L^{q}(\sigma)\|\leq C_{p,q},\qquad t>\tau_{p,q}.$
We call an  $L^{p}$ -to- $L^{q}$  bound contractive if its norm is at most one.
An endpoint bound means an  $L^{p}$ -to- $L^{q}$  bound at one fixed time.
2.2. Relative entropy and entropy production
We introduce entropy production and formulate the entropy-decay
criteria for Gibbs samplers with filtered jumps.
We use the Umegaki relative entropy introduced in Section 1.1,
written  $D(\rho\|\omega)$  for a faithful reference state  $\omega$ .
Logarithms are defined by functional
calculus, with  $0\log 0=0$ ; in infinite dimension the trace expression is
understood in the extended relative-entropy sense, rather than as a
difference of two possibly infinite traces
[21, Section 2 and Remark 4.6].
We use trace-norm lower semicontinuity and data processing in this
extended sense; see [21, Theorem 4.1(i),(iv)].
Let
$B(\omega)=\bigcup_{\Gamma\geq 1}\{\rho\in\mathscr{T}_{1}(\mathcal{H}):\rho\geq 0,\ \operatorname{Tr}\rho=1,\ \Gamma^{-1}\omega\leq\rho\leq\Gamma\omega\}.$
Here the inequalities are in the operator order and  $\Gamma$  is a scalar
comparison constant. The notation  $B(\omega)$  denotes this set of
states, whereas  $B(\mathcal{H})$  denotes the algebra of bounded operators.
For  $\rho\in D(\mathcal{L})\cap B(\omega)$  and an invariant state
$\omega$ , the entropy production is
$\operatorname{EP}_{\mathcal{L}}(\rho)=-\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(\mathcal{L}(\rho)(\log\rho-\log\omega)\bigr).$
The logarithmic difference has a bounded extension on  $B(\omega)$ ,
so this trace is defined. A modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality
(MLSI) with rate  $\alpha>0$  is
$\alpha D(\rho\|\omega)\leq\operatorname{EP}_{\mathcal{L}}(\rho)$  on this domain.
The precise Stroock–Varopoulos (SV) assumption in Theorem 1.1
is that, for every  $\rho\in D(\mathcal{L})\cap B(\sigma)$ ,
(2.6)
$\sqrt{\rho}\in D(\mathcal{E}),\qquad 4\mathcal{E}(\sqrt{\rho})\leq\operatorname{EP}_{\mathcal{L}}(\rho).$
KMS symmetry alone does not imply this comparison; see
Proposition 2.10. Under the assumptions of
Theorem 1.1, the proof also gives the equivalent MLSI,
$\alpha_{\rm HC}D(\rho\|\sigma)\leq\operatorname{EP}_{\mathcal{L}}(\rho),\qquad\rho\in D(\mathcal{L})\cap B(\sigma),$
with the same rate  $\alpha_{\rm HC}$  as in Theorem 1.1.
Theorem 1.2 applies to the filtered samplers as follows.
Corollary 2.1.
Let  $\sigma_{E}\in(0,\infty]$  and let
$\Phi_{t}=e^{t\mathcal{L}_{\sigma_{E}}}$  be any of the
conservative KMS-symmetric semigroups constructed in
[4], with invariant Gibbs state
$\sigma_{\beta}$ . Assume the irreducibility hypotheses giving
$\ker L_{\sigma_{E}}=\mathbb{C}\sqrt{\sigma_{\beta}}$ , and put
$L=L_{\sigma_{E}}\geq 0$  in the sign convention of
(2.4). If
$\|T_{s}^{(2)}:L^{2}(\sigma_{\beta})\to L^{4}(\sigma_{\beta})\|\leq C>1,$
then  $\lambda=\operatorname{gap}(L)>0$  and
(1.2) holds with
(2.7)
$\alpha_{\rm KMS}=\left(2s+\frac{2\log C+1}{\lambda}\right)^{-1}.$
For  $C=1$ , the rate  $(2s)^{-1}$  holds without a gap. This includes the
original generator at  $\sigma_{E}=\infty$  and every Gaussian width  $0<\sigma_{E}<\infty$ ; it does not use the Davies limit  $\sigma_{E}=0$ .
For the same  $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{4}$  bound at time  $s$ , with constant  $C>1$
and spectral gap  $\lambda>0$ , the two entropy-decay rates are
$\alpha_{\rm HC}=\left(s+\frac{\log C+1/2}{\lambda}\right)^{-1},\qquad\alpha_{\rm KMS}=\frac{1}{2}\alpha_{\rm HC}.$
Theorem 1.1 gives the first rate when the Stroock–Varopoulos
comparison holds. Theorem 1.2 gives the second rate
without that comparison. The KMS argument therefore gives half the rate obtained with SV. Proposition 2.10
shows why the comparison cannot be assumed for cross-frequency
generators; it does not show that this factor of two is optimal.
Hyperboundedness gives an  $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{4}$  bound after the
waiting time  $\tau_{2,4}$  in (2.5). Under primitivity,
compactness gives a positive gap, and Theorem 1.2
therefore gives exponential relative-entropy decay. If the Stroock–Varopoulos comparison also
holds, Theorem 1.1 gives the faster rate above.
A unique invariant state does not by itself ensure a positive gap in
infinite dimension. When the  $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{4}$  bound has norm at most
one, Theorem 1.2 gives the rate  $(2s)^{-1}$  without a gap.
If the Stroock–Varopoulos comparison holds as well,
Theorem 1.1 improves this rate to  $s^{-1}$ .
The following table compares the two entropy-decay criteria. In the
first two rows the endpoint bound has constant  $C>1$ , and its
automatically positive spectral gap enters the rate; in the last two
rows the endpoint is contractive ( $C=1$ ), so the rate needs no gap value.
Norm bound
Other assumptions
Entropy-decay rate
$L^{2}\to L^{4}$  at  $(s,C)$
SV
$\displaystyle\left(s+\frac{\log C+1/2}{\lambda}\right)^{-1}$
$L^{2}\to L^{q_{0}}$  at  $(s,C)$
KMS symmetry
$\displaystyle\frac{1-2/q_{0}}{s+\lambda^{-1}(\log C+1-2/q_{0})}$
contractive  $L^{2}\to L^{4}$
SV
$s^{-1}$
contractive  $L^{2}\to L^{q_{0}}$
KMS symmetry
$(1-2/q_{0})s^{-1}$
To prove Theorem 1.1, we first derive a logarithmic Sobolev
inequality. We interpolate the  $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{4}$  bound to small times and
differentiate at time zero. This gives a  $2$ -logarithmic Sobolev
inequality with an additional squared-norm term, called the defect. The Rothaus
estimate transfers the defect to the component orthogonal to the
invariant vector, and the Poincaré inequality bounds this component
by the Dirichlet energy. Combining the tight inequality with the Stroock–Varopoulos comparison
gives the modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality. Exponential
relative-entropy decay then follows. When  $C=1$ , differentiation already gives a tight inequality,
so the gap is unnecessary.
The proof of Theorem 1.2 derives entropy contraction
directly from the weighted  $L^{p}$  estimates. For  $C>1$ , interpolation,
noncommutative  $L^{q}$  smoothness, and decay of centred observables under
the spectral gap yield contractive  $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{q}$  bounds after an
explicit additional time. KMS symmetry then allows interpolation
with the  $L^{1}$  contraction to give a strong data-processing inequality
for relative entropy. We divide the time interval into equal pieces and iterate the
short-time estimate. Letting the number of pieces tend to infinity
gives exponential decay. Optimizing the interpolation
parameter gives the rate in Theorem 1.2. For  $C=1$ , the argument starts from
the given contractive endpoint and again requires no gap.
The remainder of Section 2 proves these criteria and
identifies the cross-frequency obstruction to the
Stroock–Varopoulos comparison. Its infinite-dimensional Davies
criterion is conditional on the stated exhaustion hypotheses, which
must be verified for any proposed application.
Section 3 proves stability of the norm bounds under
bounded perturbations, and of  $2$ -logarithmic Sobolev inequalities
under changes of the Gibbs weight on a finite energy subspace.
Section 4 treats polynomial jumps, Bose–Hubbard
samplers with hopping, and finite-rank Coulomb perturbations of tensor
quantum Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (qOU) semigroups. It also gives the
periodic charging example.
2.3. Modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality
We relate the modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality to entropy decay
and express relative entropy in the Hilbert–Schmidt representation.
If
$\Gamma^{-1}\omega\leq\rho\leq\Gamma\omega$ , operator monotonicity of
the logarithm shows that the quadratic-form difference
$\log\rho-\log\omega$  extends to a bounded self-adjoint operator, with
$\|\log\rho-\log\omega\|_{\infty}\leq\log\Gamma;$
see [19]. Thus its pairing with
$\mathcal{L}(\rho)\in\mathscr{T}_{1}(\mathcal{H})$  is defined for
$\rho\in D(\mathcal{L})\cap B(\omega)$ .
Lemma 2.2.
Let  $\omega$  be a faithful invariant state of  $\Phi_{t}=e^{t\mathcal{L}}$  and let  $\alpha>0$ . The estimate  $D(\Phi_{t}(\rho)\|\omega)\leq e^{-\alpha t}D(\rho\|\omega)$  for all states and all  $t\geq 0$  is equivalent to
$\alpha D(\rho\|\omega)\leq\operatorname{EP}_{\mathcal{L}}(\rho),\qquad\rho\in D(\mathcal{L})\cap B(\omega).$
This is the equivalence between MLSI and entropy decay in infinite
dimension; see [13, Lemma A.1 and Theorem 2.7].
The hypercontractive estimates use the spaces  $L^{p}(\sigma)$ , whereas
the Dirichlet form acts on the fixed Hilbert space
$\mathscr{T}_{2}(\mathcal{H})$ . We identify an observable  $X$
with
$Y=\iota_{2,\sigma}(X)=\sigma^{1/4}X\sigma^{1/4}.$
This identification is isometric:  $\|Y\|_{2}=\|X\|_{2,\sigma}$ .
The norm of the same observable in  $L^{p}(\sigma)$  is obtained by
changing the weights from
$\sigma^{1/4}$  to  $\sigma^{1/(2p)}$ . In terms of  $Y$ , this gives
(2.8)
$\|Y\|_{p\leftarrow 2,\sigma}:=\|\sigma^{1/(2p)-1/4}Y\sigma^{1/(2p)-1/4}\|_{p}=\|X\|_{p,\sigma},\qquad 1\leq p<\infty,$
whenever these norms are finite. The subscript  $p\leftarrow 2$  denotes
the weighted  $L^{p}$  norm in the Hilbert–Schmidt coordinates fixed at
$p=2$ . At  $p=2$ , it is the ordinary Hilbert–Schmidt norm.
For  $p>2$ , the exponent of  $\sigma$  in
(2.8) is negative. Since the eigenvalues of
$\sigma$  can approach zero, this expression need not be finite for
every Hilbert–Schmidt operator. We define it by finite spectral cutoffs. Choose increasing finite-rank spectral
projections  $P_{n}$  of  $\sigma$  with  $P_{n}\to I$  strongly, and set
$\|Y\|_{p\leftarrow 2,\sigma}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\|\sigma^{1/(2p)-1/4}P_{n}YP_{n}\sigma^{1/(2p)-1/4}\|_{p}\in[0,\infty].$
All powers in each term act on the finite-dimensional range of  $P_{n}$ .
The norms increase with  $n$ , and their limit is independent of the
chosen exhaustion. The domain consists of those  $Y$  for which this
limit is finite; on that domain the reweighted operator belongs to
$\mathscr{T}_{p}(\mathcal{H})$ . The proof of Theorem 2.3 constructs the form core used to
differentiate the semigroup.
For  $Y\in\mathscr{T}_{2}(\mathcal{H})\setminus\{0\}$ , define
$\displaystyle\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Y):=\frac{\|Y\|_{2}^{2}}{2}\bigg[$
$\displaystyle D\left(\frac{Y^{\dagger}Y}{\|Y\|_{2}^{2}}\middle\|\sigma\right)+D\left(\frac{YY^{\dagger}}{\|Y\|_{2}^{2}}\middle\|\sigma\right)\bigg],$
with  $\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(0)=0$  and infinite values allowed. Both
normalized operators inside the relative entropies are states, and
this functional is lower semicontinuous in the Hilbert–Schmidt norm.
For  $Y$  supported on a finite spectral subspace of  $\sigma$ ,
differentiating (2.8) gives
$\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Y)=4\|Y\|_{2}^{2}\left.\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}p}\log\|Y\|_{p\leftarrow 2,\sigma}\right|_{p=2},\qquad Y\neq 0.$
Here  $Y$  is fixed while  $p$  varies. In infinite dimension we use
the relative-entropy formula above; the cutoff argument in
Theorem 2.3 below proves the required norm comparison.
In particular, a state  $\rho$  is represented in the positive cone of
Hilbert–Schmidt space by its square root  $Y=\sqrt{\rho}$ . Then
$Y^{\dagger}Y=YY^{\dagger}=\rho$  and  $\|Y\|_{2}^{2}=\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$ , so
$\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(\sqrt{\rho})=D(\rho\|\sigma).$
The equilibrium state corresponds to  $\sqrt{\sigma}$ , which is also
the image of the identity observable under  $\iota_{2,\sigma}$ .
Thus an inequality for  $\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Y)$  gives a relative-entropy
inequality by taking  $Y=\sqrt{\rho}$ .
2.4. The Gross and Rothaus steps
We differentiate the hypercontractive bound and use the Rothaus and
Poincaré inequalities to obtain a tight logarithmic Sobolev inequality.
For standard-form vectors use the complex Hilbert–Schmidt inner
product  $\langle X,Y\rangle:=\operatorname{Tr}(X^{\dagger}Y)$ . Thus
$\langle\sqrt{\sigma},X\rangle\sqrt{\sigma}$  is the orthogonal projection
of  $X$  onto the invariant line  $\mathbb{C}\sqrt{\sigma}$ .
Theorem 2.3.
Under the semigroup assumptions of Theorem 1.1, the endpoint (1.1) implies, for every standard-form vector  $X\in D(\mathcal{E})\subset\mathscr{T}_{2}(\mathcal{H})$ ,
(2.9)
$\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(X)\leq 4s\mathcal{E}(X)+4\log C\|X\|_{2}^{2}.$
Consequently, for every state  $\rho$  with  $\sqrt{\rho}\in D(\mathcal{E})$ ,
(2.10)
$D(\rho\|\sigma)\leq 4s\mathcal{E}(\sqrt{\rho})+(4\log C+2)\|\sqrt{\rho}-\langle\sqrt{\sigma},\sqrt{\rho}\rangle\sqrt{\sigma}\|_{2}^{2}.$
If the gap is  $\lambda>0$ , then
(2.11)
$D(\rho\|\sigma)\leq c_{\rm LS}\mathcal{E}(\sqrt{\rho}),\qquad c_{\rm LS}=4s+\frac{4\log C+2}{\lambda}.$
For  $C=1$ , (2.9) directly gives (2.11) with  $c_{\rm LS}=4s$  and no gap assumption.
Proof.
Step 1: a spectral form core.
Let  $E_{R}=\mathbf{1}_{[0,R]}(L)$  and set
$\mathcal{C}=\bigcup_{R>0}E_{R}\mathscr{T}_{2}(\mathcal{H})$ .
For  $X\in D(\mathcal{E})$ , the spectral truncations  $X_{R}=E_{R}X$  satisfy
$\|X-X_{R}\|_{\mathcal{E}}^{2}=\|(I-E_{R})X\|_{2}^{2}+\|(I-E_{R})L^{1/2}X\|_{2}^{2}\longrightarrow 0,$
where  $\|X\|_{\mathcal{E}}^{2}=\|X\|_{2}^{2}+\mathcal{E}(X)$ . Thus
$\mathcal{C}$  is a form core. If  $X\in E_{R}\mathscr{T}_{2}(\mathcal{H})$ ,
then  $e^{sL}X$  is well defined and has norm at most  $e^{sR}\|X\|_{2}$ .
The assumed endpoint therefore gives
$\|X\|_{4\leftarrow 2,\sigma}=\|e^{-sL}e^{sL}X\|_{4\leftarrow 2,\sigma}\leq C\|e^{sL}X\|_{2}\leq Ce^{sR}\|X\|_{2}.$
Thus the transported  $L^{4}$  norm is bounded by a constant times
the Hilbert–Schmidt norm on each spectral subspace. We first prove the estimates for a nonzero
$X\in E_{R}\mathscr{T}_{2}(\mathcal{H})$ ; the case  $X=0$  is immediate.
Step 2: endpoint interpolation.
Apply Stein interpolation [22, Chapter V],
in its weighted noncommutative form
[23, Theorem 2.10], on
$0\leq\operatorname{Re}z\leq 1$  to the analytic family  $e^{-szL}$ . On the first boundary  $e^{-isyL}$  is
unitary on  $L^{2}$ , and on the second boundary the factorization
$e^{-s(1+iy)L}=e^{-sL}e^{-isyL}$  gives the  $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{4}$  bound
$C$ , for every  $y\in\mathbb{R}$ . Consequently, for  $0\leq t\leq s$ ,
$\|e^{-tL}X\|_{q(t)\leftarrow 2,\sigma}\leq C^{t/s}\|X\|_{2},\qquad\frac{1}{q(t)}=\frac{1-t/s}{2}+\frac{t/s}{4}.$
The exponent is  $q(t)=4s/(2s-t)$ . Apply the estimate to
$e^{tL}X$ , which is well defined on the spectral subspace from
Step 1. Since  $e^{-tL}e^{tL}X=X$ , it follows that
$\log\frac{\|X\|_{q(t)\leftarrow 2,\sigma}}{\|X\|_{2}}\leq\frac{t}{s}\log C+\log\frac{\|e^{tL}X\|_{2}}{\|X\|_{2}},\qquad 0<t\leq s.$
Step 3: finite cutoffs and the defect.
Let  $P_{n}$  be the finite spectral projections of  $\sigma$  used above
and put  $X_{n}=P_{n}XP_{n}$ . For all sufficiently large  $n$ ,  $X_{n}\neq 0$ .
Fix  $0<t\leq s$  and define, for  $0\leq u\leq t$ ,
$g_{n}(u)=\log\|X_{n}\|_{q(u)\leftarrow 2,\sigma}.$
Weighted interpolation makes  $g_{n}$  convex, since  $1/q(u)$  is affine
in  $u$ ; see [17, 23].
We differentiate only finite matrices on the range of  $P_{n}$ . The finite-matrix entropy formula and  $q^{\prime}(0)=1/s$  give
$\frac{\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(X_{n})}{4s\|X_{n}\|_{2}^{2}}=g_{n}^{\prime}(0)\leq\frac{g_{n}(t)-g_{n}(0)}{t}.$
The weight here is the restriction of  $\sigma$ , without renormalizing
its trace. Thus this is precisely  $\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(X_{n})$ , with no
normalization correction.
By the definition of the transported norm,
$\|X_{n}\|_{2}\longrightarrow\|X\|_{2},\qquad\|X_{n}\|_{q(t)\leftarrow 2,\sigma}\longrightarrow\|X\|_{q(t)\leftarrow 2,\sigma}<\infty.$
Lower semicontinuity of the entropy and the bound on  $g_{n}^{\prime}(0)$  give
$\displaystyle\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(X)$
$\displaystyle\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(X_{n})$
$\displaystyle\leq\frac{4s\|X\|_{2}^{2}}{t}\log\frac{\|X\|_{q(t)\leftarrow 2,\sigma}}{\|X\|_{2}}$
$\displaystyle\leq 4\log C\|X\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{4s\|X\|_{2}^{2}}{t}\log\frac{\|e^{tL}X\|_{2}}{\|X\|_{2}}.$
Only the last Hilbert–Schmidt norm needs to be differentiated.
The operator  $L$  is bounded on  $E_{R}\mathscr{T}_{2}(\mathcal{H})$ , so
$\left.\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}t}\log\|e^{tL}X\|_{2}\right|_{t=0}=\frac{\operatorname{Re}\langle X,LX\rangle}{\|X\|_{2}^{2}}=\frac{\mathcal{E}(X)}{\|X\|_{2}^{2}}.$
Letting  $t\downarrow 0$  proves (2.9) on
$\mathcal{C}$ . The argument applies to complex  $X$  even when the spectral
projections of  $L$  and  $\sigma$  do not commute.
Step 4: the centred estimate.
Write  $a=\langle\sqrt{\sigma},X\rangle$  and
$X_{0}=X-a\sqrt{\sigma}$ . Since  $\|\sqrt{\sigma}\|_{2}=1$  and
$\sqrt{\sigma}\in\ker L$ , we have
$\langle\sqrt{\sigma},X_{0}\rangle=0,\qquad\|X\|_{2}^{2}=|a|^{2}+\|X_{0}\|_{2}^{2},\qquad\mathcal{E}(X_{0})=\mathcal{E}(X).$
Moreover  $X_{0}\in\mathcal{C}$ , because every  $E_{R}$  fixes
$\sqrt{\sigma}$ . The entropy-domain Rothaus inequality proved in
Lemma 2.4 below gives
$\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(X)\leq\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(X_{0})+2\|X_{0}\|_{2}^{2}.$
Applying (2.9) to  $X_{0}$  and using
$\mathcal{E}(X_{0})=\mathcal{E}(X)$  now gives
$\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(X)\leq 4s\mathcal{E}(X)+(4\log C+2)\|X_{0}\|_{2}^{2}.$
Thus the defect depends only on the component orthogonal to the
invariant vector.
Step 5: extension to the form domain and the gap.
For general  $X\in D(\mathcal{E})$ , use the truncations  $X_{R}=E_{R}X$
from Step 1. They satisfy
$\mathcal{E}(X_{R})\to\mathcal{E}(X)$  and  $\|X_{R}\|_{2}\to\|X\|_{2}$ .
Since  $E_{R}\sqrt{\sigma}=\sqrt{\sigma}$ , their centred components are
$(X_{R})_{0}=E_{R}X_{0}$  and converge to  $X_{0}$  in  $L^{2}$ .
For the defective bound, lower semicontinuity gives
$\displaystyle\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(X)$
$\displaystyle\leq\liminf_{R\to\infty}\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(X_{R})$
$\displaystyle\leq\lim_{R\to\infty}\bigl(4s\mathcal{E}(X_{R})+4\log C\|X_{R}\|_{2}^{2}\bigr)=4s\mathcal{E}(X)+4\log C\|X\|_{2}^{2}.$
Using the centred bound from Step 4 instead gives
$\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(X)\leq\lim_{R\to\infty}\bigl(4s\mathcal{E}(X_{R})+(4\log C+2)\|E_{R}X_{0}\|_{2}^{2}\bigr)=4s\mathcal{E}(X)+(4\log C+2)\|X_{0}\|_{2}^{2}.$
Thus both inequalities hold throughout  $D(\mathcal{E})$ . With  $X=\sqrt{\rho}$ , the identity
$\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(\sqrt{\rho})=D(\rho\|\sigma)$  then gives
(2.10).
If  $\lambda>0$ , the definition of the spectral gap on the orthogonal
complement of  $\sqrt{\sigma}$  gives
$\lambda\|X_{0}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\mathcal{E}(X_{0})=\mathcal{E}(X)$ .
Substitution into the centred bound, again with  $X=\sqrt{\rho}$ ,
yields
$D(\rho\|\sigma)\leq\left(4s+\frac{4\log C+2}{\lambda}\right)\mathcal{E}(\sqrt{\rho}),$
which is (2.11). Finally, when  $C=1$ , the defect
$4\log C\|X\|_{2}^{2}$  in (2.9) vanishes.
Applying that inequality directly to  $\sqrt{\rho}$  gives the constant
$4s$ , without centering or a spectral-gap assumption.
∎
Lemma 2.4 (Rothaus inequality on the entropy domain).
Let  $\sigma$  be a faithful density matrix on  $\mathcal{H}$ . For every
$Y\in\mathscr{T}_{2}(\mathcal{H})$  and  $a\in\mathbb{C}$ ,
(2.12)
$\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Y+a\sqrt{\sigma})\leq\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Y)+2\|Y\|_{2}^{2}.$
Infinite values are allowed. In particular, the estimate applies to
the centred vector  $Y=X-\langle\sqrt{\sigma},X\rangle\sqrt{\sigma}$
whenever its entropy is finite.
Proof.
Finite dimension.
For  $2\leq q\leq 4$ , set
$B_{q}=\sigma^{1/(2q)-1/4}Y\sigma^{1/(2q)-1/4}$ .
The first variation of the squared Schatten norm at
$a\sigma^{1/q}$  is
$\left.\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}u}\|a\sigma^{1/q}+uB_{q}\|_{q}^{2}\right|_{u=0}=2\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\bar{a}\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma^{1-1/q}B_{q})\bigr)=2\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\bar{a}\langle\sqrt{\sigma},Y\rangle\bigr).$
For  $a=0$  both sides vanish. The Ball–Carlen–Lieb smoothness
inequality [24] therefore gives
$\|Y+a\sqrt{\sigma}\|_{q\leftarrow 2,\sigma}^{2}\leq|a|^{2}+2\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\bar{a}\langle\sqrt{\sigma},Y\rangle\bigr)+(q-1)\|Y\|_{q\leftarrow 2,\sigma}^{2}.$
This is an equality at  $q=2$ , without a centering assumption.
The middle term is independent of  $q$ . For any fixed  $Z$ ,
$\left.\partial_{q}\|Z\|_{q\leftarrow 2,\sigma}^{2}\right|_{q=2+}=2\|Z\|_{2}^{2}\left.\partial_{q}\log\|Z\|_{q\leftarrow 2,\sigma}\right|_{q=2+}=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Z).$
Since equality holds at  $q=2$ , the right derivatives satisfy
$\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Y+a\sqrt{\sigma})\leq\|Y\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Y).$
This is (2.12). When  $Z=0$  its squared
norm is identically zero, so the same argument includes  $Y=0$  and
$Y+a\sqrt{\sigma}=0$ .
Entropy recovery under spectral cutoffs.
For a positive trace-class operator  $A$  of trace  $m>0$ , write
$\mathfrak{D}_{\sigma}(A):=mD(A/m\|\sigma)+m\log m,\qquad\mathfrak{D}_{\sigma}(0):=0.$
This definition avoids subtracting possibly infinite energy and
entropy traces. The functional is lower semicontinuous in trace
norm [21, Theorem 4.1(i)] and satisfies
$\mathfrak{D}_{\sigma}(A)\geq m\log m$ .
Choose increasing finite-rank spectral projections  $P_{n}$  of  $\sigma$
with  $P_{n}\to I$  strongly, and put  $Q_{n}=I-P_{n}$ ,  $Y_{n}=P_{n}YP_{n}$ .
We claim that finite  $\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Y)$  implies
(2.13)
$\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Y_{n})\longrightarrow\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Y).$
To see this, set
$A=Y^{\dagger}Y,\qquad A_{n}=Y_{n}^{\dagger}Y_{n},\qquad R_{n}=P_{n}Y^{\dagger}Q_{n}YP_{n},\qquad S_{n}=Q_{n}AQ_{n}.$
Then  $A_{n}+R_{n}=P_{n}AP_{n}$ . On the finite block, the reference-logarithm
terms cancel in the difference
$\displaystyle\mathfrak{D}_{\sigma}(A_{n}+R_{n})-\mathfrak{D}_{\sigma}(A_{n})-\mathfrak{D}_{\sigma}(R_{n})={}$
$\displaystyle\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(A_{n}[\log(A_{n}+R_{n})-\log A_{n}]\bigr)$
$\displaystyle+\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(R_{n}[\log(A_{n}+R_{n})-\log R_{n}]\bigr)\geq 0.$
The last inequality follows from operator monotonicity of the logarithm
[25, Chapter V], with regularization at zero.
Data processing [21, Theorem 4.1(iv)] for the
pinching  $A\mapsto P_{n}AP_{n}+Q_{n}AQ_{n}$ , which fixes  $\sigma$ , gives the second:
$\mathfrak{D}_{\sigma}(A_{n})+\mathfrak{D}_{\sigma}(R_{n})+\mathfrak{D}_{\sigma}(S_{n})\leq\mathfrak{D}_{\sigma}(P_{n}AP_{n})+\mathfrak{D}_{\sigma}(S_{n})\leq\mathfrak{D}_{\sigma}(A).$
The discarded masses tend to zero because
$r_{n}:=\operatorname{Tr}R_{n}=\|Q_{n}YP_{n}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\|Q_{n}Y\|_{2}^{2}\longrightarrow 0,\qquad s_{n}:=\operatorname{Tr}S_{n}=\|YQ_{n}\|_{2}^{2}\longrightarrow 0.$
Since  $\mathfrak{D}_{\sigma}(R_{n})\geq r_{n}\log r_{n}$  and
$\mathfrak{D}_{\sigma}(S_{n})\geq s_{n}\log s_{n}$ , it follows that
$\mathfrak{D}_{\sigma}(A_{n})\leq\mathfrak{D}_{\sigma}(A)-r_{n}\log r_{n}-s_{n}\log s_{n}.$
The trace-norm convergence follows from the ideal inequality:
$\|A_{n}-A\|_{1}\leq(\|Y_{n}\|_{2}+\|Y\|_{2})\|Y_{n}-Y\|_{2}\longrightarrow 0.$
Combining the upper bound with lower semicontinuity gives
$\mathfrak{D}_{\sigma}(A)\leq\liminf_{n}\mathfrak{D}_{\sigma}(A_{n})\leq\limsup_{n}\mathfrak{D}_{\sigma}(A_{n})\leq\mathfrak{D}_{\sigma}(A).$
Applying this argument to  $Y^{\dagger}$  also yields
$\mathfrak{D}_{\sigma}(Y_{n}Y_{n}^{\dagger})\to\mathfrak{D}_{\sigma}(YY^{\dagger})$ .
The identity
$\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Y)=\tfrac{1}{2}\mathfrak{D}_{\sigma}(Y^{\dagger}Y)+\tfrac{1}{2}\mathfrak{D}_{\sigma}(YY^{\dagger})-\|Y\|_{2}^{2}\log\|Y\|_{2}^{2}$
and  $\|Y_{n}\|_{2}\to\|Y\|_{2}$  prove
(2.13).
Passage to the entropy domain.
Assume  $\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Y)<\infty$ , since otherwise the inequality is immediate. Put  $z_{n}=\operatorname{Tr}(P_{n}\sigma)$  and
$\sigma_{n}=P_{n}\sigma P_{n}/z_{n}$ , considered on  $P_{n}\mathcal{H}$ .
For every  $Z=P_{n}ZP_{n}$ ,
$\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma_{n}}(Z)=\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Z)+\|Z\|_{2}^{2}\log z_{n}.$
With  $X=Y+a\sqrt{\sigma}$ , its compression is
$X_{n}=Y_{n}+a\sqrt{z_{n}}\sqrt{\sigma_{n}}$ . The finite-dimensional
inequality gives
$\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma_{n}}(X_{n})\leq\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma_{n}}(Y_{n})+2\|Y_{n}\|_{2}^{2}.$
Returning to the original reference state, this reads
$\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(X_{n})\leq\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Y_{n})+2\|Y_{n}\|_{2}^{2}+(\|Y_{n}\|_{2}^{2}-\|X_{n}\|_{2}^{2})\log z_{n}.$
Here  $z_{n}\to 1$ , both norm sequences are bounded, and  $X_{n}\to X$
in Hilbert–Schmidt norm. Thus (2.13) gives
$\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(X)\leq\liminf_{n}\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(X_{n})\leq\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Y)+2\|Y\|_{2}^{2},$
as required.
∎
2.5. Entropy decay from KMS symmetry
We prove Theorem 1.2 by turning the hypercontractive
bound into entropy contraction through weighted interpolation and
noncommutative  $L^{q}$  smoothness.
We use the standard centred smoothness estimate
(2.14)
$\|aI+Y\|_{q,\sigma}^{2}\leq|a|^{2}+(q-1)\|Y\|_{q,\sigma}^{2},\qquad 2\leq q<\infty,\quad\langle Y\rangle_{\sigma}=0.$
It is the Ball–Carlen–Lieb inequality [24]
applied at  $a\sigma^{1/q}$  in direction  $\iota_{q,\sigma}(Y)$ ;
the first variation vanishes by centering. Schatten-norm density
extends the matrix inequality to the present Hilbert space. This is
also the estimate used in [5, Lemma 2.3].
The next lemma gives the extra time needed to make the norm at most one.
Lemma 2.5.
Let  $T_{t}$  be a  $\sigma$ -preserving Markov semigroup with scalar fixed
space and let  $\lambda>0$ . Suppose that, for every  $\sigma$ -centred  $Y\in L^{2}(\sigma)$ ,
$\|T_{t}Y\|_{2,\sigma}\leq e^{-\lambda t}\|Y\|_{2,\sigma}.$
If, for some  $u>0$ ,  $q>2$ , and  $K\geq 1$ ,
$\|T_{u}:L^{2}(\sigma)\to L^{q}(\sigma)\|\leq K,$
then  $\|T_{u+r}:L^{2}(\sigma)\to L^{q}(\sigma)\|\leq 1$  for
(2.15)
$r=\lambda^{-1}\bigl(\log K+\tfrac{1}{2}\log(q-1)\bigr).$
Proof.
Write  $X=aI+Y$ , where  $a=\langle X\rangle_{\sigma}$  and
$\langle Y\rangle_{\sigma}=0$ . Invariance and orthogonality give
$\langle T_{t}Y\rangle_{\sigma}=0,\qquad T_{t}I=I,\qquad\|X\|_{2,\sigma}^{2}=|a|^{2}+\|Y\|_{2,\sigma}^{2}.$
Apply the gap estimate before using the endpoint:
$\|T_{u}T_{r}Y\|_{q,\sigma}\leq K\|T_{r}Y\|_{2,\sigma}\leq Ke^{-\lambda r}\|Y\|_{2,\sigma}.$
The centred smoothness inequality (2.14) then gives
$\displaystyle\|T_{u+r}X\|_{q,\sigma}^{2}$
$\displaystyle=\|aI+T_{u}T_{r}Y\|_{q,\sigma}^{2}$
$\displaystyle\leq|a|^{2}+(q-1)\|T_{u}T_{r}Y\|_{q,\sigma}^{2}\leq|a|^{2}+(q-1)K^{2}e^{-2\lambda r}\|Y\|_{2,\sigma}^{2}.$
The time in (2.15) solves  $(q-1)K^{2}e^{-2\lambda r}=1$ . The last expression is
therefore  $\|X\|_{2,\sigma}^{2}$ .
∎
Lemma 2.6.
For every state  $\rho$  there are  $\rho_{k}\in B(\sigma)$  such that
(2.16)
$\|\rho_{k}-\rho\|_{1}\longrightarrow 0,\qquad D(\rho_{k}\|\sigma)\longrightarrow D(\rho\|\sigma)$
in the extended nonnegative reals.
Proof.
In finite dimension, put  $\rho_{\varepsilon}=(1-\varepsilon)\rho+\varepsilon\sigma$ . Faithfulness of  $\sigma$  makes
$\rho_{\varepsilon}\in B(\sigma)$ , and
$\|\rho_{\varepsilon}-\rho\|_{1}\leq 2\varepsilon,\qquad D(\rho_{\varepsilon}\|\sigma)\leq(1-\varepsilon)D(\rho\|\sigma).$
Lower semicontinuity gives the matching lower limit.
In infinite dimension, choose increasing finite-rank spectral
projections  $E_{n}\to I$  of  $\sigma$ , and put  $Q_{n}=I-E_{n}$ .
Faithfulness gives  $\operatorname{Tr}(Q_{n}\sigma)>0$ . Define the normal channel
$\mathsf{E}_{n}(\rho)=E_{n}\rho E_{n}+\operatorname{Tr}(Q_{n}\rho)\frac{Q_{n}\sigma Q_{n}}{\operatorname{Tr}(Q_{n}\sigma)}.$
It replaces the discarded block by the corresponding Gibbs tail.
It preserves the trace and fixes  $\sigma$ :
$\operatorname{Tr}\mathsf{E}_{n}(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}(E_{n}\rho)+\operatorname{Tr}(Q_{n}\rho)=1,\qquad\mathsf{E}_{n}(\sigma)=\sigma.$
Moreover
$\|\mathsf{E}_{n}(\rho)-\rho\|_{1}\leq\|E_{n}\rho E_{n}-\rho\|_{1}+\operatorname{Tr}(Q_{n}\rho)\longrightarrow 0.$
To control the operator order, let  $m_{n}>0$  be the smallest eigenvalue
of  $E_{n}\sigma E_{n}$  on  $E_{n}\mathcal{H}$ , and set
$c_{n}=\max\left\{\frac{\|E_{n}\rho E_{n}\|_{\infty}}{m_{n}},\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(Q_{n}\rho)}{\operatorname{Tr}(Q_{n}\sigma)}\right\}.$
The two blocks separately satisfy
$E_{n}\rho E_{n}\leq c_{n}E_{n}\sigma E_{n},\qquad\operatorname{Tr}(Q_{n}\rho)\frac{Q_{n}\sigma Q_{n}}{\operatorname{Tr}(Q_{n}\sigma)}\leq c_{n}Q_{n}\sigma Q_{n},$
so  $\mathsf{E}_{n}(\rho)\leq c_{n}\sigma$ .
Choose  $\varepsilon_{n}=1/(n+1)$  and put
$\rho_{n}=(1-\varepsilon_{n})\mathsf{E}_{n}(\rho)+\varepsilon_{n}\sigma$ .
Then
$\varepsilon_{n}\sigma\leq\rho_{n}\leq\bigl((1-\varepsilon_{n})c_{n}+\varepsilon_{n}\bigr)\sigma,\qquad\|\rho_{n}-\rho\|_{1}\leq\|\mathsf{E}_{n}(\rho)-\rho\|_{1}+2\varepsilon_{n}\to 0.$
Thus  $\rho_{n}\in B(\sigma)$ . If  $D(\rho\|\sigma)<\infty$ ,
convexity, data processing, and lower semicontinuity yield
$\displaystyle D(\rho_{n}\|\sigma)$
$\displaystyle\leq(1-\varepsilon_{n})D(\mathsf{E}_{n}(\rho)\|\sigma)\leq(1-\varepsilon_{n})D(\rho\|\sigma),$
$\displaystyle D(\rho\|\sigma)$
$\displaystyle\leq\liminf_{n}D(\rho_{n}\|\sigma).$
These bounds prove entropy convergence. If  $D(\rho\|\sigma)=\infty$ ,
the second line alone forces  $D(\rho_{n}\|\sigma)\to\infty$ .
∎
The norm-to-entropy implication below is
[26, Proposition 5.4] in finite dimension.
We give the proof for unbounded Gibbs weights and arbitrary
normal states.
Lemma 2.7.
Let  $\Phi$  be a normal channel with faithful invariant state  $\sigma$ ,
let  $T=\Phi^{*}$ , and assume that  $T$  is  $\sigma$ -KMS symmetric and extends
consistently to positive contractions on  $L^{r}(\sigma)$  for
$1\leq r\leq\infty$ . Suppose that, for some  $1\leq K<\infty$ ,
(2.17)
$\|T:L^{p}(\sigma)\to L^{q}(\sigma)\|\leq K,\qquad 1<p\leq q<\infty.$
Then
(2.18)
$D(\Phi(\rho)\|\sigma)\leq\frac{(p-1)q}{p(q-1)}D(\rho\|\sigma)+\frac{q}{q-1}\log K$
for every state  $\rho$ .
Proof.
For  $\rho\in B(\sigma)$ , the observable
$X=\iota_{1,\sigma}^{-1}(\rho)$  is bounded and positive.
We use the inverse only on this range. KMS symmetry gives
$\Phi\iota_{1,\sigma}=\iota_{1,\sigma}T$ . Weighted complex interpolation
[17] of (2.17) with
the  $L^{1}$  contraction yields, for
$0\leq\vartheta<1$ ,
$\frac{1}{p_{\vartheta}}=\vartheta+\frac{1-\vartheta}{p},\quad\frac{1}{q_{\vartheta}}=\vartheta+\frac{1-\vartheta}{q},\quad\|TX\|_{q_{\vartheta},\sigma}\leq K^{1-\vartheta}\|X\|_{p_{\vartheta},\sigma}.$
For  $r>1$ , define the sandwiched Rényi relative entropy
[23, Section 3] by
$\widetilde{D}_{r}(\rho\|\sigma):=\frac{1}{r-1}\log\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\left(\sigma^{(1-r)/(2r)}\rho\sigma^{(1-r)/(2r)}\right)^{r}\right].$
For  $\rho\in B(\sigma)$ , the positive product belongs to the
required Schatten class, and
$\log\|\iota_{1,\sigma}^{-1}(\rho)\|_{r,\sigma}=\frac{r-1}{r}\widetilde{D}_{r}(\rho\|\sigma).$
Since  $\Phi$  preserves
$\sigma$  and order,  $\Phi(\rho)\in B(\sigma)$  as well. The interpolated
bound therefore becomes
$\widetilde{D}_{q_{\vartheta}}(\Phi(\rho)\|\sigma)\leq\frac{(p_{\vartheta}-1)q_{\vartheta}}{p_{\vartheta}(q_{\vartheta}-1)}\widetilde{D}_{p_{\vartheta}}(\rho\|\sigma)+\frac{(1-\vartheta)q_{\vartheta}}{q_{\vartheta}-1}\log K.$
The interpolation identities imply
$\frac{p_{\vartheta}-1}{p_{\vartheta}}=(1-\vartheta)\frac{p-1}{p},\qquad\frac{q_{\vartheta}-1}{q_{\vartheta}}=(1-\vartheta)\frac{q-1}{q}.$
The coefficients are therefore independent of  $\vartheta$ :
$\frac{(p_{\vartheta}-1)q_{\vartheta}}{p_{\vartheta}(q_{\vartheta}-1)}=\frac{(p-1)q}{p(q-1)},\qquad\frac{(1-\vartheta)q_{\vartheta}}{q_{\vartheta}-1}=\frac{q}{q-1}.$
Letting  $\vartheta\uparrow 1$  proves
(2.18) on  $B(\sigma)$  because
$\widetilde{D}_{r}(\rho\|\sigma)\to D(\rho\|\sigma)$  as  $r\downarrow 1$
for comparable states [23, Proposition 3.8(ii)].
For a general state with finite input entropy, choose  $\rho_{k}$  from
Lemma 2.6. Trace-norm contractivity gives
$\|\Phi(\rho_{k})-\Phi(\rho)\|_{1}\leq\|\rho_{k}-\rho\|_{1}\to 0$ .
Consequently
$\displaystyle D(\Phi(\rho)\|\sigma)$
$\displaystyle\leq\liminf_{k}D(\Phi(\rho_{k})\|\sigma)$
$\displaystyle\leq\lim_{k}\left(\frac{(p-1)q}{p(q-1)}D(\rho_{k}\|\sigma)+\frac{q}{q-1}\log K\right)$
$\displaystyle=\frac{(p-1)q}{p(q-1)}D(\rho\|\sigma)+\frac{q}{q-1}\log K.$
For infinite input entropy the right-hand side is infinite, so the
assertion holds in the extended sense.
∎
Proof of Theorem 1.2.
We use the interpolation argument of
[5, Theorem 3.3], using the preceding lemmas to justify each step in infinite dimension. Put  $\delta=1-2/q_{0}$ ,
so  $0<\delta<1$ .
Interpolation and removal of the endpoint constant.
For  $0<\theta\leq 1$ , weighted Stein interpolation gives
$\frac{1}{q_{\theta}}=\frac{1-\theta}{2}+\frac{\theta}{q_{0}}=\frac{1-\theta\delta}{2},\qquad\|T_{\theta s}:L^{2}(\sigma)\to L^{q_{\theta}}(\sigma)\|\leq C^{\theta}.$
When  $C>1$ , Lemma 2.5, with  $K=C^{\theta}$ ,
gives a contractive endpoint at
(2.19)
$S_{\theta}=\theta s+\frac{\theta\log C+\frac{1}{2}\log(q_{\theta}-1)}{\lambda}.$
Interpolate this endpoint with the  $L^{2}$  bound at time zero. For
$0\leq u\leq S_{\theta}$ , define  $r_{\theta}(u)$  by
$\frac{1}{r_{\theta}(u)}=\frac{1-u/S_{\theta}}{2}+\frac{u/S_{\theta}}{q_{\theta}}=\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{\theta\delta u}{S_{\theta}}\right).$
Then  $\|T_{u}:L^{2}(\sigma)\to L^{r_{\theta}(u)}(\sigma)\|\leq 1$ .
For  $u>0$ , Lemma 2.7 applies with
$p=2$ ,  $q=r_{\theta}(u)$ , and  $K=1$ . Its coefficient is
$\frac{r_{\theta}(u)}{2(r_{\theta}(u)-1)}=\frac{1}{1+(\theta\delta/S_{\theta})u}.$
We have therefore obtained the short-time estimate
$D(\Phi_{u}(\rho)\|\sigma)\leq\frac{D(\rho\|\sigma)}{1+(\theta\delta/S_{\theta})u},\qquad 0\leq u\leq S_{\theta}.$
Iteration and the limiting rate.
Assume  $D(\rho\|\sigma)<\infty$ , fix  $t>0$ , and take an integer
$n$  large enough that  $t/n\leq S_{\theta}$ . Applying the last estimate
successively to  $\rho,\Phi_{t/n}(\rho),\ldots,\Phi_{(n-1)t/n}(\rho)$  gives
$D(\Phi_{t}(\rho)\|\sigma)\leq\left(1+\frac{\theta\delta t}{nS_{\theta}}\right)^{-n}D(\rho\|\sigma)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}e^{-(\theta\delta/S_{\theta})t}D(\rho\|\sigma).$
To compute the limit as  $\theta\downarrow 0$ , use
$q_{\theta}-1=\frac{1+\theta\delta}{1-\theta\delta},\qquad\frac{\log(q_{\theta}-1)}{2\theta}=\frac{\log(1+\theta\delta)-\log(1-\theta\delta)}{2\theta}\longrightarrow\delta.$
It follows that
$\frac{\theta\delta}{S_{\theta}}=\frac{\delta}{s+\lambda^{-1}\left(\log C+\frac{\log(q_{\theta}-1)}{2\theta}\right)}\longrightarrow\frac{\delta}{s+\lambda^{-1}(\log C+\delta)}.$
The entropy bound holds for every  $\theta>0$ , so passing to this
limit proves (1.2).
For  $C=1$ , interpolation starts directly from  $(s,q_{0})$ :
$\frac{1}{r(u)}=\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{\delta u}{s}\right),\qquad\|T_{u}:L^{2}(\sigma)\to L^{r(u)}(\sigma)\|\leq 1,\qquad 0\leq u\leq s.$
The same norm-to-entropy calculation and iteration give the rate
$\delta/s$ .
∎
Proof of Corollary 2.1.
The construction is a conservative KMS-symmetric QMS of positive
contractions on the weighted scale, with invariant state  $\sigma_{\beta}$ .
Its Hilbert–Schmidt semigroup is  $e^{-tL_{\sigma_{E}}}$ .
Thus the nonnegative operator in (2.4) is
$L_{\sigma_{E}}$ . The endpoint implies compact resolvent, so the
kernel assumption gives a positive gap and allows us to apply
Theorem 1.2; taking  $q_{0}=4$  gives
(2.7), without separating the Bohr frequencies.
∎
2.6. Stroock–Varopoulos inequality
We recall the standard finite-dimensional Davies comparison, then
identify the cross-frequency obstruction and give conditions for passing to infinite dimension.
We use the following frequency convention throughout this subsection. Write the Hamiltonian as
$H=\sum_{E\in\operatorname{Sp}(H)}EP_{E}$ , where  $P_{E}$  is the orthogonal projection
onto its  $E$ -eigenspace, and set
$\sigma=\sigma_{\beta}$ . Every faithful matrix state has this Gibbs
representation.
For each bare jump  $A^{\alpha}$ , its component at frequency  $\nu$  is
$A_{\nu}^{\alpha}:=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}E,E^{\prime}\in\operatorname{Sp}(H)\\
E^{\prime}-E=\nu\end{subarray}}P_{E^{\prime}}A^{\alpha}P_{E},\qquad\nu\in\Omega(H).$
Thus  $[H,A_{\nu}^{\alpha}]=\nu A_{\nu}^{\alpha}$  and
$[\log\sigma,A_{\nu}^{\alpha}]=-\beta\nu A_{\nu}^{\alpha}$ .
Adjoint closure of the bare family gives
$(A_{\nu}^{\alpha})^{\dagger}=A_{-\nu}^{\bar{\alpha}}$ .
Proposition 2.8 (Finite-dimensional Davies comparison).
Let  $\dim\mathcal{H}<\infty$  and use the adjoint-closed frequency decomposition
above. Suppose
$\mathcal{L}=\sum_{\alpha,\nu}r_{\alpha,\nu}\mathcal{D}_{A_{\nu}^{\alpha}},\qquad\mathcal{D}_{A}(\rho)=A\rho A^{\dagger}-\tfrac{1}{2}\{A^{\dagger}A,\rho\},\qquad r_{\bar{\alpha},-\nu}=e^{\beta\nu}r_{\alpha,\nu}\geq 0.$
Then every faithful state  $\rho$  satisfies
$4\mathcal{E}(\sqrt{\rho})\leq\operatorname{EP}_{\mathcal{L}}(\rho)$ .
This is [10, Theorem 14] at  $p=1$ ,  $q=2$ .
The rate pairing makes  $-\mathcal{L}^{*}$  self-adjoint for
$\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma X^{\dagger}Y)$ , which is the strong reversibility assumed
there. Under the standard-form identification, their  $2$ -Dirichlet
form is  $\mathcal{E}(\sqrt{\rho})$  and their  $1$ -Dirichlet form is
$\operatorname{EP}_{\mathcal{L}}(\rho)/4$ ; this accounts for the factor four.
For the filtered Davies generator,  $r_{\alpha,\nu}=|\widehat{f}(\nu)|^{2}$
and the filter KMS identity supplies the rate pairing.
2.6.1. The cross-frequency obstruction
The Davies comparison uses frequency diagonality. When different frequencies are coupled, the paired identity below
still holds, but the scalar chain inequality does not control the
mixed terms.
In finite dimension, retain the adjoint-closed frequency decomposition
above. For  $0<\sigma_{E}\leq\infty$ , set
$\displaystyle q_{\nu\mu}^{(\sigma_{E})}$
$\displaystyle:={e^{-(\nu-\mu)^{2}/(8\sigma_{E}^{2})}}\overline{\widehat{f}(\nu)}\widehat{f}(\mu),\qquad d_{\nu\mu}:=\frac{\beta(\nu-\mu)}{4},$
$\displaystyle c_{\nu\mu}^{(\sigma_{E})}$
$\displaystyle:=q_{\nu\mu}^{(\sigma_{E})}\frac{e^{\beta(\nu+\mu)/4}}{2\cosh d_{\nu\mu}}.$
The state-side cross-frequency generator is
(2.20)
$\mathcal{L}_{\sigma_{E}}(\rho)=\sum_{\alpha,\nu,\mu}q_{\nu\mu}^{(\sigma_{E})}\Bigl(A_{\mu}^{\alpha}\rho(A_{\nu}^{\alpha})^{\dagger}-\frac{e^{d_{\nu\mu}}}{2\cosh d_{\nu\mu}}(A_{\nu}^{\alpha})^{\dagger}A_{\mu}^{\alpha}\rho-\frac{e^{-d_{\nu\mu}}}{2\cosh d_{\nu\mu}}\rho(A_{\nu}^{\alpha})^{\dagger}A_{\mu}^{\alpha}\Bigr).$
All frequency sums here and below run over  $\Omega(H)$ .
At  $\sigma_{E}=\infty$  this is the original generator; finite
$\sigma_{E}$  retains the cross terms with a Gaussian weight.
Lemma 2.9.
Let  $\rho$  be a faithful state,
$K_{\rho}=\log\rho-\log\sigma_{\beta}$ , and write
$a_{\nu}=\beta\nu/2$ . Define
$\displaystyle U_{\alpha,\nu}$
$\displaystyle:=e^{-a_{\nu}/2}A_{\nu}^{\alpha}\sqrt{\rho}-e^{a_{\nu}/2}\sqrt{\rho}A_{\nu}^{\alpha},$
$\displaystyle W_{\alpha,\nu}$
$\displaystyle:=e^{-a_{\nu}}A_{\nu}^{\alpha}\rho-e^{a_{\nu}}\rho A_{\nu}^{\alpha},\qquad V_{\alpha,\nu}:=[A_{\nu}^{\alpha},K_{\rho}].$
Let  $\mathcal{E}_{\sigma_{E}}$  be the standard-form Dirichlet form associated
with  $\mathcal{L}_{\sigma_{E}}$ . Its energy and the entropy production
satisfy
(2.21)
$\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\sigma_{E}}(\sqrt{\rho})$
$\displaystyle=\operatorname{Re}\sum_{\alpha,\nu,\mu}c_{\nu\mu}^{(\sigma_{E})}\operatorname{Tr}(U_{\alpha,\nu}^{\dagger}U_{\alpha,\mu}),$
(2.22)
$\displaystyle\operatorname{EP}_{\mathcal{L}_{\sigma_{E}}}(\rho)$
$\displaystyle=\operatorname{Re}\sum_{\alpha,\nu,\mu}c_{\nu\mu}^{(\sigma_{E})}\operatorname{Tr}(W_{\alpha,\nu}^{\dagger}V_{\alpha,\mu}).$
Proof.
Put  $Y=\sqrt{\rho}$ . The four terms in the first pairing are
$\displaystyle\operatorname{Tr}(U_{\alpha,\nu}^{\dagger}U_{\alpha,\mu})={}$
$\displaystyle e^{-(a_{\nu}+a_{\mu})/2}\operatorname{Tr}(Y(A_{\nu}^{\alpha})^{\dagger}A_{\mu}^{\alpha}Y)$
$\displaystyle-e^{(a_{\mu}-a_{\nu})/2}\operatorname{Tr}(Y(A_{\nu}^{\alpha})^{\dagger}YA_{\mu}^{\alpha})$
$\displaystyle-e^{(a_{\nu}-a_{\mu})/2}\operatorname{Tr}((A_{\nu}^{\alpha})^{\dagger}YA_{\mu}^{\alpha}Y)$
$\displaystyle+e^{(a_{\nu}+a_{\mu})/2}\operatorname{Tr}((A_{\nu}^{\alpha})^{\dagger}Y^{2}A_{\mu}^{\alpha}).$
Multiply by  $c_{\nu\mu}^{(\sigma_{E})}$  and sum. Using
$\sigma_{\beta}^{t}A_{\nu}^{\alpha}\sigma_{\beta}^{-t}=e^{-2ta_{\nu}}A_{\nu}^{\alpha}$  and pairing the adjoint rows turns this sum into
$-\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(Y\sigma_{\beta}^{-1/4}\mathcal{L}_{\sigma_{E}}(\sigma_{\beta}^{1/4}Y\sigma_{\beta}^{1/4})\sigma_{\beta}^{-1/4}\right)=\mathcal{E}_{\sigma_{E}}(Y).$
This is the first formula. For the second, the modular relation
$[\log\sigma_{\beta},A_{\nu}^{\alpha}]=-2a_{\nu}A_{\nu}^{\alpha}$  gives
$V_{\alpha,\nu}=A_{\nu}^{\alpha}\log(e^{-a_{\nu}}\rho)-\log(e^{a_{\nu}}\rho)A_{\nu}^{\alpha}.$
The KMS identity for the filter reads
$\widehat{f}(-\nu)=e^{a_{\nu}}\overline{\widehat{f}(\nu)}$ , hence
(2.23)
$c_{-\mu,-\nu}^{(\sigma_{E})}=c_{\nu\mu}^{(\sigma_{E})}\quad\text{under}\quad(\alpha,\nu,\mu)\longmapsto(\bar{\alpha},-\mu,-\nu).$
Expansion and cyclicity give the real part of
$\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha,\nu,\mu}c_{\nu\mu}^{(\sigma_{E})}\big[{}$
$\displaystyle e^{-a_{\nu}}\operatorname{Tr}(\rho(A_{\nu}^{\alpha})^{\dagger}A_{\mu}^{\alpha}K_{\rho})-e^{-a_{\nu}}\operatorname{Tr}(A_{\mu}^{\alpha}\rho(A_{\nu}^{\alpha})^{\dagger}K_{\rho})$
$\displaystyle-e^{a_{\nu}}\operatorname{Tr}((A_{\nu}^{\alpha})^{\dagger}\rho A_{\mu}^{\alpha}K_{\rho})+e^{a_{\nu}}\operatorname{Tr}(A_{\mu}^{\alpha}(A_{\nu}^{\alpha})^{\dagger}\rho K_{\rho})\big].$
Reindexing the last two terms by (2.23), and writing
$p_{\nu\mu}:=\frac{e^{d_{\nu\mu}}}{2\cosh d_{\nu\mu}},$
use
$\displaystyle c_{\nu\mu}^{(\sigma_{E})}e^{-a_{\nu}}$
$\displaystyle=q_{\nu\mu}^{(\sigma_{E})}(1-p_{\nu\mu}),\ c_{\nu\mu}^{(\sigma_{E})}e^{-a_{\mu}}=q_{\nu\mu}^{(\sigma_{E})}p_{\nu\mu},\text{ and }c_{\nu\mu}^{(\sigma_{E})}(e^{-a_{\nu}}+e^{-a_{\mu}})=q_{\nu\mu}^{(\sigma_{E})}.$
to obtain
$\displaystyle\operatorname{Re}\sum_{\alpha,\nu,\mu}q_{\nu\mu}^{(\sigma_{E})}\big[{}$
$\displaystyle-\operatorname{Tr}(A_{\mu}^{\alpha}\rho(A_{\nu}^{\alpha})^{\dagger}K_{\rho})+p_{\nu\mu}\operatorname{Tr}((A_{\nu}^{\alpha})^{\dagger}A_{\mu}^{\alpha}\rho K_{\rho})$
$\displaystyle+(1-p_{\nu\mu})\operatorname{Tr}(\rho(A_{\nu}^{\alpha})^{\dagger}A_{\mu}^{\alpha}K_{\rho})\big],$
This is  $-\operatorname{Tr}(\mathcal{L}_{\sigma_{E}}(\rho)K_{\rho})$  by
(2.20).
∎
For a fixed frequency, spectral decomposition and the scalar inequality
$4(\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{x})^{2}\leq(y-x)(\log y-\log x)$  give
$4\|U_{\alpha,\nu}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\operatorname{Re}\langle W_{\alpha,\nu},V_{\alpha,\nu}\rangle.$
The diagonal estimates do not control the terms with  $\nu\neq\mu$  in
(2.21)–(2.22).
The following example shows that the Stroock–Varopoulos comparison
can fail even for a single self-adjoint bare jump.
Proposition 2.10.
For the filter (2.3), there exist a Hamiltonian  $H$ , a
self-adjoint bare jump  $A$ , and a faithful state  $\rho$  on  $\mathbb{C}^{2}$  such that
$\operatorname{EP}_{\mathcal{L}_{\sigma_{E}}}(\rho)<4\mathcal{E}_{\sigma_{E}}(\sqrt{\rho}),\qquad\sigma_{E}\in\{30,\infty\}.$
Proof.
Take
$H=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\
0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\
1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\beta=\frac{1}{4}.$
Set  $v=(2,-3)^{\mathsf{T}}/\sqrt{13}$  and
$\rho=\frac{1}{2000}I+\frac{999}{1000}|v\rangle\langle v|$ .
The eigenvalues of  $\rho$  are  $1/2000$  and  $1999/2000$ , so  $\rho$  is
faithful. The corresponding matrix functions are
$\sqrt{\rho}=\frac{I+(\sqrt{1999}-1)|v\rangle\langle v|}{\sqrt{2000}},\qquad\log\rho=-(\log 2000)I+(\log 1999)|v\rangle\langle v|.$
Substitution into
(2.21)–(2.22) gives
$\operatorname{EP}_{\mathcal{L}_{\infty}}(\rho)<\frac{9}{1000}<4\mathcal{E}_{\infty}(\sqrt{\rho}),\qquad\operatorname{EP}_{\mathcal{L}_{30}}(\rho)<\frac{1}{100}<4\mathcal{E}_{30}(\sqrt{\rho}).$
This proves both assertions.
For  $\sigma_{E}=\infty$ , the filtered jump is
$L^{1}=\begin{pmatrix}\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(0)&\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(-1)\\
\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(1)&0\end{pmatrix}.$
Here the filter values are
$\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(0)=e^{-1/4},\qquad\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(\pm 1)=e^{-(\sqrt{17}\pm 1)/16},\qquad\langle 0|[L^{1},(L^{1})^{\dagger}]|0\rangle=\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(-1)^{2}-\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(1)^{2}>0.$
Thus  $L^{1}$  is non-normal. Every proper unital  $*$ -subalgebra of
$M_{2}(\mathbb{C})$  is commutative and contains only normal matrices.
Consequently  $L^{1}$  and  $(L^{1})^{\dagger}$  generate  $M_{2}(\mathbb{C})$ , proving
irreducibility.
∎
2.6.2. Unbounded Davies generators
We give conditions under which finite-dimensional Davies comparisons
pass to the infinite-dimensional generator.
An unweighted sum over energy pairs diverges already on the diagonal,
since  $|\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(0)|^{2}=e^{-1/2}$ . We must instead sum the transition blocks with their Gibbs
weights. The result below gives sufficient approximation conditions;
these must be checked for each model.
Assume now that  $H$  has pure point spectrum with finite multiplicities,
$Z_{\beta}<\infty$ , and  $P_{E}\mathcal{H}\subset D(A^{\alpha})$  for all  $E,\alpha$ .
The component  $A_{\nu}^{\alpha}$  is initially defined on
$\mathcal{D}_{\rm fin}(H):=\operatorname{span}\{P_{E}\mathcal{H}:E\in\operatorname{Sp}(H)\}$
by the same transition-block formula. In the following expressions,
products with states are understood through their Hilbert–Schmidt
extensions whenever these exist. Write  $A$  for the whole family
$(A^{\alpha})_{\alpha\in\mathcal{A}}$ , and define its Gibbs-weighted transition
activity by
(2.24)
$\mathfrak{J}_{\widehat{f}}(H,A):=\frac{1}{Z_{\beta}}\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal{A}}\sum_{E,E^{\prime}\in\operatorname{Sp}(H)}e^{-\beta E}|\widehat{f}(E^{\prime}-E)|^{2}\|P_{E^{\prime}}A^{\alpha}P_{E}\|_{2}^{2}.$
Assume  $\mathfrak{J}_{\widehat{f}}(H,A)<\infty$ . For a state satisfying
$\Gamma^{-1}\sigma_{\beta}\leq\rho\leq\Gamma\sigma_{\beta}$ , the expressions
$U_{\alpha,\nu}$  from Lemma 2.9 have Hilbert–Schmidt
extensions whenever  $\widehat{f}(\nu)\neq 0$ , and obey the following bound,
with zero-weight frequencies omitted:
$\sum_{\alpha,\nu}e^{\beta\nu/2}|\widehat{f}(\nu)|^{2}\|U_{\alpha,\nu}\|_{2}^{2}\leq 4\Gamma\,\mathfrak{J}_{\widehat{f}}(H,A).$
Indeed,  $\rho\leq\Gamma\sigma_{\beta}$  gives, first on spectral cutoffs,
$\|A_{\nu}^{\alpha}\sqrt{\rho}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\Gamma\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_{\beta}(A_{\nu}^{\alpha})^{\dagger}A_{\nu}^{\alpha}),\qquad\|\sqrt{\rho}A_{\nu}^{\alpha}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\Gamma\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_{\beta}A_{\nu}^{\alpha}(A_{\nu}^{\alpha})^{\dagger}).$
The transition-block decomposition yields
$\displaystyle\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_{\beta}(A_{\nu}^{\alpha})^{\dagger}A_{\nu}^{\alpha})$
$\displaystyle=Z_{\beta}^{-1}\sum_{E^{\prime}-E=\nu}e^{-\beta E}\|P_{E^{\prime}}A^{\alpha}P_{E}\|_{2}^{2},$
$\displaystyle\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_{\beta}A_{\nu}^{\alpha}(A_{\nu}^{\alpha})^{\dagger})$
$\displaystyle=e^{-\beta\nu}\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_{\beta}(A_{\nu}^{\alpha})^{\dagger}A_{\nu}^{\alpha}).$
Consequently the two terms defining  $U_{\alpha,\nu}$  satisfy
$\displaystyle e^{\beta\nu/2}|\widehat{f}(\nu)|^{2}\|U_{\alpha,\nu}\|_{2}^{2}$
$\displaystyle\leq 2|\widehat{f}(\nu)|^{2}\bigl(\|A_{\nu}^{\alpha}\sqrt{\rho}\|_{2}^{2}+e^{\beta\nu}\|\sqrt{\rho}A_{\nu}^{\alpha}\|_{2}^{2}\bigr)$
$\displaystyle\leq 4\Gamma|\widehat{f}(\nu)|^{2}\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_{\beta}(A_{\nu}^{\alpha})^{\dagger}A_{\nu}^{\alpha}).$
Summing proves the activity bound and the existence of the
Hilbert–Schmidt extensions. This controls the Dirichlet form.
The logarithmic term needs a separate estimate.
Definition 2.11.
Let  $P_{n}$  be increasing finite-rank spectral projections of  $H$  that
converge strongly to  $I$ .
For  $\rho\in D(\mathcal{L}_{0})\cap B(\sigma_{\beta})$ , use  $K_{\rho}$  as in
Lemma 2.9. Discard any initial indices with
$\operatorname{Tr}(P_{n}\rho)=0$  and set
$\sigma_{n}=\frac{P_{n}\sigma_{\beta}P_{n}}{\operatorname{Tr}(P_{n}\sigma_{\beta})},\qquad\rho_{n}=\frac{P_{n}\rho P_{n}}{\operatorname{Tr}(P_{n}\rho)},\qquad K_{n}=\log\rho_{n}-\log\sigma_{n}$
on  $P_{n}\mathcal{H}$ . Let  $\mathcal{L}_{n}$  be the finite-dimensional Davies generator
obtained by keeping the transitions whose initial and final energy
spaces both lie in  $P_{n}\mathcal{H}$ . Write  $\mathcal{E}_{n}$  for its standard-form Dirichlet form
and take  $\operatorname{EP}_{\mathcal{L}_{n}}$  relative to  $\sigma_{n}$ . Extend the matrices
$\rho_{n},\sigma_{n}$  and their square roots by zero to  $\mathcal{H}$  when
comparing different  $n$ . We interpret a closed Dirichlet form as
$+\infty$  outside its domain. The exhaustion is
SV-admissible for  $\rho$  if
(2.25)
$\displaystyle\sqrt{\rho_{n}}\longrightarrow\sqrt{\rho}\quad\text{in }\mathscr{T}_{2}(\mathcal{H}),\qquad\mathcal{E}_{0}(\sqrt{\rho})\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mathcal{E}_{n}(\sqrt{\rho_{n}}),$
(2.26)
$\displaystyle\sup_{n}\|K_{n}\|_{\infty}<\infty,\qquad P_{n}K_{n}P_{n}\longrightarrow K_{\rho}\quad\text{strongly},$
(2.27)
$\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{n}(\rho_{n})\longrightarrow\mathcal{L}_{0}(\rho)\quad\text{in trace norm}.$
Here  $K_{n}$  is extended by zero on  $(P_{n}\mathcal{H})^{\perp}$ . The exhaustion is SV-admissible on a class of states if these conditions hold for every state in that class.
Uniform boundedness and strong convergence of  $K_{n}$ , together with
trace-norm generator convergence, imply
(2.28)
$\operatorname{EP}_{\mathcal{L}_{n}}(\rho_{n})=-\operatorname{Tr}(\mathcal{L}_{n}(\rho_{n})K_{n})\longrightarrow-\operatorname{Tr}(\mathcal{L}_{0}(\rho)K_{\rho})=\operatorname{EP}_{\mathcal{L}_{0}}(\rho).$
To check the passage to the limit, extend  $K_{n}$  by zero as above
and subtract the two trace pairings:
$\displaystyle|\operatorname{Tr}(\mathcal{L}_{n}(\rho_{n})K_{n})-\operatorname{Tr}(\mathcal{L}_{0}(\rho)K_{\rho})|\leq{}$
$\displaystyle\|\mathcal{L}_{n}(\rho_{n})-\mathcal{L}_{0}(\rho)\|_{1}\|K_{n}\|_{\infty}$
$\displaystyle+|\operatorname{Tr}(\mathcal{L}_{0}(\rho)(K_{n}-K_{\rho}))|\longrightarrow 0.$
The first term vanishes by (2.27).
For the second, approximate  $\mathcal{L}_{0}(\rho)$  in trace norm by a
finite-rank operator. Strong convergence handles that finite-rank
pairing, and the uniform bound on  $K_{n}$  controls the approximation error.
Theorem 2.12.
Suppose that an SV-admissible exhaustion exists on
$D(\mathcal{L}_{0})\cap B(\sigma_{\beta})$ . Then the Stroock–Varopoulos hypothesis (2.6) of Theorem 1.1 holds on this class. Consequently, Theorem 1.1 applies whenever its remaining hypotheses—the identification (2.4), positive contractions on the weighted spaces, the bound (1.1), and a positive gap when  $C>1$ —are satisfied.
Proof.
By Proposition 2.8,
$4\mathcal{E}_{n}(\sqrt{\rho_{n}})\leq\operatorname{EP}_{\mathcal{L}_{n}}(\rho_{n})$ . Taking lower limits and using
(2.25) and (2.28) gives
$4\mathcal{E}_{0}(\sqrt{\rho})\leq 4\liminf_{n}\mathcal{E}_{n}(\sqrt{\rho_{n}})\leq\lim_{n}\operatorname{EP}_{\mathcal{L}_{n}}(\rho_{n})=\operatorname{EP}_{\mathcal{L}_{0}}(\rho)<\infty.$
Finiteness follows because  $\mathcal{L}_{0}(\rho)$  is trace class and
$K_{\rho}$  is bounded. Since the closed form is interpreted as
$+\infty$  outside its domain, the same inequality proves
$\sqrt{\rho}\in D(\mathcal{E}_{0})$  as well as the SV bound.
∎
Corollary 2.13.
For a primitive finite-dimensional Davies generator,
Proposition 2.8 proves the SV inequality. Hence Theorem 1.1
applies if the weighted extensions are positive contractions, satisfy
(2.4), and obey (1.1). The same conclusion
holds in infinite dimension under Definition 2.11.
Proof of Theorem 1.1.
Combining (2.11) and the assumed inequality (2.6) gives
$\frac{4}{c_{\rm LS}}D(\rho\|\sigma)\leq 4\mathcal{E}(\sqrt{\rho})\leq\operatorname{EP}_{\mathcal{L}}(\rho).$
This holds on  $D(\mathcal{L})\cap B(\sigma)$ : the SV assumption places  $\sqrt{\rho}$  in the form domain and gives
the last inequality. Thus Lemma 2.2 applies with
$\alpha_{\rm HC}=\frac{4}{c_{\rm LS}}=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\left(s+\frac{\log C+1/2}{\lambda}\right)^{-1},&C>1,\\[4.0pt]
s^{-1},&C=1.\end{cases}$
Under (2.5), fix its constant  $C_{2,4}$  and apply the
estimate at each  $s>\tau_{2,4}$ . For finite input entropy the
right-hand side is continuous in  $s$ , so letting
$s\downarrow\tau_{2,4}$  gives the corresponding limiting rate.
Infinite input entropy requires no limit argument.
∎
3. Perturbative hypercontractivity
We prove two stability results. With the Gibbs weight fixed, a
product formula controls changes of the generator that are bounded
along a hypercontractive curve. When the weight changes on a finite
energy subspace, entropy and form comparisons preserve a tight
logarithmic Sobolev inequality, provided the new generator has a
positive gap.
3.1. Interpolation and bounded perturbations
We transfer bounds along a hypercontractive curve under perturbations
that are bounded on each weighted space along the curve.
We use weighted Stein interpolation
[22, 17] in the form established
in Step 2 of Theorem 2.3; a weighted three-lines theorem is
[23, Theorem 2.10]. For a KMS-symmetric
semigroup as in Section 2, an endpoint
$\|T_{\tau}:L^{2}(\sigma)\to L^{q}(\sigma)\|\leq C$  with
$\tau>0$  and  $2<q<\infty$  gives
$\|T_{t}:L^{2}(\sigma)\to L^{q(t)}(\sigma)\|\leq C^{t/\tau},\qquad\frac{1}{q(t)}=\frac{1-t/\tau}{2}+\frac{t/\tau}{q},\quad 0\leq t\leq\tau.$
The next theorem assumes a bound between every two points on
the exponent curve. It is related to the Holley–Stroock
principles of [1, 12].
For the bounded perturbation theorem and the Trotter product formula
on a fixed Banach space, see
[27, Theorem III.1.3 and Corollary III.5.8].
Theorem 3.1.
Let  $\sigma$  be a faithful density matrix, fix  $t_{*}>0$  and
$2\leq p_{*}<\infty$ , and let  $T_{t}^{(r)}$  and  $S_{t}^{(r)}$  be strongly
continuous, consistent semigroups on  $L^{r}(\sigma)$  for
$2\leq r\leq p_{*}$ . Fix  $\omega\in\mathbb{R}$  and a continuous
nondecreasing exponent curve  $p:[0,t_{*}]\to[2,p_{*}]$  with  $p(0)=2$ .
Suppose that
$\|T_{t-s}:L^{p(s)}(\sigma)\to L^{p(t)}(\sigma)\|\leq e^{\omega(t-s)},\qquad 0\leq s\leq t\leq t_{*}.$
Let  $\mathscr{C}$  be a common dense subspace of
$\bigcap_{2\leq r\leq p_{*}}L^{r}(\sigma)$  on which the realizations of
the semigroups agree. One may take  $B(\mathcal{H})$  when all maps are
initially defined there. Let  $\mathcal{V}$  be a linear map with bounded
realizations  $\mathcal{V}^{(r)}:L^{r}(\sigma)\to L^{r}(\sigma)$  that
agree on  $\mathscr{C}$ . We assume that adding  $\mathcal{V}$  to the
generator of  $T_{t}$  generates the semigroup  $S_{t}$ , in the precise sense
that, for  $0\leq t\leq t_{*}$ , the following  $L^{2}$  Trotter formula holds:
$S_{t}^{(2)}=\operatorname*{s-lim}_{n\to\infty}\bigl(T_{t/n}^{(2)}e^{(t/n)\mathcal{V}^{(2)}}\bigr)^{n}.$
Here  $\operatorname*{s-lim}$  denotes convergence on each vector of
$L^{2}(\sigma)$  in its norm. Assume that the perturbation bound
$M_{t_{*}}:=\sup_{2\leq r\leq p(t_{*})}\|\mathcal{V}^{(r)}:L^{r}(\sigma)\to L^{r}(\sigma)\|$
is finite.
Then, for  $0\leq s\leq t\leq t_{*}$ ,
(3.1)
$\|S_{t-s}:L^{p(s)}(\sigma)\to L^{p(t)}(\sigma)\|\leq e^{(\omega+M_{t_{*}})(t-s)}.$
In particular,
$\|S_{t}:L^{2}(\sigma)\to L^{p(t)}(\sigma)\|\leq e^{(\omega+M_{t_{*}})t}$ . If the reverse Trotter formula holds with
$T$  and  $S$  interchanged and perturbation  $-\mathcal{V}$ , the same
statement transfers a curve from  $S$  back to  $T$ .
Proof.
Fix  $0\leq s<t\leq t_{*}$  and a positive integer  $n$ . Put
$h=(t-s)/n$  and  $s_{k}=s+kh$ . For  $X\in\mathscr{C}$ , define
$X_{0,n}=X,\qquad X_{k,n}=T_{h}e^{h\mathcal{V}}X_{k-1,n}\quad(1\leq k\leq n).$
The products agree wherever two of the weighted spaces overlap,
by consistency. The exponential series gives
$\|e^{h\mathcal{V}^{(p(s_{k-1}))}}\|\leq\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{h^{j}M_{t_{*}}^{j}}{j!}=e^{hM_{t_{*}}}.$
Apply the assumed two-time bound to the other factor. At the  $k$ th step,
$\|X_{k,n}\|_{p(s_{k}),\sigma}\leq e^{\omega h}\|e^{h\mathcal{V}}X_{k-1,n}\|_{p(s_{k-1}),\sigma}\leq e^{(\omega+M_{t_{*}})h}\|X_{k-1,n}\|_{p(s_{k-1}),\sigma}.$
Iteration yields a bound independent of  $n$ :
$\|X_{n,n}\|_{p(t),\sigma}\leq e^{(\omega+M_{t_{*}})(t-s)}\|X\|_{p(s),\sigma}.$
We now pass to the limit in  $L^{p(t)}(\sigma)$ . For  $2\leq q<\infty$ ,
Hölder’s inequality and  $\operatorname{Tr}\sigma=1$  give the continuous inclusion
$L^{q}(\sigma)\subset L^{2}(\sigma)$ :
$\|X\|_{2,\sigma}=\|\sigma^{1/4-1/(2q)}\iota_{q,\sigma}(X)\sigma^{1/4-1/(2q)}\|_{2}\leq\|X\|_{q,\sigma}.$
The bounded sequence  $(X_{n,n})_{n}$  has a weakly convergent subsequence
in the reflexive space  $L^{p(t)}(\sigma)$ , say with limit  $Y$ .
The same subsequence converges weakly to  $Y$  in  $L^{2}(\sigma)$ .
The Trotter formula also gives
