$X_{n,n}=(T_{h}e^{h\mathcal{V}})^{n}X\longrightarrow S_{t-s}^{(2)}X\quad\hbox{in }L^{2}(\sigma).$
Uniqueness of the weak limit therefore gives  $Y=S_{t-s}X$ .
Weak lower semicontinuity now proves
$\|S_{t-s}X\|_{p(t),\sigma}\leq\liminf_{j}\|X_{n_{j},n_{j}}\|_{p(t),\sigma}\leq e^{(\omega+M_{t_{*}})(t-s)}\|X\|_{p(s),\sigma}.$
By density of  $\mathscr{C}$ , this bound holds on all of
$L^{p(s)}(\sigma)$ . Consistency identifies the limit with  $S_{t-s}$ .
For  $s=t$  the bound is the identity estimate. Replacing
$\mathcal{V}$  by  $-\mathcal{V}$  proves the reverse statement whenever
the reverse product formula holds.
∎
3.2. Finite-core changes of the Gibbs weight
We now allow the Gibbs weight to change on a finite-dimensional
energy subspace and compare the resulting entropies and Dirichlet forms.
Lemma 3.2.
Let  $\sigma_{0}$  and  $\sigma$  be faithful density matrices on  $\mathcal{H}$ .
Assume that  $P$  is a finite-rank orthogonal projection satisfying
$P\sigma_{0}=\sigma_{0}P$  and  $P\sigma=\sigma P$ . Set  $Q=I-P$  and suppose that
$Q\sigma Q=c\,Q\sigma_{0}Q$
for a scalar  $c>0$ . Then there is a constant  $0\leq\kappa<\infty$
such that, for every Hilbert–Schmidt operator
$Y\in\mathscr{T}_{2}(\mathcal{H})$  with finite  $\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma_{0}}(Y)$ ,
(3.2)
$\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Y)\leq\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma_{0}}(Y)+\kappa\|Y\|_{2}^{2}.$
Proof.
The quadratic-form difference  $K=\log\sigma_{0}-\log\sigma$  has a
bounded self-adjoint extension. Indeed, block functional calculus gives
$K=P(\log\sigma_{0}-\log\sigma)P-(\log c)Q,\qquad\|K\|_{\infty}\leq\max\{\|P(\log\sigma_{0}-\log\sigma)P\|_{\infty},|\log c|\}<\infty.$
The  $P$ -block is finite dimensional and both compressed states are
strictly positive there. Since the difference of the reference logarithms is bounded,
relative entropy satisfies, whenever  $D(\rho\|\sigma_{0})<\infty$ ,
$D(\rho\|\sigma)=D(\rho\|\sigma_{0})+\operatorname{Tr}(\rho K).$
This identity holds also when the individual energy and von Neumann
entropy traces are infinite, by bounded perturbation of the reference
logarithm in the extended relative-entropy definition;
see [21, Appendix B.1] for bounded relative Hamiltonians.
Apply it to  $Y^{\dagger}Y/\|Y\|_{2}^{2}$  and  $YY^{\dagger}/\|Y\|_{2}^{2}$
in the explicit relative-entropy formula for  $\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}$ .
For  $Y\neq 0$  this gives
$\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Y)-\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma_{0}}(Y)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Tr}\bigl((Y^{\dagger}Y+YY^{\dagger})K\bigr)\leq\|K\|_{\infty}\|Y\|_{2}^{2}.$
For  $Y=0$  the claim is immediate. Thus one may take
$\kappa=\|\log\sigma_{0}-\log\sigma\|_{\infty}$ .
∎
Proposition 3.3.
Let  $T_{t}^{0}$  and  $T_{t}$  be primitive KMS-symmetric Markov semigroups with
faithful invariant states  $\sigma_{0}$  and  $\sigma$ , and let
$L_{0},L\geq 0$  be their standard-form generators with closed forms
$\mathcal{E}_{0},\mathcal{E}$  on  $\mathscr{T}_{2}(\mathcal{H})$ .
Assume the finite-core relation of Lemma 3.2,
and choose its comparison constant  $\kappa\geq 0$ . Suppose that,
for some finite  $c_{0}>0$ ,
$\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma_{0}}(Y)\leq c_{0}\mathcal{E}_{0}(Y),\qquad Y\in D(\mathcal{E}_{0}).$
Assume also that  $D(\mathcal{E})\subset D(\mathcal{E}_{0})$  and that there are finite
constants  $A>0$  and  $B\geq 0$  such that
(3.3)
$\mathcal{E}_{0}(Y)\leq A\mathcal{E}(Y)+B\|Y\|_{2}^{2},\qquad Y\in D(\mathcal{E}).$
If  $L$  has gap  $\lambda>0$ , define
$c_{\rm fc}=c_{0}A+(c_{0}B+\kappa+2)/\lambda$ . Then
(3.4)
$\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Y)\leq c_{\rm fc}\mathcal{E}(Y),\qquad Y\in D(\mathcal{E}).$
This conclusion concerns the  $2$ -logarithmic Sobolev inequality.
We do not deduce a hypercontractive bound from these assumptions.
Proof.
Fix  $X\in D(\mathcal{E})$  and define its centred vector by
$Y=X-\langle\sqrt{\sigma},X\rangle\sqrt{\sigma}$ .
Since  $\sqrt{\sigma}\in\ker L$ , both  $X$  and  $Y$  belong to
$D(\mathcal{E})\subset D(\mathcal{E}_{0})$ . The free logarithmic Sobolev
inequality and Lemma 3.2 first give
$\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Y)\leq\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma_{0}}(Y)+\kappa\|Y\|_{2}^{2}\leq c_{0}\mathcal{E}_{0}(Y)+\kappa\|Y\|_{2}^{2}<\infty.$
Thus Lemma 2.4 applies to  $Y$  without an
endpoint assumption. Combining it with (3.3) gives
$\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(X)\leq\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Y)+2\|Y\|_{2}^{2}\leq c_{0}A\mathcal{E}(X)+(c_{0}B+\kappa+2)\|Y\|_{2}^{2}.$
The centering does not change the energy, and the gap controls its norm:
$L^{1/2}Y=L^{1/2}X,\qquad\lambda\|Y\|_{2}^{2}\leq\|L^{1/2}Y\|_{2}^{2}=\mathcal{E}(X).$
Substitution removes the squared-norm term:
$\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(X)\leq\left(c_{0}A+\frac{c_{0}B+\kappa+2}{\lambda}\right)\mathcal{E}(X)=c_{\rm fc}\mathcal{E}(X).$
To deduce hypercontractivity from a logarithmic Sobolev inequality,
one needs regularity of the  $L^{p}$  Dirichlet forms
[8, 9].
We prove an  $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{4}$  bound directly for the Coulomb sampler
in Section 4.2.
∎
4. Applications and obstructions
We apply the entropy-decay criteria to bosonic Gibbs samplers and
examine how the jump operators affect hypercontractivity. We classify one-mode polynomial jumps by their order and then
treat Bose–Hubbard models with hopping. For finite-rank Coulomb
perturbations, we use a weighted oscillator estimate. A periodic charging
model then shows that a positive spectral gap can coexist with failure
of every  $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{p}$  endpoint with  $p>2$ .
4.1. Polynomial jumps and multimode Bose–Hubbard models
We first compare the growth of a one-mode number Hamiltonian with the
order of the bosonic jumps. This gives a classification of the
hypercontractive endpoints and explains why cubic jumps suffice for
quadratic number Hamiltonians. We then prove exponential entropy
decay for a full multimode Bose–Hubbard sampler with hopping and
repulsive density interactions in Theorem 4.3.
Entropy decay for quantum Ornstein–Uhlenbeck semigroups, with
Hamiltonians quadratic in the creation and annihilation operators,
is well understood; see, for example,
[28, 29, 30].
Here the Hamiltonian is a nonlinear polynomial of the number operator,
and the filtered transition rates depend strongly on occupation number.
We use the bosonic operators of Section 2.1 on the
one-mode space  $\mathcal{H}=\ell^{2}(\mathbb{N}_{0})$ , omitting their mode index.
Let  $H=h(N)$ , where  $h$  is a real polynomial of degree  $m\geq 2$  with
positive leading coefficient, and fix  $\beta>0$ . The occupation number
is denoted by  $n$ , and  $Z_{\beta}=\sum_{n\geq 0}e^{-\beta h(n)}$ .
A jump of order  $d\geq 1$  creates or annihilates  $d$  particles; we use the
adjoint pair  $\mathcal{A}_{d}=\{a^{d},(a^{\dagger})^{d}\}$ . Choose a finite nonempty set  $D\subset\{1,2,\ldots\}$  of jump orders,
put  $d_{*}:=\max D$ , and take the bare family
$\mathcal{A}_{D}:=\bigcup_{d\in D}\mathcal{A}_{d}$ .
The set  $D$  is unrelated to the relative entropy  $D(\rho\|\sigma)$ .
Theorem 4.2 gives three regimes: no hypercontractive
endpoint when  $d_{*}<m$ , a positive waiting time when  $d_{*}=m$ , and an
endpoint at every positive time when  $d_{*}>m$ . When  $d_{*}=m$ , the theorem gives the threshold but excludes
the boundary time from its statement.
The proof compares the growth of the Gibbs weight, governed by
$h(n)$ , with the diagonal damping of order  $n^{d_{*}}$ . The remaining terms
are uniformly bounded over compact intervals of finite exponents and
can be treated by Theorem 3.1. A no-jump lower
bound in the invariant diagonal sector gives the converse estimates.
Separating the diagonal loss.
We first work with one jump pair and identify the unbounded part of
its generator. We first prove the matrix formulas on the
finite-rank core  $\operatorname{span}\{E_{nk}:n,k\geq 0\}$ , where
$E_{nk}=|n\rangle\langle k|$ .
For the filter (2.3), the dressed creation and annihilation
jumps are denoted by
$L_{d}^{+}$  and  $L_{d}^{-}$ , respectively:
$L_{d}^{+}=(a^{\dagger})^{d}\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(h(N+d)-h(N)),\qquad L_{d}^{-}=a^{d}\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(h(N-d)-h(N)).$
Put
$\Delta_{d}^{+}h(n)=h(n+d)-h(n),\qquad\Delta_{d}^{-}h(n)=h(n-d)-h(n),$
Here  $h(n-d)$  means evaluation of the polynomial at the integer
$n-d$ . For  $n<d$ , the lowering jump is zero, so no transition to
a negative occupation occurs. Every falling factorial below
is defined to be zero when  $n<d$ .
To use the perturbation theorem, we need bounds on the weighted
generator. Conjugation changes the gain operators and leaves the
diagonal losses unchanged. On the symmetric Schatten realization of
$L^{p}(\sigma_{\beta})$ , for  $2\leq p<\infty$  define
$g_{d,\pm,p}(n)=\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(\Delta_{d}^{\pm}h(n))e^{\beta(p-1)\Delta_{d}^{\pm}h(n)/(2p)}=\exp\left[-\frac{\sqrt{1+(\beta\Delta_{d}^{\pm}h(n))^{2}}}{4}+\frac{(p-2)\beta\Delta_{d}^{\pm}h(n)}{4p}\right]$
and
$\displaystyle B_{d,+,p}$
$\displaystyle=(a^{\dagger})^{d}g_{d,+,p}(N),$
$\displaystyle B_{d,-,p}$
$\displaystyle=a^{d}g_{d,-,p}(N),$
$\displaystyle b_{d,+}(N)$
$\displaystyle=\prod_{j=1}^{d}(N+j)|\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(\Delta_{d}^{+}h(N))|^{2},$
$\displaystyle b_{d,-}(N)$
$\displaystyle=\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}(N-j)|\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(\Delta_{d}^{-}h(N))|^{2}.$
The symbols  $B_{d,\pm,p}$  denote the transported Heisenberg gain
operators, and  $b_{d,\pm}(N)$  denote the diagonal loss operators.
Indeed, transport of the gain  $L^{\dagger}XL$  gives
$\sigma_{\beta}^{1/(2p)}L^{\dagger}\sigma_{\beta}^{-1/(2p)}$ .
Relabelling the adjoint pair and using the KMS relation gives the
factor  $(p-1)/(2p)$  above. In particular the transported generator
annihilates  $\sigma_{\beta}^{1/p}$ , the vector representing  $I$ . The weighted
generator of the  $d$ th jump pair, acting on its symmetric Schatten
realization, is
$\mathscr{L}_{p,h,d}(X)=B_{d,+,p}XB_{d,+,p}^{\dagger}+B_{d,-,p}XB_{d,-,p}^{\dagger}-\frac{1}{2}\{b_{d,+}(N)+b_{d,-}(N),X\}.$
The next lemma bounds the gains and the upward loss. The downward
loss is the only unbounded part of the reference generator.
For nonnegative sequences  $(u_{n})$  and  $(v_{n})$  in this subsection,
$u_{n}\lesssim v_{n}$  means  $u_{n}\leq Cv_{n}$  for all
sufficiently large  $n$ , with a constant  $C$  independent of  $n$ ;
$u_{n}\gtrsim v_{n}$  means  $v_{n}\lesssim u_{n}$ , and  $u_{n}\asymp v_{n}$  means
both inequalities. For a linear map  $\mathscr{V}$  on  $\mathscr{T}_{p}(\mathcal{H})$ ,
write  $\|\mathscr{V}\|_{p\to p}$  for its Schatten- $p$  operator norm.
Lemma 4.1.
For every  $2\leq p_{*}<\infty$ , the operators  $B_{d,\pm,p}$  and
$b_{d,+}(N)$  are bounded uniformly for  $2\leq p\leq p_{*}$ . Hence
$\mathscr{V}_{d,p}(X):=B_{d,+,p}XB_{d,+,p}^{\dagger}+B_{d,-,p}XB_{d,-,p}^{\dagger}-\frac{1}{2}\{b_{d,+}(N),X\}$
satisfies
(4.1)
$\sup_{2\leq p\leq p_{*}}\|\mathscr{V}_{d,p}\|_{p\to p}<\infty.$
Proof.
For  $x=\beta\Delta_{d}^{\pm}h(n)$  and  $2\leq p\leq p_{*}$ ,
$|g_{d,\pm,p}(n)|\leq e^{-|x|/(2p_{*})}.$
For  $x\geq 0$  the exponent is at most  $-x/(2p)$ .
For  $x<0$  it is at most  $-(p-1)|x|/(2p)\leq-|x|/(2p_{*})$ .
The polynomial expansion gives
$\Delta_{d}^{+}h(n)=ma_{m}d\,n^{m-1}+O(n^{m-2}),\qquad\Delta_{d}^{-}h(n)=-ma_{m}d\,n^{m-1}+O(n^{m-2}),$
where  $a_{m}>0$  is the leading coefficient. Thus, for all sufficiently
large  $n$ ,  $|\Delta_{d}^{\pm}h(n)|\geq c_{d}n^{m-1}$  and
$\Delta_{d}^{+}h(n)\geq c_{d}n^{m-1}$ . This exponential decay dominates
the polynomial ladder coefficients. For the positive increment,
put  $x=\beta\Delta_{d}^{+}h(n)$ ; then
$|\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(\Delta_{d}^{+}h(n))|^{2}=e^{-(\sqrt{1+x^{2}}+x)/2}\leq e^{-x},$
so  $b_{d,+}(n)\lesssim n^{d}e^{-cn^{m-1}}$  for some  $c>0$ .
In particular,
$\|B_{d,\pm,p}\|_{\infty}\leq C\sup_{n\geq 0}(1+n)^{d/2}e^{-cn^{m-1}/p_{*}}<\infty.$
The ideal property and the anticommutator bound now give
$\|\mathscr{V}_{d,p}\|_{p\to p}\leq\|B_{d,+,p}\|_{\infty}^{2}+\|B_{d,-,p}\|_{\infty}^{2}+\|b_{d,+}(N)\|_{\infty},$
uniformly for  $2\leq p\leq p_{*}$ .
∎
Combining the jump orders.
We now sum the generators over  $d\in D$  and include all downward
losses in one diagonal operator. This separates the unbounded part, so
Theorem 3.1 applies to the full family. Set
(4.2)
$\displaystyle A_{D}(N)$
$\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{d\in D}b_{d,-}(N),$
$\displaystyle\mathscr{A}_{D}(X)$
$\displaystyle:=-(A_{D}(N)X+XA_{D}(N)),$
(4.3)
$\displaystyle\mathscr{V}_{D,p}$
$\displaystyle:=\sum_{d\in D}\mathscr{V}_{d,p},$
$\displaystyle\mathscr{L}_{p,h,D}$
$\displaystyle=\mathscr{A}_{D}+\mathscr{V}_{D,p}.$
Here  $\mathscr{L}_{p,h,D}=\sum_{d\in D}\mathscr{L}_{p,h,d}$ .
By Lemma 4.1,
$M_{D,p_{*}}:=\sup_{2\leq p\leq p_{*}}\|\mathscr{V}_{D,p}\|_{p\to p}<\infty.$
The diagonal loss satisfies
(4.4)
$A_{D}(n)\asymp n^{d_{*}},$
because for each fixed  $d$ ,
$\frac{b_{d,-}(n)}{n^{d}}=\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}\left(1-\frac{j}{n}\right)|\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(\Delta_{d}^{-}h(n))|^{2}\longrightarrow 1,\qquad\frac{2A_{D}(n)}{n^{d_{*}}}\longrightarrow 1.$
Thus the largest jump order determines the damping at large
occupation. The estimate (4.4) concerns
large  $n$  only; lowering jumps can vanish at small occupations.
The diagonal semigroup is
$T_{t}^{D}(X)=e^{-tA_{D}(N)}Xe^{-tA_{D}(N)}.$
Its gain in integrability is measured by the following estimate,
which reduces the weighted norm bound to a scalar supremum: for
$2\leq r\leq q<\infty$ ,
(4.5)
$\|T_{t}^{D}:L^{r}(\sigma_{\beta})\to L^{q}(\sigma_{\beta})\|\leq Z_{\beta}^{1/r-1/q}\sup_{n\geq 0}\exp\!\left[\beta(1/r-1/q)h(n)-2tA_{D}(n)\right].$
Indeed, if  $X\in L^{r}(\sigma_{\beta})$  and
$Y=\iota_{r,\sigma_{\beta}}(X)\in\mathscr{T}_{r}(\mathcal{H})$ , the transported
output is  $K_{t,r,q}YK_{t,r,q}$ , where
$K_{t,r,q}=e^{-tA_{D}(N)}\sigma_{\beta}^{1/(2q)-1/(2r)}.$
The estimate follows from
$\|K_{t,r,q}YK_{t,r,q}\|_{q}\leq\|K_{t,r,q}\|_{\infty}^{2}\|Y\|_{r}$ .
The positive term in the exponent of (4.5)
is the cost of changing the Gibbs weight from  $L^{r}$  to  $L^{q}$ ; the
negative term is the damping supplied by the jumps. Comparing their
growth gives the three cases above.
Classification and entropy decay.
We pass from the diagonal estimate to the full sampler, then use
the gap criterion of Theorem 1.2 to deduce entropy decay.
Write  $S_{t}^{D}$  for the consistent weighted semigroup whose Schatten
realizations satisfy
$\iota_{p,\sigma_{\beta}}S_{t}^{D}\iota_{p,\sigma_{\beta}}^{-1}=e^{t\mathscr{L}_{p,h,D}}.$
Let  $\Phi_{t}^{D}$  be its Schrödinger-picture semigroup on trace-class
operators.
Theorem 4.2.
Let  $h$  be a real polynomial of degree  $m\geq 2$  with positive leading
coefficient, let  $D\subset\{1,2,\ldots\}$  be finite and nonempty, and put
$d_{*}=\max D$ . For the sampler with bare jumps  $\mathcal{A}_{D}$  and filter
(2.3), the following statements hold.
(1)
If  $m>d_{*}$ , the sampler has no bounded  $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{4}$  map at any finite
positive time.
(2)
If  $m=d_{*}$  and  $a_{m}>0$  is the leading coefficient of  $h$ ,
then, for every  $p>2$ , the sampler is bounded
$L^{2}(\sigma_{\beta})\to L^{p}(\sigma_{\beta})$  for
(4.6)
$t>\beta a_{m}(1/2-1/p),$
and unbounded between these spaces for
$0<t<\beta a_{m}(1/2-1/p)$ .
The boundary time is excluded from this statement.
(3)
If  $m<d_{*}$ , it is bounded  $L^{2}(\sigma_{\beta})\to L^{p}(\sigma_{\beta})$  for every  $p>2$  and every  $t>0$ .
Quantitative bound. Fix a slope  $\delta>0$  and define
$p_{\delta}(u)=(1/2-\delta u)^{-1},\qquad 0\leq u<(2\delta)^{-1}.$
For every time  $s\in(0,(2\delta)^{-1})$ , define
$\omega_{D,\delta,s}:=\max\!\left\{0,\,\delta\log Z_{\beta}+\sup_{n\geq 0}\{\beta\delta h(n)-2A_{D}(n)\}+M_{D,p_{\delta}(s)}\right\}.$
Whenever the supremum is finite, the full semigroup  $S_{t}^{D}$  satisfies
(4.7)
$\|S_{t-u}^{D}:L^{p_{\delta}(u)}(\sigma_{\beta})\to L^{p_{\delta}(t)}(\sigma_{\beta})\|\leq e^{\omega_{D,\delta,s}(t-u)},\qquad 0\leq u\leq t\leq s.$
Kernel and entropy decay. The mixed semigroup is conservative,
and its nonnegative standard-form operator  $L_{D}=-\mathscr{L}_{2,h,D}$
has compact resolvent. Put  $g=\gcd(D)$  and let  $P_{r}$  project onto
occupations  $n\equiv r\pmod{g}$ . Then
$\ker L_{D}=\operatorname{span}\{\sqrt{\sigma_{\beta}}P_{r}:0\leq r<g\}.$
In particular, the sampler is primitive exactly when  $g=1$ .
Assume henceforth  $g=1$ , and let  $\lambda_{D}>0$  be its smallest
positive eigenvalue. If  $d_{*}=m$ , (4.7) reaches
$p=4$  for every  $s>\beta a_{m}/4$ ; if  $d_{*}>m$ , it does so for every  $s>0$ .
For either of these two regimes, fix such an admissible  $s$
and, with  $\delta=1/(4s)$ , put
(4.8)
$C_{D}(s):=e^{s\omega_{D,1/(4s),s}}.$
Then every state  $\rho$  satisfies
(4.9)
$D(\Phi_{t}^{D}(\rho)\|\sigma_{\beta})\leq e^{-\alpha_{D}(s)t}D(\rho\|\sigma_{\beta}),\qquad\alpha_{D}(s)=\left(2s+\frac{2\log C_{D}(s)+1}{\lambda_{D}}\right)^{-1}.$
Proof.
Step 1: construction of the sampler.
The sampler is obtained from the infinite-dimensional form
construction of [4, Section 2].
Indeed, choose a scalar  $c\in\mathbb{R}$  that makes the Hamiltonian positive.
Put  $\widetilde{H}=h(N)+cI\asymp(N+1)^{m}$ . For either
$A=a^{d}$  or  $A=(a^{\dagger})^{d}$ , the ladder coefficients give
$\|A\widetilde{H}^{-d/(2m)}\|_{\infty}+\|\widetilde{H}^{d/(2m)}A\widetilde{H}^{-d/m}\|_{\infty}<\infty.$
All jumps are closed on their respective maximal domains and have
the finite occupation span as a common core. For the finite family,
the same ladder estimates give the common energy-bound exponents  $\gamma=d_{*}/(2m)$  and  $\mu=d_{*}/m$ .
The filter
(2.3) is nonvanishing and satisfies the required KMS and
boundedness conditions. Thus the closed form of
[4, Propositions 2.4 and 2.8]
generates a conservative KMS-symmetric QMS for every polynomial  $h$
covered by Theorem 4.2.
We identify its generator before applying the perturbation theorem.
On Hilbert–Schmidt matrix units,
$\mathscr{A}_{D}E_{nk}=-(A_{D}(n)+A_{D}(k))E_{nk}.$
Finite matrices form an operator core for this self-adjoint diagonal
operator. The remainder  $\mathscr{V}_{D,2}$  is bounded by
Lemma 4.1 and symmetric by KMS reversibility.
Consequently  $\mathscr{A}_{D}+\mathscr{V}_{D,2}$  is essentially
self-adjoint on that core. The standard-form generator supplied by
the construction agrees there with
(4.3), so uniqueness of the
self-adjoint closure identifies it with this bounded perturbation.
The bounded perturbation product formula
[27, Corollary III.5.8] now gives
$e^{t\mathscr{L}_{2,h,D}}=\operatorname*{s-lim}_{n\to\infty}\bigl(e^{(t/n)\mathscr{A}_{D}}e^{(t/n)\mathscr{V}_{D,2}}\bigr)^{n}\quad\text{on }\mathscr{T}_{2}(\mathcal{H}).$
For the other exponents, transporting  $\mathscr{V}_{D,p}$  back by
$\iota_{p,\sigma_{\beta}}$  gives the same map on finite matrix
observables. These observables are dense in every  $L^{p}(\sigma_{\beta})$
with  $p<\infty$ ; the diagonal semigroups are consistent there as well.
Together with the QMS extensions, this verifies the consistency
and product-formula assumptions of Theorem 3.1.
Step 2: hypercontractive upper bounds.
Fix the exponent curve  $p_{\delta}$  and a time  $s$  for which the
supremum in  $\omega_{D,\delta,s}$  is finite. The identity
$1/p_{\delta}(u)-1/p_{\delta}(t)=\delta(t-u)$  turns
(4.5) into a bound along this curve, with
growth constant
$\omega_{0}=\delta\log Z_{\beta}+\sup_{n\geq 0}\{\beta\delta h(n)-2A_{D}(n)\},\qquad\|T_{t-u}^{D}:L^{p_{\delta}(u)}\to L^{p_{\delta}(t)}\|\leq e^{\omega_{0}(t-u)}.$
By Lemma 4.1, the perturbation in
(4.3) is bounded uniformly for all exponents
along this curve. Applying
Theorem 3.1 adds  $M_{D,p_{\delta}(s)}$  to this
constant and proves (4.7).
It remains to choose the curve. If  $a_{m}$  is the leading coefficient
of  $h$ , then
$\beta\delta h(n)-2A_{D}(n)=\beta\delta a_{m}n^{m}-n^{d_{*}}+o(n^{m}+n^{d_{*}}).$
For  $d_{*}>m$ , this tends to  $-\infty$  for every  $\delta>0$ .
For  $d_{*}=m$ , its leading coefficient is  $\beta\delta a_{m}-1$ .
To reach  $p>2$  at time  $t$ , choose
$\delta=\frac{1/2-1/p}{t},\qquad\beta\delta a_{m}<1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad t>\beta a_{m}(1/2-1/p).$
This proves the claimed upper bounds in both regimes.
Step 3: the no-jump obstruction.
To rule out earlier bounds, we use the invariant classical sector of diagonal observables,
whose outgoing rate is
$r(n)=\sum_{d\in D}(b_{d,+}(n)+b_{d,-}(n))\sim n^{d_{*}}$ .
Writing  $\pi_{n}=Z_{\beta}^{-1}e^{-\beta h(n)}$ , test the semigroup on
the normalized observable  $\pi_{n}^{-1/2}|n\rangle\langle n|$ .
The probability of remaining at occupation  $n$  without a jump until
time  $t$  is  $e^{-tr(n)}$ , so
$\|S_{t}^{D}:L^{2}(\sigma_{\beta})\to L^{p}(\sigma_{\beta})\|\geq e^{-tr(n)}\pi_{n}^{1/p-1/2}.$
The logarithm of this lower bound is
$-tr(n)+(1/2-1/p)(\beta h(n)+\log Z_{\beta})=\beta a_{m}(1/2-1/p)n^{m}-tn^{d_{*}}+o(n^{m}+n^{d_{*}}).$
It tends to  $+\infty$  for  $m>d_{*}$  at every finite  $t$ , and for
$m=d_{*}$  whenever  $t<\beta a_{m}(1/2-1/p)$ . This proves both obstructions directly
for the full sampler.
Step 4: the kernel, gap and entropy decay.
By Step 1,  $L_{D}=-\mathscr{A}_{D}-\mathscr{V}_{D,2}$  is a bounded
symmetric perturbation of the nonnegative diagonal operator
$-\mathscr{A}_{D}$ . The latter has eigenvectors  $E_{nk}$  and eigenvalues
$A_{D}(n)+A_{D}(k)\to\infty$  as  $n+k\to\infty$ .
If  $\mathsf{P}_{J}$  projects onto the span of  $E_{nk}$  with  $n+k\leq J$ ,
then
$\|(I-\mathsf{P}_{J})(I-\mathscr{A}_{D})^{-1}\|_{2\to 2}=\sup_{n+k>J}\frac{1}{1+A_{D}(n)+A_{D}(k)}\longrightarrow 0.$
Thus  $(I-\mathscr{A}_{D})^{-1}$  is a norm limit of finite-rank maps.
The bounded perturbation transfers this compactness through
$(L_{D}+I)^{-1}=(I-\mathscr{A}_{D})^{-1}+(I-\mathscr{A}_{D})^{-1}\mathscr{V}_{D,2}(L_{D}+I)^{-1}.$
Hence  $L_{D}$  has compact resolvent.
For  $Y\in\ker L_{D}$ , every nonnegative paired form vanishes.
The paired identity (2.21) extends from finite
matrices by the loss bound  $C(N+I)^{d_{*}}$  and the form-core property
proved in Step 1. Since its integration weight is strictly positive,
each paired derivation vanishes. Each matrix entry involves finitely
many Bohr frequencies; extracting their coefficients, using the
nonvanishing filter and its KMS relation, gives
$[X,a^{d}]=[X,(a^{\dagger})^{d}]=0\quad(d\in D),\qquad X=\sigma_{\beta}^{-1/4}Y\sigma_{\beta}^{-1/4},$
entrywise. These products are defined entrywise because the jumps
are weighted shifts; no boundedness of  $X$  is required. For any fixed
$d\in D$ ,  $X$  therefore commutes with
$a^{d}(a^{\dagger})^{d}=\prod_{j=1}^{d}(N+j)$ , whose eigenvalues are strictly
increasing. Hence  $X$  is diagonal, and its entries obey
$x_{n+d}=x_{n}$  for all  $d\in D$ . Bézout’s identity writes  $g=A-B$
with  $A,B$  nonnegative integer combinations of elements of  $D$ , so
$x_{n}=x_{n+A}=x_{n+g+B}=x_{n+g}$ . Thus  $X$  is constant on residue
classes modulo  $g$ . Conversely, each  $\sqrt{\sigma_{\beta}}P_{r}$  belongs
to the form domain by its Gibbs tail and is annihilated by all paired
derivations. This proves the stated kernel formula. When  $g=1$ ,
compact resolvent and simplicity of zero give  $\lambda_{D}>0$ .
When  $d_{*}=m$ , the critical threshold in
(4.6) is  $\beta a_{m}/4$  at  $p=4$ .
When  $d_{*}>m$ , every  $s>0$  is allowed. Finally apply
Theorem 1.2 with  $q_{0}=4$  and norm bound
(4.8) to obtain
(4.9).
∎
The full multimode Bose–Hubbard Hamiltonian.
With hopping, the filtered jumps are no longer explicit in the
occupation basis. Total particle number is still conserved, so we
can estimate the filters on finite-dimensional particle sectors.
The cubic losses dominate the errors in these estimates.
Theorem 4.3 (Multimode Bose–Hubbard sampler with hopping).
Let  $k\geq 1$ ,  $\beta>0$ , and let  $a_{j},a_{j}^{\dagger},N_{j}=a_{j}^{\dagger}a_{j}$
be the usual mode operators on  $\ell^{2}(\mathbb{N}_{0}^{k})$ . Consider
$H=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\left[\frac{U_{j}}{2}N_{j}(N_{j}-I)-\mu_{j}N_{j}\right]+\sum_{i<j}V_{ij}N_{i}N_{j}-\sum_{i<j}\left(J_{ij}a_{i}^{\dagger}a_{j}+\overline{J_{ij}}a_{j}^{\dagger}a_{i}\right),$
where  $U_{j}>0$ ,  $\mu_{j}\in\mathbb{R}$ ,  $V_{ij}\geq 0$ , and  $J_{ij}\in\mathbb{C}$  are
arbitrary. Put  $\sigma_{\beta}=Z_{\beta}^{-1}e^{-\beta H}$ , with
$Z_{\beta}=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H})<\infty$ . In each mode take the bare jumps
$a_{j},a_{j}^{\dagger},a_{j}^{3},(a_{j}^{\dagger})^{3}$ , with filter
$\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(\nu)=\exp\left[-\frac{\sqrt{1+(\beta\nu)^{2}}+\beta\nu}{4}\right].$
Writing  $P_{E}$  for the spectral projections of  $H$ , define on finite
particle sectors
$L^{\alpha}=\sum_{E,E^{\prime}}\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(E^{\prime}-E)P_{E^{\prime}}A^{\alpha}P_{E},\qquad C_{H}=\sum_{\alpha}(L^{\alpha})^{\dagger}L^{\alpha},$
and choose the correction Hamiltonian by
$P_{E}BP_{E^{\prime}}=\frac{i}{2}\tanh\!\left(\frac{\beta(E-E^{\prime})}{4}\right)P_{E}C_{H}P_{E^{\prime}}.$
The generator
$\mathcal{L}(\rho)=-i[B,\rho]+\sum_{\alpha}\left(L^{\alpha}\rho(L^{\alpha})^{\dagger}-\frac{1}{2}\{(L^{\alpha})^{\dagger}L^{\alpha},\rho\}\right)$
has a conservative KMS-symmetric realization with  $\sigma_{\beta}$  as
its unique invariant state. Its nonnegative standard-form generator
$L$  has compact resolvent and a positive gap  $\lambda$ . If
$0=\lambda_{1}\leq\lambda_{2}\leq\cdots$  are its eigenvalues with multiplicity,
then, for the fixed model,
$1+\lambda_{j}\asymp j^{3/(2k)},\qquad\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathscr{T}_{2}}(e^{-tL})\asymp t^{-2k/3}\quad(0<t\leq 1).$
Here the trace is on Hilbert–Schmidt space; the comparison constants
may depend on all model parameters. Its Heisenberg semigroup satisfies
$\|T_{t}:L^{2}(\sigma_{\beta})\to L^{p}(\sigma_{\beta})\|<\infty\qquad(2<p<\infty,\ t>0).$
For any  $s>0$ , choose  $C(s)\geq 1$  bounding the  $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{4}$  norm
of  $T_{s}$ . Then every state  $\rho$  satisfies
$D(\Phi_{t}(\rho)\|\sigma_{\beta})\leq e^{-\alpha(s)t}D(\rho\|\sigma_{\beta}),\qquad\alpha(s)=\left(2s+\frac{2\log C(s)+1}{\lambda}\right)^{-1}>0.$
Alternatively, take the bare jumps  $a_{j},a_{j}^{\dagger},a_{j}^{2},(a_{j}^{\dagger})^{2}$ .
The resulting sampler is again conservative and primitive, with compact
resolvent and a positive gap. Let  $W=(w_{ij})$  be real symmetric with
$w_{ii}=U_{i}$ ,  $w_{ij}=V_{ij}$  for  $i\neq j$ , and put
$\Lambda=\lambda_{\max}(W)>0$ . In this case a bounded
$L^{2}(\sigma_{\beta})$ -to- $L^{p}(\sigma_{\beta})$  endpoint is available whenever
$2<p<\infty,\qquad t>\frac{\beta\Lambda}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{p}\right).$
The same entropy estimate holds with its own gap and endpoint constant
at every  $s>\beta\Lambda/8$ . No assertion is made at the boundary time.
There is no occupation cutoff or smallness assumption on the hopping.
The constants may depend on all model parameters, including  $k$ .
Proof.
The main estimate is that the cubic losses grow like the cube of
the total particle number, whereas the weighted gains grow only
linearly. We first prove these bounds on particle sectors, then use
them to control the full semigroup.
Step 1:
Write  $H=H_{0}+T$ , where  $H_{0}$  contains the number-diagonal terms and
$T$  is the hopping term. Set  $\mathsf{N}=\sum_{j}N_{j}$ , let
$Q_{n}=\mathbf{1}_{\{n\}}(\mathsf{N})$ , and put
$\mathcal{H}^{[n]}=Q_{n}\mathcal{H}$ . Each term of  $H$  preserves  $\mathcal{H}^{[n]}$ ,
whose dimension is  $\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}$ . Let  $h_{\rm hop}$  be the Hermitian  $k\times k$  matrix with
zero diagonal and off-diagonal entries  $-J_{ij}$  and
$-\overline{J_{ij}}$ . On the
symmetric  $n$ -particle space,
$T|_{\mathcal{H}^{[n]}}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}(h_{\rm hop})_{\ell},\qquad\|TQ_{n}\|\leq n\|h_{\rm hop}\|.$
If  $U_{\min}=\min_{j}U_{j}>0$ , the number-diagonal part satisfies
$H_{0}\geq\frac{U_{\min}}{2}\sum_{j}N_{j}^{2}-C\mathsf{N},\qquad H_{0}\leq C\left(\sum_{j}N_{j}^{2}+\mathsf{N}+I\right).$
Moreover,
$\sum_{j}N_{j}^{2}\geq k^{-1}\mathsf{N}^{2},\qquad N_{i}N_{j}\leq\tfrac{1}{2}(N_{i}^{2}+N_{j}^{2}).$
The positive onsite coefficients and nonnegative density couplings
therefore give, after a scalar shift,
$c(\mathsf{N}+I)^{2}\leq\widetilde{H}:=H+c_{0}I\leq C(\mathsf{N}+I)^{2},\qquad\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta\widetilde{H}})\leq\sum_{n\geq 0}\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}e^{-\beta c(n+1)^{2}}<\infty.$
The inequalities hold separately on every particle sector. For a lowering or raising jump of order  $d\in\{1,3\}$ ,
$\|a_{i}^{d}Q_{n}\|^{2}\leq n(n-1)\cdots(n-d+1),\qquad\|(a_{i}^{\dagger})^{d}Q_{n}\|^{2}\leq(n+1)\cdots(n+d),$
where the first expression is zero for  $n<d$ . Each jump changes
$n$  by at most three. Combining these estimates with the lower and
upper bounds on  $\widetilde{H}$  gives
$\|A^{\alpha}\widetilde{H}^{-3/4}\|+\|\widetilde{H}^{3/4}A^{\alpha}\widetilde{H}^{-3/2}\|<\infty.$
The jumps are closed on their respective maximal domains and share
the finite particle span as a spectral core. These are the common
energy bounds required in
[4, Condition A and Proposition 2.4].
The filter satisfies its KMS and boundedness conditions, so the form
construction gives a conservative KMS-symmetric sampler.
Every spectral sum defining a jump between fixed particle sectors
is finite. Below, constants are independent of the sector index  $n$ .
Step 2:
Extend  $V_{ij}$  symmetrically and set
$w_{ii}=U_{i}$ ,  $w_{ij}=V_{ij}$  for  $i\neq j$ . Fix a mode  $i$  and put
$A=a_{i}^{3},\qquad D_{i}=b_{i}I+3\sum_{j}w_{ij}N_{j},\qquad c_{i}=b_{i}+6U_{i}+3\mu_{i},$
where  $b_{i}$  is sufficiently large that  $D_{i}\geq 4I$  and its values
at occupations differing by one hop are comparable. Write  $\varepsilon(\mathbf{n})$  for the value of  $H_{0}$  at the
occupation vector  $\mathbf{n}$ . For  $n_{i}\geq 3$ ,
$\displaystyle\varepsilon(\mathbf{n}-3e_{i})-\varepsilon(\mathbf{n})$
$\displaystyle=\frac{U_{i}}{2}\bigl[(n_{i}-3)(n_{i}-4)-n_{i}(n_{i}-1)\bigr]+3\mu_{i}-3\sum_{j\neq i}V_{ij}n_{j}$
$\displaystyle=-3\sum_{j}w_{ij}n_{j}+6U_{i}+3\mu_{i}=-D_{i}(\mathbf{n})+c_{i}.$
Applying this identity to each occupation vector gives
$[H_{0},A]=-A(D_{i}-c_{i}I).$
For  $\operatorname{Re}z\geq-1$ , put  $K_{z}=A(z+D_{i})^{-1}$ .
Since  $D_{i}(\mathbf{n})\geq c(n_{i}+1)$  and
$|z+D_{i}(\mathbf{n})|\geq D_{i}(\mathbf{n})-1\geq\tfrac{3}{4}D_{i}(\mathbf{n})$ ,
$\|K_{z}Q_{n}\|=\max_{|\mathbf{n}|=n}\frac{\sqrt{n_{i}(n_{i}-1)(n_{i}-2)}}{|z+D_{i}(\mathbf{n})|}\leq C\sqrt{n+1}.$
For a hopping term  $T_{rs}=a_{r}^{\dagger}a_{s}$ ,  $r\neq s$ , put
$R_{i}(z)=(z+D_{i})^{-1}$  and  $\Delta_{rs}=3(w_{ir}-w_{is})$ .
The product rule gives
$[T_{rs},K_{z}]=[T_{rs},A]R_{i}(z)+A[T_{rs},R_{i}(z)],\qquad[T_{rs},A]=-3\mathbf{1}_{\{r=i\}}a_{i}^{2}a_{s}.$
The first term has norm at most  $C\sqrt{n+1}$  on  $\mathcal{H}^{[n]}$ :
its coefficient is bounded by
$C(n_{i}+1)\sqrt{n_{s}}/D_{i}(\mathbf{n})$  when  $r=i$ .
For the second term, evaluate the commutator on  $|\mathbf{n}\rangle$ :
$\displaystyle[T_{rs},R_{i}(z)]|\mathbf{n}\rangle$
$\displaystyle=\sqrt{(n_{r}+1)n_{s}}\left(\frac{1}{z+D_{i}(\mathbf{n})}-\frac{1}{z+D_{i}(\mathbf{n})+\Delta_{rs}}\right)|\mathbf{n}+e_{r}-e_{s}\rangle$
$\displaystyle=\frac{\Delta_{rs}\sqrt{(n_{r}+1)n_{s}}}{(z+D_{i}(\mathbf{n}))(z+D_{i}(\mathbf{n})+\Delta_{rs})}|\mathbf{n}+e_{r}-e_{s}\rangle.$
The choice of  $b_{i}$  bounds the modulus of each denominator below by
$cD_{i}(\mathbf{n})$ . After applying  $A$ , the coefficient is bounded by
$C\frac{(n_{i}+1)^{3/2}|w_{ir}-w_{is}|\sqrt{(n_{r}+1)n_{s}}}{(b_{i}+3\sum_{j}w_{ij}n_{j})^{2}}\leq C\sqrt{n+1}.$
Indeed, nonnegativity of the  $w_{ij}$  and  $w_{ii}>0$  bounds the first
factor  $(n_{i}+1)^{3/2}$  by  $CD_{i}(\mathbf{n})^{3/2}$  and gives
$|w_{ir}-w_{is}|\sqrt{(n_{r}+1)n_{s}}\leq CD_{i}(\mathbf{n})^{1/2}\sqrt{n+1}.$
Each term is a weighted occupation shift, so a bound on its
coefficients is an operator-norm bound. Summing the finitely many hopping terms therefore proves
$\|K_{z}Q_{n}\|+\|[T,K_{z}]Q_{n}\|\leq C\sqrt{n+1},\qquad\operatorname{Re}z\geq-1.$
On maps from  $\mathcal{H}^{[n]}$  to  $\mathcal{H}^{[n-3]}$ , let
$\mathcal{D}_{n}X=H_{n-3}X-XH_{n}$ , where  $H_{n}=H|_{\mathcal{H}^{[n]}}$ .
Since  $H_{0}$  commutes with  $D_{i}$ , we have
$\displaystyle[H,K_{z}]$
$\displaystyle=-A(D_{i}-c_{i}I)(z+D_{i})^{-1}+[T,K_{z}]$
$\displaystyle=-A+zK_{z}+c_{i}K_{z}+[T,K_{z}].$
Thus
$(z-\mathcal{D}_{n})K_{z}Q_{n}=AQ_{n}-R_{z}Q_{n},\qquad R_{z}=c_{i}K_{z}+[T,K_{z}],\qquad\|R_{z}Q_{n}\|\leq C\sqrt{n+1}.$
In particular, with  $K=AD_{i}^{-1}$  and  $R=c_{i}K+[T,K]$ ,
$A=-[H,K]+R,\qquad\|KQ_{n}\|+\|RQ_{n}\|\leq C\sqrt{n+1}.$
The finitely many sectors  $n<3$  contribute zero to  $A$ .
Step 3:
We use the resolvent identity to estimate the energy filter on
each half of the frequency axis. The group
$e^{it\mathcal{D}_{n}}X=e^{itH_{n-3}}Xe^{-itH_{n}}$  consists of
operator-norm isometries. Hence
$\|(z-\mathcal{D}_{n})^{-1}\|_{\infty\to\infty}\leq|\operatorname{Im}z|^{-1},\qquad\|g(\mathcal{D}_{n})\|_{\infty\to\infty}\leq\|\check{g}\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R})},$
where  $g(\nu)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\check{g}(t)e^{it\nu}\,\mathrm{d}t$  in the second
inequality. Also  $\operatorname{spec}(\mathcal{D}_{n})\subset[-M_{n},M_{n}]$ ,
where  $M_{n}=C(n+1)^{2}$ .
Choose a smooth  $\chi$  equal to zero on  $(-\infty,-1]$  and to
one on  $[0,\infty)$ . Restricted to this spectral interval, it is a
sum of  $O(1+\log(n+2))$  smooth functions  $\chi_{\ell}$  supported
in  $[-1,\infty)$  on dyadic intervals of length  $2^{\ell}$ , with
$|\chi_{\ell}^{(r)}|\leq C_{r}2^{-\ell r}$ . Each has an almost analytic
extension  $\widetilde{\chi}_{\ell}$  with
$\int_{\mathbb{C}}\frac{|\partial_{\bar{z}}\widetilde{\chi}_{\ell}(z)|}{|\operatorname{Im}z|}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y\leq C,\qquad\operatorname{supp}\widetilde{\chi}_{\ell}\subset\{\operatorname{Re}z\geq-1\}.$
For example, use the first-order extension
$(\chi_{\ell}(x)+iy\chi_{\ell}^{\prime}(x))\eta(y/2^{\ell})$  with a fixed
smooth cutoff  $\eta$ . On  $|y|\lesssim 2^{\ell}$ , its derivative obeys
$|\partial_{\bar{z}}\widetilde{\chi}_{\ell}(x+iy)|\leq C|y|2^{-2\ell}+C2^{-\ell}\mathbf{1}_{\{|y|\asymp 2^{\ell}\}},$
on an  $x$ -interval of length  $O(2^{\ell})$ . Dividing by  $|y|$  and
integrating therefore gives a constant independent of  $\ell$ .
The Cauchy–Green, or Helffer–Sjöstrand, formula
[31, Section 2] and Step 2 give
$\displaystyle\chi_{\ell}(\mathcal{D}_{n})AQ_{n}$
$\displaystyle=A\chi_{\ell}(-D_{i})Q_{n}-\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{\mathbb{C}}\partial_{\bar{z}}\widetilde{\chi}_{\ell}(z)(z-\mathcal{D}_{n})^{-1}R_{z}Q_{n}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y,$
$\displaystyle\|\chi_{\ell}(\mathcal{D}_{n})AQ_{n}\|$
$\displaystyle\leq C\sqrt{n+1}.$
The first term vanishes because  $D_{i}\geq 4I$ . The formula can also
be checked entry by entry in the two finite energy eigenbases;
the resolvent estimate makes its bound independent of their dimensions.
Summing the dyadic pieces yields
$\|\chi(\mathcal{D}_{n})AQ_{n}\|\leq C\sqrt{n+1}\log(n+2).$
Write  $f=\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}$  in this proof and set
$g_{-}(\nu)=f(\nu)-1+\chi(\nu)$  and
$g_{+}(\nu)=f(-\nu)-\chi(\nu)$ . For every integer  $r\geq 0$ ,
$|g_{\pm}^{(r)}(\nu)|\leq C_{r}(1+|\nu|)^{-1-r}.$
A dyadic partition and the Fourier estimate above imply
$\|g_{\pm}(\mathcal{D}_{n})\|_{\infty\to\infty}\leq C,\qquad\|(\nu g_{\pm})(\mathcal{D}_{n})\|_{\infty\to\infty}\leq C\log(n+2).$
Here is the dyadic estimate. For a smooth  $u$  supported in a fixed
bounded interval, put  $u_{\ell}(\nu)=u(2^{-\ell}\nu)$ .
Plancherel, Cauchy–Schwarz, and a change of variables give
$\|\check{u}\|_{1}\leq C(\|u\|_{2}+\|u^{\prime}\|_{2}),\qquad\check{u}_{\ell}(t)=2^{\ell}\check{u}(2^{\ell}t),\qquad\|\check{u}_{\ell}\|_{1}=\|\check{u}\|_{1}.$
The rescaled pieces of  $g_{\pm}$  have size  $O(2^{-\ell})$ , while
those of  $\nu g_{\pm}$  have size  $O(1)$ . If  $L_{n}$  is the number of
dyadic scales meeting  $[-M_{n},M_{n}]$ , the two bounds follow from
$\sum_{\ell=0}^{L_{n}}C2^{-\ell}\leq 2C,\qquad\sum_{\ell=0}^{L_{n}}C\leq C\log(n+2).$
Apply the multiplier to  $A=-\mathcal{D}_{n}K+R$  on this block:
$\displaystyle g_{\pm}(\mathcal{D}_{n})AQ_{n}$
$\displaystyle=-(\nu g_{\pm})(\mathcal{D}_{n})KQ_{n}+g_{\pm}(\mathcal{D}_{n})RQ_{n},$
$\displaystyle\|g_{\pm}(\mathcal{D}_{n})AQ_{n}\|$
$\displaystyle\leq C\log(n+2)\|KQ_{n}\|+C\|RQ_{n}\|.$
Step 2 now gives
$\|g_{\pm}(\mathcal{D}_{n})AQ_{n}\|\leq C\sqrt{n+1}\log(n+2).$
Thus, denoting the filtered cubic lowering and raising jumps by
$L_{i,3}^{-}$  and  $L_{i,3}^{+}$ ,
$\|(L_{i,3}^{-}-a_{i}^{3})Q_{n}\|+\|(L_{i,3}^{+})^{\dagger}Q_{n}\|\leq C\sqrt{n+1}\log(n+2).$
The second term uses
$(L_{i,3}^{+})^{\dagger}Q_{n}=f(-\mathcal{D}_{n})AQ_{n}$ .
Taking adjoints and shifting  $n$  by three bounds  $L_{i,3}^{+}Q_{n}$
as well. The same dyadic Fourier argument for  $f$  itself gives
$\|L_{i,1}^{\pm}Q_{n}\|\leq C\sqrt{n+1}\log(n+2)$  for the linear
jumps. Consequently, for  $\psi\in\mathcal{H}^{[n]}$ ,
$\displaystyle\langle\psi,C_{H}\psi\rangle$
$\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}\|a_{i}^{3}\psi\|^{2}-C(n+1)\log^{2}(n+2)\|\psi\|^{2},$
$\displaystyle\sum_{i}(a_{i}^{\dagger})^{3}a_{i}^{3}$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{i}N_{i}(N_{i}-I)(N_{i}-2I)\geq k^{-2}\mathsf{N}^{3}-C(\mathsf{N}+I)^{2}.$
The last lower bound uses
$\sum_{i}n_{i}^{3}\geq k^{-2}(\sum_{i}n_{i})^{3}$  and
$n_{i}(n_{i}-1)(n_{i}-2)=n_{i}^{3}-3n_{i}^{2}+2n_{i}$ .
For every  $\varepsilon>0$ ,
$(n+1)^{2}+(n+1)\log^{2}(n+2)\leq\varepsilon(n+1)^{3}+C_{\varepsilon}.$
This absorbs the error into the cubic term. For the upper bound,
the filtered lowering jumps have norm at most  $C(n+1)^{3/2}$ ,
and the remaining jumps satisfy the smaller bounds above. Thus
$c(\mathsf{N}+I)^{3}-CI\leq C_{H}\leq C(\mathsf{N}+I)^{3}.$
Step 4:
For a bare jump  $A^{\alpha}$ , its standard-form gain operator is
$B_{\alpha}=e^{\beta H/4}L^{\alpha}e^{-\beta H/4}=F_{0}(\operatorname{ad}_{H})A^{\alpha},\qquad F_{\theta}(\nu)=\exp\!\left[-\frac{\sqrt{1+(\beta\nu)^{2}}}{4}+\theta\nu\right].$
Here  $\operatorname{ad}_{H}(X)=[H,X]$  is used only on the finite
particle blocks. Fix  $0\leq\theta_{*}<\beta/4$ .
Both  $F_{\theta}$  and  $\nu F_{\theta}$  have inverse Fourier transforms
with uniformly bounded  $L^{1}$  norms for  $|\theta|\leq\theta_{*}$ .
For a cubic lowering jump, the identity in Step 2 gives
$\displaystyle B_{\alpha,\theta}Q_{n}$
$\displaystyle:=(e^{\theta H}B_{\alpha}e^{-\theta H})Q_{n}=F_{\theta}(\mathcal{D}_{n})AQ_{n}=-(\nu F_{\theta})(\mathcal{D}_{n})KQ_{n}+F_{\theta}(\mathcal{D}_{n})RQ_{n}.$
The Fourier bounds therefore imply
$\sup_{|\theta|\leq\theta_{*}}\|B_{\alpha,\theta}Q_{n}\|\leq C_{\theta_{*}}(\|KQ_{n}\|+\|RQ_{n}\|)\leq C_{\theta_{*}}\sqrt{n+1}.$
For cubic raising jumps this follows by adjunction and
$F_{\theta}(-\nu)=F_{-\theta}(\nu)$ ; for linear jumps it follows
directly from their  $C\sqrt{n+1}$  bare bound.
The correction  $B$  in the statement is essential when hopping is
present. Transporting the full generator, including this correction,
gives on finite particle matrices
$LX=DX+XD-\sum_{\alpha}B_{\alpha}XB_{\alpha}^{\dagger},\qquad D=\frac{1}{2\cosh((\beta/4)\operatorname{ad}_{H})}(C_{H}).$
To check the drift and its sign, set
$M=-iB-C_{H}/2$  and  $x=\beta(E-E^{\prime})/4$ . The definition of  $B$  gives
$P_{E}MP_{E^{\prime}}=-\frac{1-\tanh x}{2}P_{E}C_{H}P_{E^{\prime}}=-\frac{e^{-x}}{2\cosh x}P_{E}C_{H}P_{E^{\prime}}.$
Conjugating by  $e^{\beta H/4}$  multiplies this block by  $e^{x}$ .
Hence  $e^{\beta H/4}Me^{-\beta H/4}=-D$ , and the two drift terms
in the nonnegative standard-form generator are  $DX+XD$ .
For  $D_{\theta}=e^{\theta H}De^{-\theta H}$ , its Hermitian part is
$\operatorname{Re}D_{\theta}=\frac{\cosh(\theta\operatorname{ad}_{H})}{2\cosh((\beta/4)\operatorname{ad}_{H})}(C_{H})=\int_{\mathbb{R}}m_{\theta}(t)e^{itH}C_{H}e^{-itH}\,\mathrm{d}t,$
where an elementary Fourier transform gives
$m_{\theta}(t)=\frac{\cos(2\pi\theta/\beta)\cosh(2\pi t/\beta)}{\beta\,[\sinh^{2}(2\pi t/\beta)+\cos^{2}(2\pi\theta/\beta)]}\geq 0,\qquad\int_{\mathbb{R}}m_{\theta}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t=\frac{1}{2}.$
Since  $H$  commutes with  $\mathsf{N}$ , Step 3 implies, uniformly for
$|\theta|\leq\theta_{*}$ ,
$\operatorname{Re}D_{\theta}\geq c(\mathsf{N}+I)^{3}-CI,\qquad\|D_{\theta}Q_{n}\|\leq C_{\theta_{*}}(n+1)^{3}.$
For the norm estimate, use the integrable inverse Fourier transform
of  $e^{\theta\nu}/(2\cosh(\beta\nu/4))$  and the upper bound on  $C_{H}$ .
Step 5:
On Hilbert–Schmidt space set
$\mathcal{K}_{r}X=(\mathsf{N}+I)^{r}X+X(\mathsf{N}+I)^{r}\text{ for }r=1,2,3,\qquad W_{\theta}X=e^{\theta\widetilde{H}}Xe^{\theta\widetilde{H}}.$
The loss operator  $X\mapsto DX+XD$  is a self-adjoint direct sum
on the blocks  $Q_{n}XQ_{m}$ , with domain  $D(\mathcal{K}_{3})$  and finite
particle matrices as an operator core. The gain operator and its
conjugates are lower order. In fact, each bare row has a fixed
particle-number change  $d_{\alpha}\in\{-3,-1,1,3\}$ , and
$W_{\theta}\bigl(B_{\alpha}XB_{\alpha}^{\dagger}\bigr)=B_{\alpha,\theta}(W_{\theta}X)B_{\alpha,\theta}^{\dagger}.$
Write  $X_{nm}=Q_{n}XQ_{m}$ , with a block understood to be zero if
an index is negative. For one gain term,
$\|B_{\alpha,\theta}X_{nm}B_{\alpha,\theta}^{\dagger}\|_{2}\leq C\sqrt{(n+1)(m+1)}\|X_{nm}\|_{2},$
and its output lies in block  $(n+d_{\alpha},m+d_{\alpha})$ .
For fixed  $\alpha$ , distinct input blocks have orthogonal outputs.
Squaring and summing gives
$\|B_{\alpha,\theta}XB_{\alpha,\theta}^{\dagger}\|_{2}^{2}\leq C\sum_{n,m}(n+1)(m+1)\|X_{nm}\|_{2}^{2}\leq C\|\mathcal{K}_{1}X\|_{2}^{2}.$
For the form bound, put  $x_{nm}=\|X_{nm}\|_{2}$  and use
$\displaystyle|\langle X,B_{\alpha,\theta}XB_{\alpha,\theta}^{\dagger}\rangle|$
$\displaystyle\leq C\sum_{n,m}\sqrt{(n+1)(m+1)}\,x_{nm}x_{n+d_{\alpha},m+d_{\alpha}}$
$\displaystyle\leq C\sum_{n,m}(n+m+2)x_{nm}^{2}=C\langle X,\mathcal{K}_{1}X\rangle.$
The second inequality uses  $2ab\leq a^{2}+b^{2}$  and the comparability
of the weights before and after a shift of at most three.
Summing over  $\alpha$  proves
$\displaystyle\left\|\sum_{\alpha}B_{\alpha,\theta}XB_{\alpha,\theta}^{\dagger}\right\|_{2}$
$\displaystyle\leq C_{\theta_{*}}\|\mathcal{K}_{1}X\|_{2},$
$\displaystyle\left|\sum_{\alpha}\langle X,B_{\alpha,\theta}XB_{\alpha,\theta}^{\dagger}\rangle\right|$
$\displaystyle\leq C_{\theta_{*}}\langle X,\mathcal{K}_{1}X\rangle.$
At  $\theta=0$  the gain is symmetric because each  $B_{\alpha}$  is
paired with its adjoint. For every  $\varepsilon>0$ , the scalar
inequality  $r\leq\varepsilon r^{3}+C_{\varepsilon}$  gives
$\|\mathcal{K}_{1}X\|_{2}\leq\varepsilon\|\mathcal{K}_{3}X\|_{2}+C_{\varepsilon}\|X\|_{2}.$
Thus the gain has relative operator bound zero with respect to
the loss operator. The self-adjoint
perturbation theorem [19] therefore identifies the closure on finite
particle matrices with the standard-form generator from Step 1;
the Gibbs vector belongs to its domain by the Gaussian particle-number
tail. Its form domain is  $D(\mathcal{K}_{3}^{1/2})$ . For the weighted form, Step 4 first gives
$\displaystyle\operatorname{Re}\langle X,W_{\theta}LW_{\theta}^{-1}X\rangle$
$\displaystyle\geq c\langle X,\mathcal{K}_{3}X\rangle-C\langle X,\mathcal{K}_{1}X\rangle-C\|X\|_{2}^{2},$
$\displaystyle\langle X,\mathcal{K}_{1}X\rangle$
$\displaystyle\leq\varepsilon\langle X,\mathcal{K}_{3}X\rangle+C_{\varepsilon}\|X\|_{2}^{2}.$
Choose  $\varepsilon$  so that  $C\varepsilon<c/2$ . We obtain
$\operatorname{Re}\langle X,W_{\theta}LW_{\theta}^{-1}X\rangle\geq c_{*}\langle X,\mathcal{K}_{3}X\rangle-C_{*}\|X\|_{2}^{2},\qquad 0\leq\theta\leq\theta_{*}<\beta/4,$
on the finite particle core. The constants are uniform in  $\theta$
on this interval.
Step 6: smoothing at every positive time.
Fix  $s>0$  and  $2<p<\infty$ , and choose
$\delta_{p}=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{p},\qquad\theta_{*}=\frac{\beta\delta_{p}}{2}<\frac{\beta}{4},\qquad\theta(t)=\frac{\theta_{*}t}{s}\text{ for }0\leq t\leq s.$
Let  $\Pi_{M}X=Q_{\leq M}XQ_{\leq M}$ , with
$Q_{\leq M}=\sum_{n=0}^{M}Q_{n}$ , and let  $L_{M}$  be the form compression
of  $L$  to its range. These projections commute with  $W_{\theta}$ .
For  $U_{M}(t)=W_{\theta(t)}e^{-tL_{M}}\Pi_{M}X$ , differentiation
in the finite-dimensional range gives
$U_{M}^{\prime}(t)=\frac{\theta_{*}}{s}(\widetilde{H}U_{M}(t)+U_{M}(t)\widetilde{H})-W_{\theta(t)}L_{M}W_{\theta(t)}^{-1}U_{M}(t).$
The compression keeps every loss term: it is  $\Pi_{M}L\Pi_{M}$  on
its range, rather than a new sampler with truncated jumps.
Since  $\Pi_{M}$  commutes with the weight, Step 5 gives
$\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}t}\|U_{M}(t)\|_{2}^{2}$
$\displaystyle\leq\frac{\theta_{*}}{s}\langle U_{M},\widetilde{H}U_{M}+U_{M}\widetilde{H}\rangle-c_{*}\langle U_{M},\mathcal{K}_{3}U_{M}\rangle+C_{*}\|U_{M}\|_{2}^{2}\leq b_{s}\|U_{M}(t)\|_{2}^{2},$
where one may take
$b_{s}=C_{*}+2\sup_{r\geq 1}\left\{\frac{C\theta_{*}}{s}r^{2}-c_{*}r^{3}\right\}<\infty.$
Here  $\widetilde{H}\leq C(\mathsf{N}+I)^{2}$  is from Step 1.
Integration gives  $\|U_{M}(s)\|_{2}\leq e^{sb_{s}}\|X\|_{2}$ ,
uniformly in  $M$ . To remove  $M$ , set  $u=(L+I)^{-1}X$  and
$u_{M}=(L_{M}+I)^{-1}\Pi_{M}X$ . The variational equations give
$\mathcal{E}(u-u_{M},v)+\langle u-u_{M},v\rangle=0\quad(v\in\operatorname{Ran}\Pi_{M}),\qquad\|u-u_{M}\|_{\mathcal{E}}\leq\inf_{v\in\operatorname{Ran}\Pi_{M}}\|u-v\|_{\mathcal{E}}\longrightarrow 0.$
Here  $\mathcal{E}(\cdot,\cdot)$  is the sesquilinear form associated with
$\mathcal{E}$ . The limit follows because finite particle matrices are a form
core. Strong resolvent convergence then gives
$e^{-sL_{M}}\Pi_{M}X\to e^{-sL}X$  in Hilbert–Schmidt norm
[27, Theorem III.4.8].
Choose a joint eigenbasis  $(\psi_{a})_{a}$  of  $\widetilde{H}$  and
$\mathsf{N}$ , with  $\widetilde{H}\psi_{a}=\widetilde{E}_{a}\psi_{a}$ .
If  $y_{ab}^{(M)}$  and  $y_{ab}$  are the corresponding coefficients
of these two outputs, Fatou’s lemma gives
$\sum_{a,b}e^{2\theta_{*}(\widetilde{E}_{a}+\widetilde{E}_{b})}|y_{ab}|^{2}\leq\liminf_{M}\sum_{a,b}e^{2\theta_{*}(\widetilde{E}_{a}+\widetilde{E}_{b})}|y_{ab}^{(M)}|^{2}\leq e^{2sb_{s}}\|X\|_{2}^{2}.$
In particular, the weighted output is Hilbert–Schmidt and
$\|e^{\theta_{*}\widetilde{H}}e^{-sL}Xe^{\theta_{*}\widetilde{H}}\|_{2}\leq e^{sb_{s}}\|X\|_{2}.$
The bound therefore holds for the full semigroup. Put  $\widetilde{Z}=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta\widetilde{H}})$ .
Since  $\|Y\|_{p}\leq\|Y\|_{2}$  for  $p\geq 2$ ,
$\|e^{-sL}X\|_{p\leftarrow 2,\sigma_{\beta}}=\widetilde{Z}^{\delta_{p}}\|e^{\theta_{*}\widetilde{H}}e^{-sL}Xe^{\theta_{*}\widetilde{H}}\|_{p}\leq\widetilde{Z}^{\delta_{p}}e^{sb_{s}}\|X\|_{2}.$
This proves the required bounds for every  $s>0$  and finite  $p>2$ .
Step 7: the kernel and the gap.
Step 5 gives a quantitative tail estimate:
$\|(I-\Pi_{M})Y\|_{2}^{2}\leq\frac{\langle Y,\mathcal{K}_{3}Y\rangle}{(M+2)^{3}}\leq\frac{\mathcal{E}(Y)+C_{*}\|Y\|_{2}^{2}}{c_{*}(M+2)^{3}}.$
Every  $\Pi_{M}$  has finite rank. Thus the form unit ball is relatively
compact in Hilbert–Schmidt space, and  $L$  has compact resolvent.
Moreover, the upper loss and gain bounds in Steps 4–5 give the
matching upper form bound, so
$c\mathcal{K}_{3}-CI\leq L\leq C\mathcal{K}_{3}+CI.$
There are  $\binom{n+k}{k}\asymp n^{k}$  occupation states with at most
$n$  particles. Counting pairs of such states gives
$\#\{\text{eigenvalues of }\mathcal{K}_{3}\leq E\}\asymp E^{2k/3}$ .
The min–max principle yields  $1+\lambda_{j}\asymp j^{3/(2k)}$ ;
summing  $e^{-t\lambda_{j}}$  gives the asserted heat-trace bounds.
These are matching powers, not exact Weyl constants.
To identify its kernel, put
$J_{\alpha}(t)=e^{itH}L^{\alpha}e^{-itH}$ . The paired Dirichlet-form
identity (2.21), at  $\sigma_{E}=\infty$ , reads
$\mathcal{E}(Y)=\sum_{\alpha}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{\|J_{\alpha}(t)Y-YJ_{\bar{\alpha}}(t)^{\dagger}\|_{2}^{2}}{\beta\cosh(2\pi t/\beta)}\,\mathrm{d}t.$
We first justify the identity for complex finite particle matrices.
For a self-adjoint  $Y$ , the difference between the two sides is a
real quadratic polynomial in its matrix entries. It vanishes on
the positive definite matrices by homogeneity and Lemma 2.9,
and hence on all self-adjoint matrices. One may work in a particle
cutoff larger than the support of  $Y$  by three, so all jump images
and loss terms are retained. For complex  $Y=Y_{1}+iY_{2}$ , with
$Y_{j}=Y_{j}^{\dagger}$ , put
$\mathcal{D}_{\alpha}(t)Y=J_{\alpha}(t)Y-YJ_{\bar{\alpha}}(t)^{\dagger}$ .
Adjoint pairing gives
$\mathcal{D}_{\alpha}(t)(Y^{\dagger})=-\bigl(\mathcal{D}_{\bar{\alpha}}(t)Y\bigr)^{\dagger},\qquad\mathcal{E}(Y)=\mathcal{E}(Y_{1})+\mathcal{E}(Y_{2}).$
The mixed terms on the right also cancel after summing over
$\alpha$ . This proves the identity on the complex finite particle core.
The growth bounds from Step 3 give, uniformly in  $t$ ,
$\sum_{\alpha}\|\mathcal{D}_{\alpha}(t)Y\|_{2}^{2}\leq C\langle Y,\mathcal{K}_{3}Y\rangle.$
Both sides therefore extend continuously to
$D(\mathcal{K}_{3}^{1/2})$ . Approximation by finite particle matrices
also shows that each  $\mathcal{D}_{\alpha}(t)Y$  is continuous in  $t$ .
The integration weight is strictly positive. Hence
$Y\in\ker L\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathcal{D}_{\alpha}(t)Y=0\quad\text{for every }\alpha\text{ and }t\in\mathbb{R}.$
On each block  $Q_{n}(\cdot)Q_{m}$ , this is a finite trigonometric sum,
because a jump has a fixed particle-number change. Indeed, the finite frequency expansion on such a block is
$\mathcal{D}_{\alpha}(t)Y=\sum_{\nu}e^{it\nu}\left[f(\nu)A_{\nu}^{\alpha}Y-f(-\nu)YA_{\nu}^{\alpha}\right].$
Distinct exponentials are linearly independent. Since
$f(-\nu)=e^{\beta\nu/2}f(\nu)$  and  $f(\nu)>0$ , each coefficient
vanishes and
$A_{\nu}^{\alpha}Y=e^{\beta\nu/2}YA_{\nu}^{\alpha}.$
Define  $X=\sigma_{\beta}^{-1/4}Y\sigma_{\beta}^{-1/4}$  blockwise;
these are finite matrices, so no boundedness of  $X$  is assumed.
The modular relation gives, blockwise,
$A_{\nu}^{\alpha}\sigma_{\beta}^{1/4}=e^{\beta\nu/4}\sigma_{\beta}^{1/4}A_{\nu}^{\alpha},\qquad\sigma_{\beta}^{1/4}A_{\nu}^{\alpha}=e^{-\beta\nu/4}A_{\nu}^{\alpha}\sigma_{\beta}^{1/4}.$
Substituting  $Y=\sigma_{\beta}^{1/4}X\sigma_{\beta}^{1/4}$  into the
preceding identity and cancelling the finite invertible weights
therefore gives  $[A_{\nu}^{\alpha},X]=0$ . Summing the finitely many frequencies in each
particle block, the linear rows yield
$[a_{j},X]=[a_{j}^{\dagger},X]=0,\qquad[N_{j},X]=0\quad(1\leq j\leq k).$
Writing  $X_{\mathbf{n}\mathbf{m}}=\langle\mathbf{n}|X|\mathbf{m}\rangle$ ,
the number commutators give
$(n_{j}-m_{j})X_{\mathbf{n}\mathbf{m}}=0\quad\text{for all }j.$
Thus  $X$  is diagonal. If  $x_{\mathbf{n}}=X_{\mathbf{n}\mathbf{n}}$ ,
the creation commutators give
$0=\langle\mathbf{n}+e_{j}|[a_{j}^{\dagger},X]|\mathbf{n}\rangle=\sqrt{n_{j}+1}\,(x_{\mathbf{n}}-x_{\mathbf{n}+e_{j}}).$
Every occupation vector is connected to the vacuum by these steps.
Hence  $X$  is scalar and  $\ker L=\mathbb{C}\sqrt{\sigma_{\beta}}$ .
Compact resolvent now gives a positive gap  $\lambda$ .
Step 8: entropy decay and uniqueness among states.
Apply Theorem 1.2 with  $p=4$  and
$C(s)=\max\{1,\widetilde{Z}^{1/4}e^{sb_{s}}\}$  to obtain the claimed
relative-entropy estimate. To check uniqueness also for invariant
states of infinite relative entropy, approximate any state  $\tau$  in
trace norm by its normalized finite particle compressions  $\rho_{M}$ .
These have finite relative entropy because each particle cutoff
has finite dimension and the Gibbs state is faithful there. Pinsker’s
inequality and the entropy estimate give
$\|\Phi_{t}(\rho_{M})-\sigma_{\beta}\|_{1}^{2}\leq 2D(\Phi_{t}(\rho_{M})\|\sigma_{\beta})\leq 2e^{-\alpha(s)t}D(\rho_{M}\|\sigma_{\beta})\longrightarrow 0.$
If  $\Phi_{t}(\tau)=\tau$ , trace-norm contractivity gives
$\|\tau-\sigma_{\beta}\|_{1}\leq\|\tau-\rho_{M}\|_{1}+\|\Phi_{t}(\rho_{M})-\sigma_{\beta}\|_{1}.$
Letting  $t\to\infty$  and then  $M\to\infty$  proves  $\tau=\sigma_{\beta}$ .
Step 9: the quadratic-jump alternative.
We record the changes needed when each cubic pair is replaced by a
quadratic pair. Step 1 applies with common energy exponents  $1/2$  and
$1$ . In Step 2 take
$A=a_{i}^{2},\qquad D_{i}=b_{i}I+2\sum_{j}w_{ij}N_{j},\qquad c_{i}=b_{i}+3U_{i}+2\mu_{i}.$
Then  $[H_{0},A]=-A(D_{i}-c_{i}I)$  exactly, and
$\|A(z+D_{i})^{-1}Q_{n}\|\leq C$  for  $\operatorname{Re}z\geq-1$ .
For a hopping term the direct commutator is
$[a_{r}^{\dagger}a_{s},a_{i}^{2}]=-2\mathbf{1}_{\{r=i\}}a_{i}a_{s}$ .
The resolvent-commutator coefficient is bounded by
$C\frac{(n_{i}+1)|w_{ir}-w_{is}|\sqrt{(n_{r}+1)n_{s}}}{D_{i}(\mathbf{n})^{2}}\leq C\sqrt{n+1},$
using the same nonnegative-interaction estimate as in Step 2.
Thus its resolvent identity holds with a remainder bounded by
$C\sqrt{n+1}$ . Step 3 consequently gives
$\|(L_{i,2}^{-}-a_{i}^{2})Q_{n}\|+\|L_{i,2}^{+}Q_{n}\|\leq C\sqrt{n+1}\log(n+2).$
For every  $\varepsilon>0$ , expanding the squared lowering norms and
using  $2ab\leq\varepsilon a^{2}+\varepsilon^{-1}b^{2}$  now gives
$C_{H}\geq(1-\varepsilon)\sum_{i}N_{i}^{2}-C_{\varepsilon}(\mathsf{N}+I)\log^{2}(\mathsf{N}+2I),\qquad C_{H}\leq C(\mathsf{N}+I)^{2}.$
The quadratic part of  $H$  is  $\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j}w_{ij}N_{i}N_{j}$ ;
hopping and the remaining terms have sector norm  $O(n+1)$ . Hence
$\widetilde{H}\leq\frac{\Lambda}{2}\sum_{i}N_{i}^{2}+C(\mathsf{N}+I),\qquad C_{H}\geq b\widetilde{H}-C_{b}I\quad(0<b<2/\Lambda),$
where the smaller logarithmic error is absorbed using
$\widetilde{H}\geq c(\mathsf{N}+I)^{2}$ .
Step 4 still gives  $\|B_{\alpha,\theta}Q_{n}\|\leq C_{\theta_{*}}\sqrt{n+1}$ .
The positive average defining  $\operatorname{Re}D_{\theta}$  has mass
$1/2$  and leaves  $\widetilde{H}$  invariant. Together with the gain
bound of Step 5, which is infinitesimal relative to the quadratic
energy, it follows that for every  $0<c<1/\Lambda$ ,
$\operatorname{Re}\langle X,W_{\theta}LW_{\theta}^{-1}X\rangle\geq c\langle X,\widetilde{H}X+X\widetilde{H}\rangle-C_{c,\theta_{*}}\|X\|_{2}^{2},\qquad 0\leq\theta\leq\theta_{*}<\beta/4.$
At  $\theta=0$  the same relative-bound argument identifies the operator
and form domains as  $D(\mathcal{K}_{2})$  and  $D(\mathcal{K}_{2}^{1/2})$ ,
with finite particle matrices as a core.
Set  $\theta_{*}=(\beta/2)(1/2-1/p)$  and choose
$\theta_{*}/s<c<1/\Lambda$ . This is possible under the strict time
condition in the statement. For the weighted compressions in Step 6,
$\frac{1}{2}\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}t}\|U_{M}(t)\|_{2}^{2}\leq(\theta_{*}/s-c)\langle U_{M},\widetilde{H}U_{M}+U_{M}\widetilde{H}\rangle+C_{c,\theta_{*}}\|U_{M}(t)\|_{2}^{2}.$
Integration and the same form-core limit and Fatou argument give
$\|T_{s}:L^{2}(\sigma_{\beta})\to L^{p}(\sigma_{\beta})\|\leq\widetilde{Z}^{1/2-1/p}e^{sC_{c,\theta_{*}}}<\infty$ .
The quadratic form domain embeds compactly into Hilbert–Schmidt
space. Step 7’s kernel argument uses only the linear rows and applies
unchanged, giving a simple kernel and a positive gap. Step 8 at any
$s>\beta\Lambda/8$  proves entropy decay and uniqueness among states.
∎
Remark 4.4.
For  $k=1$ ,  $U_{1}=2$ , and  $\mu_{1}=-1$ , the Hamiltonian is  $N^{2}$ .
The linear pair alone has no bounded  $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{4}$  endpoint by
Theorem 4.2; the quadratic pair gives a finite
waiting time, and the cubic pair gives smoothing at every positive
time. The theorem treats both enlarged families with full hopping. It does not give the same entropy estimate
for the samplers with only linear jumps in [14],
nor a rate uniform in the number of modes.
4.2. Finite-rank Coulomb truncations
We next treat a trapped Coulomb system in two or three dimensions.
The interaction is compressed to a finite Hermite subspace, while the
Hamiltonian and sampler act on the full infinite-dimensional space.
For each fixed particle number and cutoff, we prove a bounded
$L^{2}$ -to- $L^{4}$  map and exponential entropy decay.
Corollary 4.5 (Coulomb sampler with a finite-rank interaction).
Let  $d\in\{2,3\}$ ,  $n,M\geq 1$ ,  $\beta,\eta>0$ , and
$\alpha_{n,i,j}\in\mathbb{R}$ . On  $\mathcal{H}_{n}=L^{2}((\mathbb{R}^{d})^{n})$ , with
$x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})$ , define
$H_{0,n}=-\Delta+|x|^{2},\qquad W_{n}(x)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n}\alpha_{n,i,j}w_{d}(x_{i}-x_{j}),\qquad w_{2}(y)=-\log|y|,\quad w_{3}(y)=|y|^{-1}.$
Let  $P_{M}$  project onto the first  $M$  one-particle Hermite basis
vectors, ordered by energy with a fixed ordering of degeneracies, and
put
$\Pi_{M}=P_{M}^{\otimes n},\qquad W_{n,M}=\Pi_{M}W_{n}\Pi_{M},\qquad H_{n,M}=H_{0,n}+W_{n,M},\qquad\sigma_{\beta}=\frac{e^{-\beta H_{n,M}}}{\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H_{n,M}})}.$
Consider the coherent Gibbs sampler with bare jumps
$a_{ij}=(x_{ij}+\partial_{x_{ij}})/\sqrt{2}$  and
$a_{ij}^{\dagger}=(x_{ij}-\partial_{x_{ij}})/\sqrt{2}$ ,
$1\leq i\leq n$ ,  $1\leq j\leq d$ , and filter
$\widehat{f}_{\eta}(\nu)=e^{-\eta\nu^{2}-\beta\nu/4}$ .
Its conservative KMS-symmetric semigroup  $\Phi_{t}$  has
$\sigma_{\beta}$  as its unique invariant state, and its nonnegative
standard-form generator has compact resolvent and positive gap.
For its Heisenberg semigroup  $T_{t}$ , there are finite constants
$s_{n,M}>0$  and  $\alpha_{n,M}>0$  such that
$\|T_{s_{n,M}}:L^{2}(\sigma_{\beta})\to L^{4}(\sigma_{\beta})\|\leq 1,\qquad D(\Phi_{t}(\rho)\|\sigma_{\beta})\leq e^{-\alpha_{n,M}t}D(\rho\|\sigma_{\beta})$
for every state  $\rho$  and  $t\geq 0$ .
The conclusion also holds with any bounded self-adjoint
$W=\Pi_{M}W\Pi_{M}$  in place of  $W_{n,M}$ .
The constants may depend on  $n,M,\beta,\eta$ , and the interaction;
the estimates need not be uniform in the cutoff.
The compressed interaction is well defined: both Coulomb kernels
are locally integrable, and Hermite functions decay rapidly, so
$\langle\varphi_{\boldsymbol{\ell}},W_{n,M}\varphi_{\boldsymbol{r}}\rangle=\sum_{i<j}\alpha_{n,i,j}\int_{(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{n}}\overline{\varphi_{\boldsymbol{\ell}}(x)}w_{d}(x_{i}-x_{j})\varphi_{\boldsymbol{r}}(x)\,\,\mathrm{d}x\quad(1\leq\ell_{i},r_{i}\leq M)$
is finite, where  $\varphi_{\boldsymbol{\ell}}=\varphi_{\ell_{1}}\otimes\cdots\otimes\varphi_{\ell_{n}}$ .
The resulting matrix is self-adjoint, and
$H_{n,M}=H_{0,n}$  on  $(I-\Pi_{M})\mathcal{H}_{n}$ .
This finite-energy support lets us prove the  $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{4}$
bound directly. The form comparison in Proposition 3.3
alone would not give that bound.
An oscillator estimate.
Changing the Hamiltonian produces terms with one unbounded ladder
operator. The next estimate controls them.
For a general  $k$ -mode space  $\mathcal{H}^{(k)}=\ell^{2}(\mathbb{N}_{0}^{k})$ , put
$\mathsf{N}=\sum_{j=1}^{k}N_{j}$ . In the Coulomb application,
$k=dn$  and  $H_{0,n}=dn+2\mathsf{N}$  under the Hermite identification.
On  $\mathscr{T}_{2}(\mathcal{H}^{(k)})$  define the nonnegative operator
$\mathcal{K}X=\mathsf{N}X+X\mathsf{N},\qquad e^{\theta\mathcal{K}}X=e^{\theta\mathsf{N}}Xe^{\theta\mathsf{N}}.$
We first use these formulas on the span  $\mathscr{F}$  of the
oscillator matrix units. For  $r_{-}>r_{+}>0$ , set
$c=(r_{-}+r_{+})/2$ ,  $v=\sqrt{r_{-}r_{+}}$ , and define the free standard-form
qOU operator by
$L_{0}X=c\mathcal{K}X+kr_{+}X-v\sum_{j=1}^{k}(a_{j}Xa_{j}^{\dagger}+a_{j}^{\dagger}Xa_{j}).$
This is the sum of  $k$  one-mode qOU operators.
Lemma 4.6.
Let  $L\geq 0$  be self-adjoint on  $\mathscr{T}_{2}(\mathcal{H}^{(k)})$ ,
with  $\mathscr{F}$  a form core contained in  $D(L)$ , and write
$L=L_{0}+R$  on  $\mathscr{F}$ . Suppose that  $R\mathscr{F}\subset\mathscr{F}$
and that, for some  $\theta_{*}>0$ ,
$\kappa_{*}:=c-v\cosh(2\theta_{*})>0,\qquad\sup_{0\leq\theta\leq\theta_{*}}\|e^{\theta\mathcal{K}}Re^{-\theta\mathcal{K}}X\|_{2}\leq C_{R}\|(\mathcal{K}+I)^{1/2}X\|_{2}\quad(X\in\mathscr{F}).$
Then there is a finite  $C_{*}>0$  such that, with
$s_{*}=2\theta_{*}/\kappa_{*}$ ,
(4.10)
$\|e^{\theta_{*}\mathcal{K}}e^{-s_{*}L}X\|_{2}\leq e^{C_{*}s_{*}}\|X\|_{2},\qquad X\in\mathscr{T}_{2}(\mathcal{H}^{(k)}).$
Proof.
Put  $R_{\theta}=e^{\theta\mathcal{K}}Re^{-\theta\mathcal{K}}$  on
$\mathscr{F}$ . The conjugated free operator is
$e^{\theta\mathcal{K}}L_{0}e^{-\theta\mathcal{K}}X=c\mathcal{K}X+kr_{+}X-v\sum_{j}\bigl(e^{-2\theta}a_{j}Xa_{j}^{\dagger}+e^{2\theta}a_{j}^{\dagger}Xa_{j}\bigr).$
The two gain maps are Hilbert–Schmidt adjoints. Their common
quadratic-form estimate follows from
$\displaystyle 2\left|\sum_{j}\langle X,a_{j}Xa_{j}^{\dagger}\rangle\right|$
$\displaystyle=2\left|\sum_{j}\langle a_{j}^{\dagger}X,Xa_{j}^{\dagger}\rangle\right|\leq\sum_{j}\bigl(\|a_{j}^{\dagger}X\|_{2}^{2}+\|Xa_{j}^{\dagger}\|_{2}^{2}\bigr)=\langle X,\mathcal{K}X\rangle+k\|X\|_{2}^{2}.$
Consequently
$\displaystyle\operatorname{Re}\langle X,e^{\theta\mathcal{K}}L_{0}e^{-\theta\mathcal{K}}X\rangle\geq{}$
$\displaystyle(c-v\cosh(2\theta))\langle X,\mathcal{K}X\rangle+k(r_{+}-v\cosh(2\theta))\|X\|_{2}^{2}.$
Hence, uniformly for  $0\leq\theta\leq\theta_{*}$ ,
$\operatorname{Re}\langle X,e^{\theta\mathcal{K}}L_{0}e^{-\theta\mathcal{K}}X\rangle\geq\kappa_{*}\langle X,\mathcal{K}X\rangle-kv\cosh(2\theta_{*})\|X\|_{2}^{2}.$
For the perturbation, Cauchy–Schwarz and Young’s inequality give
$\displaystyle|\langle X,R_{\theta}X\rangle|$
$\displaystyle\leq C_{R}\|X\|_{2}\|(\mathcal{K}+I)^{1/2}X\|_{2}$
$\displaystyle\leq C_{R}\|X\|_{2}\langle X,\mathcal{K}X\rangle^{1/2}+C_{R}\|X\|_{2}^{2}$
$\displaystyle\leq\frac{\kappa_{*}}{2}\langle X,\mathcal{K}X\rangle+\left(C_{R}+\frac{C_{R}^{2}}{2\kappa_{*}}\right)\|X\|_{2}^{2}.$
Thus one may take
$C_{*}=kv\cosh(2\theta_{*})+C_{R}+C_{R}^{2}/(2\kappa_{*})$ , or any larger
positive constant, to obtain
(4.11)
$\operatorname{Re}\langle X,e^{\theta\mathcal{K}}Le^{-\theta\mathcal{K}}X\rangle\geq\frac{\kappa_{*}}{2}\langle X,\mathcal{K}X\rangle-C_{*}\|X\|_{2}^{2}.$
We justify the evolution estimate by finite-dimensional approximation.
Let  $\mathsf{P}_{J}=\mathbf{1}_{[0,J]}(\mathcal{K})$  and let
$L_{J}=\mathsf{P}_{J}L\mathsf{P}_{J}$  on its finite-dimensional range.
For  $X_{J}(t)=e^{-tL_{J}}\mathsf{P}_{J}X$  and
$\theta(t)=\kappa_{*}t/2$ , set  $U_{J}(t)=e^{\theta(t)\mathcal{K}}X_{J}(t)$ .
Since  $\mathsf{P}_{J}$  commutes with  $\mathcal{K}$ ,
Equation 4.11 applies to the compressed
operator with the same constants. For  $0\leq t\leq s_{*}$  it yields
$\frac{1}{2}\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}t}\|U_{J}(t)\|_{2}^{2}=\theta^{\prime}(t)\langle U_{J}(t),\mathcal{K}U_{J}(t)\rangle-\operatorname{Re}\langle U_{J}(t),e^{\theta(t)\mathcal{K}}L_{J}e^{-\theta(t)\mathcal{K}}U_{J}(t)\rangle\leq C_{*}\|U_{J}(t)\|_{2}^{2}.$
Multiplying by  $e^{-2C_{*}t}$  and integrating gives
$\|U_{J}(t)\|_{2}^{2}\leq e^{2C_{*}t}\|\mathsf{P}_{J}X\|_{2}^{2}\leq e^{2C_{*}t}\|X\|_{2}^{2},\qquad 0\leq t\leq s_{*}.$
To pass to the limit, put  $u=(L+I)^{-1}X$  and
$u_{J}=(L_{J}+I)^{-1}\mathsf{P}_{J}X$ .
The two variational equations imply orthogonality of  $u-u_{J}$  to
$\operatorname{Ran}\mathsf{P}_{J}$  for the inner product of the form
$\mathcal{E}+\|\cdot\|_{2}^{2}$ . Therefore
$\|u-u_{J}\|_{\mathcal{E}}\leq\inf_{v\in\operatorname{Ran}\mathsf{P}_{J}}\|u-v\|_{\mathcal{E}}\longrightarrow 0,$
because the increasing ranges exhaust the form core  $\mathscr{F}$ .
Strong resolvent convergence gives
$e^{-s_{*}L_{J}}\mathsf{P}_{J}X\to e^{-s_{*}L}X$  in Hilbert–Schmidt norm
[27, Theorem III.4.8].
Write the respective matrix coefficients as  $y^{(J)}_{\mathbf{m}\mathbf{n}}$
and  $y_{\mathbf{m}\mathbf{n}}$ . Since  $\theta(s_{*})=\theta_{*}$ , Fatou’s lemma yields
$\sum_{\mathbf{m},\mathbf{n}}e^{2\theta_{*}(|\mathbf{m}|+|\mathbf{n}|)}|y_{\mathbf{m}\mathbf{n}}|^{2}\leq\liminf_{J}\sum_{\mathbf{m},\mathbf{n}}e^{2\theta_{*}(|\mathbf{m}|+|\mathbf{n}|)}|y^{(J)}_{\mathbf{m}\mathbf{n}}|^{2}\leq e^{2C_{*}s_{*}}\|X\|_{2}^{2}.$
The finite left-hand side shows that the output belongs to
$D(e^{\theta_{*}\mathcal{K}})$ , and its square root proves
(4.10).
∎
Proof of Corollary 4.5.
Write  $H=H_{0,n}+W$ ,  $\sigma=\sigma_{\beta}(H)$ , and
$\sigma_{0}=\sigma_{\beta}(H_{0,n})$ .
Choose  $c_{0}$  so that  $\widetilde{H}=H+c_{0}I\geq I$ . Outside the
finite oscillator block,  $\widetilde{H}$  agrees with  $H_{0,n}+c_{0}I$ .
On the finite block all powers of  $\widetilde{H}$  are bounded.
Since a coordinate ladder changes the oscillator number by one,
each bare jump  $A$  satisfies
$\|A\widetilde{H}^{-1/2}\|+\|\widetilde{H}^{1/2}A\widetilde{H}^{-1}\|<\infty.$
The finite Hermite span is a common invariant core, and
$\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-b\widetilde{H}})<\infty$  for every  $b>0$ .
These bounds verify the energy and domain assumptions of
[4, Condition A and Proposition 2.4].
The Gaussian filter satisfies the required KMS and boundedness
conditions. The construction in that paper therefore gives a
conservative KMS-symmetric sampler.
Its standard-form operator  $L\geq 0$  is obtained by closing the form on
$\mathscr{F}+\mathbb{C}\sqrt{\sigma}$ . Here the finite  $H$ -spectral matrices
span  $\mathscr{F}$ , since  $W$  acts inside a fixed finite oscillator
block. We will show that  $\mathscr{F}$  alone is a form core.
Step 1: finite-energy changes of the coefficients.
Let  $L^{\ell}$  and  $L_{0}^{\ell}$  denote the filtered jumps for  $H$  and
$H_{0,n}$ , respectively, with  $\ell$  ranging over the  $2k$  bare
ladders. There is a finite oscillator spectral projection  $Q$  such
that
(4.12)
$L^{\ell}=L_{0}^{\ell}+F_{\ell},\qquad F_{\ell}=QF_{\ell}Q.$
Choose  $J_{0}$  with  $\Pi_{M}\leq\mathbf{1}_{[0,J_{0}]}(\mathsf{N})$  and
take  $Q=\mathbf{1}_{[0,J_{0}+1]}(\mathsf{N})$ .
For every bare coordinate ladder  $A$ ,
$(I-Q)A\Pi_{M}=0,\qquad\Pi_{M}A(I-Q)=0,$
because it changes total occupation by one. On the complement of
$\Pi_{M}$ ,  $H$  and  $H_{0,n}$  have the same spectral decomposition.
All changed matrix elements of the filtered jump therefore have
both source and target in  $Q\mathcal{H}_{n}$ :
$(I-Q)(L^{\ell}-L_{0}^{\ell})=0,\qquad(L^{\ell}-L_{0}^{\ell})(I-Q)=0.$
This proves (4.12). Diagonalizing
$H$  inside  $\Pi_{M}\mathcal{H}_{n}$  does not enlarge these spaces.
We enlarge  $Q$  below when further ladder actions occur.
Write the state generator as
$\mathcal{L}(\rho)=\sum_{\ell}L^{\ell}\rho(L^{\ell})^{\dagger}+M_{H}\rho+\rho M_{H}^{\dagger}$ .
We also need the finite-energy property for the drift, including
its correction Hamiltonian. For the bare ladder  $A^{\ell}$ , let
$A^{\ell}_{\nu,H}$  denote its frequency component relative to  $H$ .
Its free frequency is  $\nu_{\ell}\in\{-2,2\}$ . The same support argument gives, for each frequency,
$A^{\ell}_{\nu,H}=\mathbf{1}_{\{\nu=\nu_{\ell}\}}A^{\ell}+G^{\ell}_{\nu},\qquad G^{\ell}_{\nu}=QG^{\ell}_{\nu}Q,$
with only finitely many nonzero  $G^{\ell}_{\nu}$ .
Equation (2.20) at  $\sigma_{E}=\infty$  reads
$M_{H}=-\sum_{\ell,\nu,\mu}\frac{\overline{\widehat{f}_{\eta}(\nu)}\widehat{f}_{\eta}(\mu)e^{\beta(\nu-\mu)/4}}{2\cosh(\beta(\nu-\mu)/4)}(A^{\ell}_{\nu,H})^{\dagger}A^{\ell}_{\mu,H}.$
Subtracting the free expression leaves the products
$\displaystyle(A^{\ell}_{\nu,H})^{\dagger}A^{\ell}_{\mu,H}$
$\displaystyle-\mathbf{1}_{\{\nu=\nu_{\ell}\}}\mathbf{1}_{\{\mu=\nu_{\ell}\}}(A^{\ell})^{\dagger}A^{\ell}=\mathbf{1}_{\{\nu=\nu_{\ell}\}}(A^{\ell})^{\dagger}G^{\ell}_{\mu}+\mathbf{1}_{\{\mu=\nu_{\ell}\}}(G^{\ell}_{\nu})^{\dagger}A^{\ell}+(G^{\ell}_{\nu})^{\dagger}G^{\ell}_{\mu}.$
Every term has finite-energy support: multiplication by a ladder
adds at most one shell to the support of  $G^{\ell}_{\nu}$ .
After enlarging  $Q$  by that shell, we have
$M_{H}=M_{0}+F_{0}$  with  $F_{0}=QF_{0}Q$ .
Put  $Z=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H})$  and  $Z_{0}=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H_{0,n}})$ .
Since both Hamiltonians are reduced by  $\Pi_{M}$  and agree outside it,
for every real  $a$ ,
$(I-\Pi_{M})\sigma^{a}\sigma_{0}^{-a}(I-\Pi_{M})=(Z_{0}/Z)^{a}(I-\Pi_{M}).$
Inside the block the same product is a finite invertible matrix.
Conjugating to standard form still changes only finite-energy
coefficients:
$C_{\ell}:=\sigma^{-1/4}L^{\ell}\sigma^{1/4}=C_{\ell}^{0}+\widetilde{F}_{\ell},\qquad D_{H}:=\sigma^{-1/4}M_{H}\sigma^{1/4}=M_{0}+\widetilde{F}_{0}.$
Here every  $\widetilde{F}_{\ell}$  has finite-energy support; the
normalizing scalar cancels in each conjugation.
KMS symmetry identifies the standard-form operator with
$LX=-\sum_{\ell}C_{\ell}XC_{\ell}^{\dagger}-D_{H}X-XD_{H}^{\dagger}.$
For the free operator the two rates are
$r_{\pm}=|\widehat{f}_{\eta}(\pm 2)|^{2}$ , so
$r_{+}=e^{-2\beta}r_{-}$  and the formula for  $L_{0}$  above applies.
In particular, subtraction gives the explicit perturbation
$\displaystyle RX={}$
$\displaystyle-\sum_{\ell}\bigl(C_{\ell}^{0}X\widetilde{F}_{\ell}^{\dagger}+\widetilde{F}_{\ell}X(C_{\ell}^{0})^{\dagger}+\widetilde{F}_{\ell}X\widetilde{F}_{\ell}^{\dagger}\bigr)-\widetilde{F}_{0}X-X\widetilde{F}_{0}^{\dagger}.$
The terms with two  $\widetilde{F}$  factors and the two drift
terms have bounded coefficients. Each cross
term contains one free ladder and one finite-energy coefficient, so
the only unbounded maps to estimate have the form
(4.13)
$X\longmapsto FXa_{j}^{\sharp},\qquad X\longmapsto a_{j}^{\sharp}XF,\qquad F=QFQ,\qquad a_{j}^{\sharp}\in\{a_{j},a_{j}^{\dagger}\}.$
Step 2: the weighted perturbation estimate.
Choose  $J_{Q}$  so that  $Q\leq\mathbf{1}_{[0,J_{Q}]}(\mathsf{N})$ .
For  $F=QFQ$  and  $\theta\geq 0$ , spectral calculus gives
$\|e^{\pm\theta\mathsf{N}}Fe^{\mp\theta\mathsf{N}}\|_{\infty}\leq e^{\theta J_{Q}}\|F\|_{\infty}.$
These factors are uniformly bounded for
$[0,\beta/4]$ . For the ladder factors one has
$e^{\theta\mathsf{N}}a_{j}e^{-\theta\mathsf{N}}=e^{-\theta}a_{j},\qquad e^{\theta\mathsf{N}}a_{j}^{\dagger}e^{-\theta\mathsf{N}}=e^{\theta}a_{j}^{\dagger}.$
For the left multiplications, the ladder relations give
$\|a_{j}X\|_{2}^{2}=\operatorname{Tr}(X^{\dagger}N_{j}X),\qquad\|a_{j}^{\dagger}X\|_{2}^{2}=\operatorname{Tr}(X^{\dagger}(N_{j}+I)X).$
Right multiplication yields the corresponding terms with  $XN_{j}$ .
Since  $N_{j}\leq\mathsf{N}$ , each norm is at most
$\|(\mathcal{K}+I)^{1/2}X\|_{2}$ , and hence
$\|a_{j}^{\sharp}X\|_{2}+\|Xa_{j}^{\sharp}\|_{2}\leq 2\|(\mathcal{K}+I)^{1/2}X\|_{2}.$
For example, with  $F_{\theta}=e^{\theta\mathsf{N}}Fe^{-\theta\mathsf{N}}$ ,
$\|e^{\theta\mathcal{K}}(F(e^{-\theta\mathcal{K}}X)a_{j}^{\sharp})\|_{2}\leq e^{|\theta|}\|F_{\theta}\|_{\infty}\|(\mathcal{K}+I)^{1/2}X\|_{2}.$
Summing the finitely many terms gives
$\sup_{0\leq\theta\leq\beta/4}\|e^{\theta\mathcal{K}}Re^{-\theta\mathcal{K}}X\|_{2}\leq C_{R}\|(\mathcal{K}+I)^{1/2}X\|_{2}.$
At  $\theta=0$ , the lower and upper free estimates give
$(c-v)\langle X,\mathcal{K}X\rangle-kv\|X\|_{2}^{2}\leq\langle X,L_{0}X\rangle\leq(c+v)\langle X,\mathcal{K}X\rangle+k(r_{+}+v)\|X\|_{2}^{2}.$
The bound on  $R$  implies, for any  $\varepsilon>0$ ,
$|\langle X,RX\rangle|\leq\varepsilon\langle X,\mathcal{K}X\rangle+\left(C_{R}+\frac{C_{R}^{2}}{4\varepsilon}\right)\|X\|_{2}^{2}.$
Choose  $\varepsilon=(c-v)/2>0$  and absorb this term into the lower
bound. After adding a sufficiently large multiple of  $\|X\|_{2}^{2}$ ,
there are  $c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}>0$  such that
$c_{1}\|(\mathcal{K}+I)^{1/2}X\|_{2}^{2}\leq\mathcal{E}(X)+c_{2}\|X\|_{2}^{2}\leq c_{3}\|(\mathcal{K}+I)^{1/2}X\|_{2}^{2}.$
Hence the closure on  $\mathscr{F}$  has form domain
$D(\mathcal{K}^{1/2})$ . The Gibbs vector belongs even to
$D(\mathcal{K})$ : outside the finite block its diagonal coefficients
are  $Z^{-1/2}e^{-\beta(k+2|\mathbf{n}|)/2}$ , so
$\|(\mathcal{K}+I)\sqrt{\sigma}\|_{2}^{2}\leq C+C\sum_{\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{k}}(1+|\mathbf{n}|)^{2}e^{-2\beta|\mathbf{n}|}<\infty.$
Every term in the generator therefore maps  $\sqrt{\sigma}$  into
Hilbert–Schmidt space, and invariance
gives  $L\sqrt{\sigma}=0$  in this coefficient formula. Thus the closed
form on  $D(\mathcal{K}^{1/2})$  also annihilates  $\sqrt{\sigma}$ .
For  $\mathsf{P}_{J}=\mathbf{1}_{[0,J]}(\mathcal{K})$ , this gives
$\|(\mathcal{K}+I)^{1/2}(I-\mathsf{P}_{J})\sqrt{\sigma}\|_{2}\longrightarrow 0,$
so adding  $\sqrt{\sigma}$  does not change the closed form. This proves that
$\mathscr{F}$  is a form core for the constructed operator  $L$ ;
the coefficient formula also gives  $\mathscr{F}\subset D(L)$ .
The parameters in Lemma 4.6 can now be chosen as
$\theta_{*}=\beta/4,\qquad\kappa_{*}=v\bigl(\cosh\beta-\cosh(\beta/2)\bigr)>0,\qquad s_{*}=\frac{\beta}{2\kappa_{*}},$
because  $c/v=\cosh\beta$ . The lemma gives
(4.10).
Step 3: the endpoint and entropy decay.
The operator
$B_{*}=\sigma^{-1/8}e^{-\beta\mathsf{N}/4}$
has a bounded extension. Since  $H_{0,n}=k+2\mathsf{N}$ ,
its two blocks are
$B_{*}=\Pi_{M}B_{*}\Pi_{M}+Z^{1/8}e^{\beta k/8}(I-\Pi_{M}).$
The first block is a finite matrix and the second is scalar.
For  $Y\in D(e^{(\beta/4)\mathcal{K}})$ , first on finite matrices and
then by closure,
$\displaystyle\|Y\|_{4\leftarrow 2,\sigma}$
$\displaystyle=\|\sigma^{-1/8}Y\sigma^{-1/8}\|_{4}=\|B_{*}(e^{(\beta/4)\mathcal{K}}Y)B_{*}^{\dagger}\|_{4}$
$\displaystyle\leq\|B_{*}\|_{\infty}^{2}\|e^{(\beta/4)\mathcal{K}}Y\|_{4}\leq\|B_{*}\|_{\infty}^{2}\|e^{(\beta/4)\mathcal{K}}Y\|_{2}.$
Putting  $Y=e^{-s_{*}L}X$  and using the oscillator estimate gives
$\|e^{-s_{*}L}X\|_{4\leftarrow 2,\sigma}\leq\|B_{*}\|_{\infty}^{2}e^{C_{*}s_{*}}\|X\|_{2}.$
It follows that  $\|T_{s_{*}}:L^{2}(\sigma)\to L^{4}(\sigma)\|\leq C$ ,
where  $C=\max\{1,\|B_{*}\|_{\infty}^{2}e^{C_{*}s_{*}}\}<\infty$ .
The form comparison also proves compactness. For
$\mathsf{P}_{J}=\mathbf{1}_{[0,J]}(\mathcal{K})$  and integer  $J\geq 0$ ,
$\|(I-\mathsf{P}_{J})X\|_{2}^{2}\leq\frac{\|(\mathcal{K}+I)^{1/2}X\|_{2}^{2}}{J+1}\leq\frac{\mathcal{E}(X)+c_{2}\|X\|_{2}^{2}}{c_{1}(J+1)}.$
Since  $\mathsf{P}_{J}$  has finite rank, the form unit ball is relatively
compact in Hilbert–Schmidt space. This is the compact embedding
criterion for compact resolvent
[19, Sections 10.3 and 12.1].
The nonvanishing-filter kernel argument for finite-rank perturbations
in [15, Section 3.3] gives
$\ker L=\mathbb{C}\sqrt{\sigma}$ . Hence  $\lambda=\operatorname{gap}(L)>0$ .
By Lemma 2.5, one may take
$s_{n,M}=s_{*}+\frac{\log C+\frac{1}{2}\log 3}{\lambda}.$
Finally Theorem 1.2 gives the stated entropy estimate,
for example with
$\alpha_{n,M}=(2s_{*}+(2\log C+1)/\lambda)^{-1}>0$ .
∎
4.3. A bounded-rate obstruction
We show that bounded escape rates can prevent hypercontractivity
even when the Gibbs state is strongly confining and the sampler has a
positive spectral gap.
Proposition 4.7.
Let  $T_{t}$  be a conservative continuous-time Markov semigroup on a countable
set  $\Omega$  with faithful invariant probability  $\pi$ . For distinct  $x,y\in\Omega$ , let  $q(x,y)\geq 0$  be the transition rate
from  $x$  to  $y$ , and put  $q(x)=\sum_{y\neq x}q(x,y)$ , the total rate
out of  $x$ . Here  $L^{p}(\pi)$  has norm
$\|f\|_{p,\pi}=(\sum_{x\in\Omega}\pi(x)|f(x)|^{p})^{1/p}$ . If there are points  $x_{k}$  such
that
$\pi(x_{k})\longrightarrow 0,\qquad\sup_{k}q(x_{k})\leq\Lambda<\infty,$
then for every  $p>2$  and every finite  $t>0$ ,
$\|T_{t}:L^{2}(\pi)\to L^{p}(\pi)\|=\infty.$
Proof.
Let  $\mathbf{1}_{\{x_{k}\}}$  be the indicator of the singleton  $\{x_{k}\}$
and set  $f_{k}=\pi(x_{k})^{-1/2}\mathbf{1}_{\{x_{k}\}}$ , so
$\|f_{k}\|_{2,\pi}=1$ . The event that the chain makes no jump before time
$t$  has probability at least  $e^{-\Lambda t}$  when it starts from
$x_{k}$ . Hence
$(T_{t}f_{k})(x_{k})\geq e^{-\Lambda t}\pi(x_{k})^{-1/2}$
and therefore  $\|T_{t}f_{k}\|_{p,\pi}\geq e^{-\Lambda t}\pi(x_{k})^{1/p-1/2}\longrightarrow\infty.$
∎
Consider now the one-mode periodic charging model on  $\ell^{2}(\mathbb{Z})$ ,
with charge basis  $(e_{m})_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}$ . Define the charge operator
$\mathsf{n}e_{m}=me_{m}$  and the bilateral shift  $Se_{m}=e_{m+1}$ . Let
$H=h(\mathsf{n})$ , where  $h$  is a nonconstant even polynomial
( $h(-m)=h(m)$ ) with positive leading coefficient, and use bare jumps
$S,S^{\dagger},\mathsf{n}$ . The charge operator  $\mathsf{n}$  is distinct
from the particle count  $n$  of the preceding application.
The charge row alone generates the conservative dephasing semigroup
$(\Phi_{t}^{\rm charge}(\rho))_{mk}=e^{-t|\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(0)|^{2}(m-k)^{2}/2}\rho_{mk}.$
The two filtered shifts are bounded, and their loss operators are
diagonal, so the correction Hamiltonian is zero. Their bounded GKLS
generator perturbs this dephasing generator. The bounded perturbation
product formula gives a conservative completely positive semigroup;
the KMS pairing of the shifts makes the Gibbs state invariant.
For a diagonal observable  $g(\mathsf{n})$ , with  $g:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C}$ , the charge
row vanishes. The invariant diagonal sector is the birth–death chain
with generator  $Q$  given by
$(Qg)(m)=r_{m}^{+}\bigl(g(m+1)-g(m)\bigr)+r_{m}^{-}\bigl(g(m-1)-g(m)\bigr),\qquad r_{m}^{\pm}=|\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(h(m\pm 1)-h(m))|^{2}.$
The filter (2.3) gives  $0\leq r_{m}^{\pm}\leq 1$ .
Its invariant probability is
$Z_{\rm ch}=\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}e^{-\beta h(m)},\qquad\pi_{m}=Z_{\rm ch}^{-1}e^{-\beta h(m)},\qquad\sigma_{\rm ch}=\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}\pi_{m}|e_{m}\rangle\langle e_{m}|.$
Since diagonal observables satisfy
$\|g(\mathsf{n})\|_{p,\sigma_{\rm ch}}=\|g\|_{p,\pi}$ , the classical
norm bound is a lower bound for the quantum norm. One has  $\pi_{m}\to 0$  as
$|m|\to\infty$ , while the holding rates satisfy
$r_{m}^{+}+r_{m}^{-}\leq 2$ . Thus Proposition 4.7 shows that
this invariant diagonal sector, and hence the full quantum semigroup, has
no finite-time  $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{p}$  endpoint for any  $p>2$ . This gives a
periodic-charge counterpart of the  $m>d_{*}$  obstruction above. The sampler nevertheless has a positive gap. We prove this
separately on the diagonal and off-diagonal sectors.
After the unitary map  $g\mapsto(\sqrt{\pi_{m}}g(m))_{m}$ , the negative
diagonal generator is the Jacobi operator with diagonal
$r_{m}^{+}+r_{m}^{-}$  and off-diagonal entries
$-\sqrt{r_{m}^{+}r_{m+1}^{-}}$ .
Since  $h$  is an even confining polynomial,
$r_{m}^{+}+r_{m}^{-}\longrightarrow 1,\qquad\sqrt{r_{m}^{+}r_{m+1}^{-}}\longrightarrow 0\qquad(|m|\to\infty).$
Thus the transformed operator is  $I+K$ , where  $K$  is compact:
its three diagonals vanish at infinity and are norm limits of their
finite truncations. In particular its essential spectrum is  $\{1\}$ .
The reversible classical form is
$\langle g,-Qg\rangle_{L^{2}(\pi)}=\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}\pi_{m}r_{m}^{+}|g(m+1)-g(m)|^{2}.$
Every coefficient is positive. Thus zero energy forces
$g(m+1)=g(m)$  for every  $m$ , so  $g$  is constant. After the unitary
change of variables the kernel is  $\mathbb{C}(\sqrt{\pi_{m}})_{m}$ .
Since zero lies outside the essential spectrum  $\{1\}$ , it is an
isolated simple eigenvalue, and
$\lambda_{\rm diag}=\inf(\operatorname{spec}(-Q)\setminus\{0\})>0.$
The diagonal and off-diagonal Hilbert–Schmidt subspaces reduce the
standard-form generator: each shift gain moves the two charge indices
by the same amount, and the loss operators are diagonal.
The charge row contributes the nonnegative form
$\mathcal{E}_{\rm charge}(Y)=\frac{|\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(0)|^{2}}{2}\sum_{m,k\in\mathbb{Z}}(m-k)^{2}|Y_{mk}|^{2}\geq\frac{e^{-1/2}}{2}\|Y_{\rm off}\|_{2}^{2}.$
The other rows have a nonnegative total form. Consequently the full
sampler is primitive and has gap at least
$\min\{\lambda_{\rm diag},e^{-1/2}/2\}>0$ .
Thus this model has a positive gap but no bounded  $L^{2}$ -to- $L^{p}$
map at any finite time, for any  $p>2$ .

Instructions for reporting errors
We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile
support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the
methods listed below:
Click the "Report Issue" (
) button, located in the page header.
Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.
Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
all.
Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
